Case 03: Test-and-learn

  • Show All Code

Which customers do we send the offer to, and which version do we send, for the best return?

Author

Adrian Do

Published

October 21, 2026

Disclaimer. This notebook uses public data. The results are for illustration only. The data is not the data of an employer or a client. The margin and the contact cost are assumptions. The assumption register in the appendix gives the source of each assumption.

Setup: libraries, chart style, seed, paths, assumptions and format helpers 
# Purpose: Load the libraries and the chart style. Set the seed, the paths, the assumptions (as-01, as-02, as-04),
#          the test parameters and the format helpers.
# Input:   chart_style.R, the path of the raw data file.
# Output:  `N` (numbers for the text), `SEED`, `DATA_DIR`, `RAW_FILE`, `MARGIN`, `COST`, `CAMPAIGN`, `ALPHA`,
#          `POWER`, helpers `usd()`, `pct()`, `num()`, `ci_txt()`, `fmt_p()`, chart style `CS`.

library(knitr)
library(rpart)  # Recommended package. It comes with each R installation.
source("chart_style.R")  # One chart style for all notebooks (deck style guide): CS, cs_setup(), cs_title()

# Fixed seed: each run gives the same bootstrap samples, folds and placebo tests.
SEED <- 42
set.seed(SEED)

# Paths are relative to this notebook (cases/03-test-and-learn/).
DATA_DIR <- file.path("..", "..", "data")  # The raw data is not in the repository. See the README.
RAW_FILE <- file.path(DATA_DIR, "raw", "Kevin_Hillstrom_MineThatData_E-MailAnalytics_DataMiningChallenge_2008.03.20.csv")
# Stop early with a clear message if the data file is missing.
if (!file.exists(RAW_FILE)) stop("Download the Hillstrom data to ", RAW_FILE, ". See the README.")

# Assumptions (assumption register in the appendix) and test parameters.
MARGIN <- 0.30      # as-01: contribution margin on incremental spend
COST <- 0.10        # as-02: full cost of one email, $
CAMPAIGN <- 1e5     # as-04: customers in one campaign, for the dollar values
ALPHA <- 0.05       # Significance level of each test
POWER <- 0.80       # Power for the test design (Step 3c)

# Format helpers for the text and the tables. Each returns text.
usd <- function(x, d = 2) ifelse(x < 0, paste0("-$", formatC(-x, format = "f", digits = d, big.mark = ",")),
                                 paste0("$", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d, big.mark = ",")))
pct <- function(x, d = 1) paste0(formatC(100 * x, format = "f", digits = d), "%")
num <- function(x, d = 0) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d, big.mark = ",")
ci_txt <- function(lo, hi, f = usd) paste0("[", f(lo), ", ", f(hi), "]")
fmt_p <- function(p) ifelse(p < 0.001, "< 0.001", formatC(p, format = "f", digits = 3))


N <- list()  # Numbers for the text after each chunk.
# Assumption values that the text of Step 0 uses.
N$as_margin <- pct(MARGIN, 0)
N$as_cost <- usd(COST)
N$as_campaign <- num(CAMPAIGN)
N$as_alpha <- pct(ALPHA, 0)
N$as_power <- pct(POWER, 0)
N$as_breakeven <- usd(COST / MARGIN)  # Breakeven effect: the uplift on spend at which margin x uplift = contact cost

How to read this notebook.

  • The notebook hides the code. Click Show code to see the code of a step.
  • A blue block is a decision. A green block is a business note. A grey block (Technical note) gives detail for data scientists. A business reader can skip it.
  • The appendix holds the decision log, the assumptions, the glossary and the data dictionary.

Step 0. What and why

This step gives the business problem, the question for leadership and the method that answers it with a randomized test. Each later step answers one part of the question.

Purpose. This step answers: what must the campaign do for the business, and how does a test give a reliable answer? It supports this decision: the email version, the customers that get it, and the holdout after the launch.

0a. The business problem

Situation. A retailer sent an email to its customers who bought in the last year. The data source put each customer at random into one of three groups: the men’s email, the women’s email or no email. Then it measured visits, conversions and spend for two weeks. In this case, the email is a proxy for a card offer to card customers (as-05).

Complication. Each email has a contact cost: the cost to send, the creative work, and the future value that we lose when a customer unsubscribes (as-02). Most customers buy nothing in the test window, so the spend data is noisy. The mean effect can hide customers where the email loses money. Leadership asks two questions: “Which version do we send?” and “Do we send it to all customers?”

Question. Which email version do we send, and to which customers, for the most incremental profit?

Resolution. Measure the effect of each email on spend with the randomized test, and select the version. Then examine if the effect changes by segment, and if a targeting rule beats “send to all”. A decision layer changes the effect into dollars with the margin (as-01) and the contact cost (as-02). A holdout after the launch confirms the result.

Decision that this notebook supports. The email version, the customers that get it, and the size of the holdout after the launch.

Success metric. The incremental profit for each customer in the campaign: the incremental margin minus the contact cost. At the base assumptions, the margin is 30% and the contact cost is $0.10. Thus an email pays for itself if it adds more than $0.33 of spend (the breakeven effect).

0b. Method and data strategy

A technical reader asks one question first. Why does a difference of two group means give the causal effect of the email?

The answer is the random assignment. The data source, not the customer and not a model, selected the group of each customer. Thus, before the email, the three groups are the same on average. This is true for the features that we see and for the features that we do not see.

After the email, the only systematic difference between the groups is the email. Then a difference of means measures the effect of the email, with no model of customer behavior. Step 2d checks this condition with the data.

From the effect to a policy. The test gives one effect for each email. The business needs a policy: a version and a list of customers. We go from the effect to the policy in five moves. Each move uses the result of the move before it:

  1. Effect. Does the email change spend, and is the test large enough to show the effect that matters? (Step 3, Step 4a)
  2. Version. Which email gives the larger effect, also inside each product history? (Step 4b)
  3. Segments. Does the effect of the selected email change by segment, after a correction for many tests? (Step 4c)
  4. Uplift. Can a model or a simple rule rank the customers by their uplift? (Step 4d, Step 5)
  5. Decision layer. At the margin and the contact cost, which rule selects the customers? How do we confirm it after the launch? (Step 6, Step 7)

If the effect is not real, the other moves have no base. If no segment and no model finds a reliable difference, the simple policy “send to all” stays.

The champion comes from the data. The dollar assumptions are ours. Cases 01 and 02 must build their champion, because their data has no real policy. This case does not need to.

Question Answer
What is the champion here? “No email”: the control group of the test. The data source chose these customers at random, so they show what customers do with no email.
What does the data give? A real randomized test: three groups, with visits, conversions and spend for two weeks. Each effect in this notebook is a difference between real groups.
What does the data not give? The margin on extra spend (as-01), the full contact cost of one email (as-02), the effect after two weeks (as-03) and a bank customer (as-05).
Which assumptions do we add? A margin of 30% (as-01), a contact cost of $0.10 (as-02) and a campaign of 100,000 customers (as-04). They change the effect into dollars.
How can they be wrong? A higher contact cost or a lower margin can make “send to all” lose money. Then a targeting rule becomes better.
How do we test them? Step 7a gives the profit at contact costs from $0.05 to $0.30, and Step 7c at margins of 20%, 30% and 40%. Step 7a gives the contact costs at which the decision changes.
What does not depend on them? The effect of each email, the choice of the version and the order of customers by history. These results use only the test data.

Why “send to all” is the default. A targeting rule must earn its place. We set the rules of the evaluation framework before the rerun of this version (Step 3a). An ML uplift model replaces a simple rank by history only if it is clearly better in repeated tests. A targeting rule replaces “send to all” only if the interval of its gain is above zero at the base contact cost.

The proxy (as-05). The data is an email test of a retailer, not a test of a bank. A card issuer has the same decision for a card offer: which offer, to which customers, at which contact cost. The size of each effect is different for a card offer, and the margin and the contact cost are different too. The method stays the same. Part 2 applies it to a pricing test and a collections test of case 01.

The limits of the method.

  • The test window is two weeks (as-03). We do not know the long-term effect: more future purchases, or fatigue and unsubscribes.
  • The data has no unsubscribes and no costs. The margin (as-01) and the contact cost (as-02) are assumptions. Step 7c repeats the result for other values.
  • Few customers buy in the test window. Thus each segment effect has a wide interval, and a model with many features can fit noise.
  • The segments and the uplift method come from the same test. Cross-fitted estimates decrease the risk of a result that is too good, but a new test must confirm a targeting rule.
  • The data comes from one retailer in 2008. The dollar values are for this retailer.

Technical note. The method has these parts. Each later step gives the code.

  • Randomization check. For each pre-test feature \(x\), the standardized difference is \((\bar{x}_{\text{email}} - \bar{x}_{\text{control}}) / s_x\). A chi-square test compares the group sizes with an equal split (the sample-ratio check). Step 3a gives the limit of each check.
  • Average effect. The effect is \(\hat{\tau} = \bar{y}_1 - \bar{y}_0\), with the Welch standard error \(\sqrt{s_1^2/n_1 + s_0^2/n_0}\). A bootstrap, CUPED and a regression adjustment check the same effect (Step 4a).
  • Power. For \(n\) customers in each group, the MDE is about \((z_{1-\alpha/2} + z_{1-\beta}) \, s \sqrt{2/n}\). The notebook uses a significance level of 5% and a power of 80% (Step 3c).
  • Segments. An interaction F-test for each feature first. Then the effect of each segment, with the Holm correction (Step 4c).
  • Uplift. A five-fold cross-fit gives each customer an uplift from a model that did not see that customer. The Qini area compares the order of each method with a random order, in repeated cross-fits (Step 4d).
  • Decision layer. The breakeven effect is contact cost / margin. The breakeven rule sends the email if \(\text{margin} \times \widehat{\text{uplift}} > \text{contact cost}\). For each customer in the campaign, the profit of a selection is \(p \, (m \, \hat{\tau}_S - c)\). Here \(p\) is the share of customers in the selection, \(m\) the margin and \(c\) the contact cost (Step 7a).

0c. How the notebook answers the question

Each step answers one part of the question:

  • Step 1. Which data gives a randomized test of an offer, and what does it contain?
  • Step 2. Is the data clean, are the groups the same before the email, and what does a customer spend without an email?
  • Step 3. Which rules must the result pass, how does the test split the customers, and which metric decides?
  • Step 4. How large is the effect of each email? Which version do we send? Does the effect change by segment? Which method ranks the customers by uplift?
  • Step 5. What is the cross-fitted uplift of each customer, by history quartile?
  • Step 6. Does the recommended policy pass each rule of the evaluation framework?
  • Step 7. Which customers get the email, what is it worth in dollars, and how do we confirm it after the launch?
  • Part 2. How does the same method design a pricing test and a collections test for case 01?

Business note. The question is a trade between the incremental margin of each email and its contact cost. A randomized test gives the effect without a model, so the core result is a measured fact, not a model estimate. A targeting rule must beat this simple result before we use it. Step 1 shows the data that gives this test.

Step 1. Get data

Step 0 set the question and the method: measure the effect of each email with a randomized test, then build a policy in five moves. This step answers: which data gives this test, and what does it contain?

Purpose. This step gets the data and its meaning. It supports this decision: if the data can answer the business question.

1a. Why this data

The data is the MineThatData email test of Kevin Hillstrom (2008). Source: the MineThatData blog, file Kevin_Hillstrom_MineThatData_E-MailAnalytics_DataMiningChallenge_2008.03.20.csv. The data is a fair proxy for a card offer, for five reasons:

  • A real randomized test. The retailer put each customer at random into a group. Thus a difference of means gives the causal effect (Step 0b).
  • A choice like a card offer. The test has two versions of one campaign and a control group with no contact. A card issuer has the same choice: which offer, or no offer.
  • Outcomes in dollars. Spend gives the dollars that the decision layer needs. Visit and conversion help to explain the spend result.
  • Pre-test features. History, recency, product history, channel and area type describe each customer before the email. Thus we can examine segments and uplift.
  • A public source. Each reader can get the same file and repeat each result.

The data cannot show these things:

What the data does not show Why it matters What the notebook does
Bank customers and a card offer The size of each effect is different for a card offer. The email is a proxy (as-05). The method stays the same. Part 2 applies it to two tests of case 01.
Unsubscribes and the cost of an email The contact cost decides if targeting beats “send to all”. The contact cost is an assumption (as-02). Step 7c repeats the result for other costs. Step 7d watches the unsubscribe rate.
The margin of each purchase The profit needs the margin. The margin is an assumption (as-01). Step 7c repeats the result for other margins.
The long-term effect The test window is two weeks (as-03). A holdout after the launch (Step 7d).
Spend above a maximum value The data source cut the largest spend values. Step 2 examines the effect of this cap.

1b. Key variables

The table gives all columns of the file. The treatment is segment, and the primary outcome is spend (Step 3c). Appendix A also gives the coded features that Step 1c and Step 2 make.

Column Meaning in plain words Type Use
segment → arm The test group of the customer: “Mens E-Mail”, “Womens E-Mail” or “No E-Mail”. Text → category Treatment
spend The dollars that the customer spent in the two weeks after the email. **Number (\()** | **Primary outcome** | | `visit` | 1 = the customer visited the website in the two weeks after the email. | 1/0 | Secondary outcome | | `conversion` | 1 = the customer bought something in the two weeks after the email. | 1/0 | Secondary outcome | | `history` | The dollars that the customer spent in the last year, before the test. | Number (\)) Pre-test feature. Rank by history (Step 4d).
history_segment The same history in buckets, for example “1) $0 - $100”. Text → category Pre-test feature (hseg). Segment effects (Step 4c).
recency The number of months since the last purchase. Number Pre-test feature
mens 1 = the customer bought men’s products in the last year. 1/0 Pre-test feature. Product history (buyer).
womens 1 = the customer bought women’s products in the last year. 1/0 Pre-test feature. Product history (buyer).
newbie 1 = a new customer in the last year. 1/0 Pre-test feature
channel The channels where the customer bought in the last year: Phone, Web or Multichannel. Category Pre-test feature
zip_code The area type of the address: Urban, Suburban or Rural. The file writes “Surburban”. Category Pre-test feature (zip)

The email cannot change a pre-test feature, so a pre-test feature is fair input for a segment or an uplift model. An outcome is never a feature. Step 2d also uses the pre-test features to check that the groups are the same before the email.

1c. Load the data and look at it

The file is small, so the code reads it in one step with base R. The load also makes the coded columns that the later steps use:

  • arm: the test group, with the control group first. Thus each effect is “email minus control”.
  • buyer: the product history. It is “mens only”, “womens only” or “both”, from mens and womens.
  • hseg: the history bucket, without the number at the start of the label.
  • zip and channel: the area type and the channel as categories.
  • lhist: the log of history. It decreases the effect of the largest histories in a regression.
Load the data and make the coded columns 
# Purpose: Read the Hillstrom file and make the coded columns that Steps 2-7 use.
# Input:   RAW_FILE (setup chunk).
# Output:  `d` (one row for each customer, with `arm`, `buyer`, `hseg`, `zip`, `channel`, `lhist`),
#          `RAW_COLS` (the column names of the raw file), numbers for the text (`N`).

d <- read.csv(RAW_FILE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
RAW_COLS <- names(d)  # The 12 columns of the raw file, before the coded columns

# Test group. The control group is the first level, so each effect is "email minus control".
d$arm <- factor(d$segment, levels = c("No E-Mail", "Mens E-Mail", "Womens E-Mail"),
                labels = c("control", "mens", "womens"))
# Product history: men's products, women's products, or both, in the last year
d$buyer <- factor(ifelse(d$mens == 1 & d$womens == 1, "both", ifelse(d$mens == 1, "mens only", "womens only")),
                  levels = c("mens only", "womens only", "both"))
# History bucket: remove the number at the start ("1) "). The sort of the raw labels keeps the dollar order.
d$hseg <- factor(sub("^\\d\\) ", "", d$history_segment), levels = sub("^\\d\\) ", "", sort(unique(d$history_segment))))
d$zip <- factor(d$zip_code)
d$channel <- factor(d$channel)
d$lhist <- log(d$history)  # History is always more than $0, so the log is defined

N$rows <- num(nrow(d))
N$n_arm <- num(min(table(d$arm)))
N$spend_zero <- pct(mean(d$spend == 0))
N$spend_max <- usd(max(d$spend), 0)
N$conv_spend_ok <- all((d$spend > 0) == (d$conversion == 1))  # Spend > $0 if and only if a conversion

The next chunk shows the initial state of the data before any change: the size, the groups, the outcomes and the spend cap.

Initial state: size, groups, missing values, conversion and the spend cap 
# Purpose: Show the initial state of the data before any change: size, groups, outcomes and the spend cap.
# Input:   `d`, `RAW_COLS` (load-data chunk).
# Output:  Numbers for the text (`N`), table of the initial state.

n_grp <- table(d$arm)
N$s1_raw_cols <- num(length(RAW_COLS))
N$s1_cols <- num(ncol(d))
N$s1_n_ctrl <- num(n_grp[["control"]])
N$s1_n_mens <- num(n_grp[["mens"]])
N$s1_n_womens <- num(n_grp[["womens"]])
N$s1_missing <- num(sum(is.na(d[RAW_COLS])))
N$s1_buyers <- num(sum(d$conversion == 1))
N$s1_conv <- pct(mean(d$conversion), 2)
N$s1_visit <- pct(mean(d$visit), 1)
N$s1_cap_n <- num(sum(d$spend == max(d$spend)))  # Customers at the largest spend value

kable(data.frame(
  Fact = c("Rows (customers)", "Columns: raw file / after the load",
           "Customers in each group: no email / men's email / women's email", "Missing values (raw columns)",
           "Share with $0 spend in the test window", "Visit rate, all groups", "Conversion rate, all groups",
           "Buyers (conversion = 1)", "Largest spend (the spend cap)", "Customers at the spend cap",
           "Spend > $0 if and only if a conversion"),
  Value = c(N$rows, paste(N$s1_raw_cols, "/", N$s1_cols),
            paste(N$s1_n_ctrl, "/", N$s1_n_mens, "/", N$s1_n_womens), N$s1_missing,
            N$spend_zero, N$s1_visit, N$s1_conv, N$s1_buyers, N$spend_max, N$s1_cap_n,
            ifelse(N$conv_spend_ok, "Yes", "No"))),
  row.names = FALSE, align = "lr")
Fact Value
Rows (customers) 64,000
Columns: raw file / after the load 12 / 17
Customers in each group: no email / men’s email / women’s email 21,306 / 21,307 / 21,387
Missing values (raw columns) 0
Share with $0 spend in the test window 99.1%
Visit rate, all groups 14.7%
Conversion rate, all groups 0.90%
Buyers (conversion = 1) 578
Largest spend (the spend cap) $499
Customers at the spend cap 12
Spend > $0 if and only if a conversion Yes

The data has 64,000 customers and 12 columns. The load adds the coded columns, so d has 17 columns. The raw file has 0 missing values. The three groups have 21,306, 21,307 and 21,387 customers. These sizes are near to an equal split, and Step 2d tests this with the sample-ratio check.

Of all customers, 99.1% spend $0 in the test window. Only 578 customers buy something: a conversion rate of 0.90%. The visit rate is 14.7%. Thus spend is mostly zeros with a long right tail. Step 3 shows why this shape makes the test need many customers.

The largest spend is $499, and 12 customers have exactly this value. Thus the data source probably cut the spend at this value. Step 2 examines the effect of this cap. Each customer with spend more than $0 has a conversion, and each conversion has spend. Thus the two outcomes agree.

Business note. The data is a real randomized test with outcomes in dollars, so it can answer the business question. It cannot show bank customers, the contact cost or the long-term effect, and the notebook says where each limit matters. Step 2 checks the data and the randomization, and it measures what a customer spends without an email.

Step 2. Clean and prepare data

Step 1 showed that the Hillstrom file can answer the business question. It has one row for each customer, the test group of the customer and three outcomes over two weeks. But a test result is valid only if the groups were the same before the email. The spend data also has a cap and many customers with $0.

This step answers three questions. Which rows, columns and values can the analysis use? Do the groups differ only by the email? What do customers do without an email?

Purpose. This step makes sure that the test data can give a causal effect. It supports this decision: use the test result for the campaign decision, or run a new test.

The data preparation follows one tree with three levels. Each level has one split axis. Each axis divides all cases into groups that do not overlap and that together cover all cases (MECE).

Level Split axis Groups What this data needs Section
Rows Is the record a valid customer of the test? Not valid · valid Six technical checks. The test selected the customers, so each valid row is in scope. 2a
Columns When does the value exist, against the time of the email? Before the email (pre-test feature) · the test group · after the email (outcome) An outcome never goes into a model as a feature. The pre-test features show if the groups are the same (2d). 2b
Values Why is a value extreme, coded or empty? Extreme value from a cap · two outcomes that must agree · coded values · empty cells The spend cap. Spend against conversion. Five coded features. A check for missing values. 2c

Then Step 2d checks the random assignment: the evidence for branch 1 (validity) of the framework. Step 2e measures the baseline: what the control group does without an email.

2a. Rows: which customers can the analysis use?

The data source put each customer at random into one of three groups. Thus the analysis must keep all valid rows: a removed row can make the groups different. The code checks six conditions. A record is not valid if its test group is not one of the three groups, or if an outcome is not 0 or 1. It is also not valid if the spend is less than $0 or the history is $0 or less. The last check is a recency outside 1–12 months.

The data has no customer ID. Thus the code cannot find a customer who is in the file two times.

Rows: six technical checks 
# Purpose: Check that each row is a valid customer of the test (Step 2a).
# Input:   `d` (from the load chunk of Step 1).
# Output:  Table `row_checks` (rows that fail each check). N values for the text.

# Each check gives TRUE for a row that is not valid.
row_checks <- list(
  `Test group not one of the three groups` = is.na(d$arm),
  `Visit not 0 or 1` = !d$visit %in% c(0, 1),
  `Conversion not 0 or 1` = !d$conversion %in% c(0, 1),
  `Spend less than $0` = d$spend < 0,
  `History of $0 or less` = d$history <= 0,
  `Recency outside 1-12 months` = !d$recency %in% 1:12
)
invalid <- Reduce(`|`, row_checks)
N$n_rows_raw <- num(nrow(d))
N$n_invalid <- num(sum(invalid))
# A random test keeps all valid rows. The code stops if a row fails, so that a later step cannot hide it.
if (any(invalid)) stop(sum(invalid), " rows fail a technical check. Examine them before you continue.")
kable(data.frame(Check = names(row_checks), `Rows that fail` = num(sapply(row_checks, sum)),
                 check.names = FALSE), row.names = FALSE, align = "lr")
Check Rows that fail
Test group not one of the three groups 0
Visit not 0 or 1 0
Conversion not 0 or 1 0
Spend less than $0 0
History of $0 or less 0
Recency outside 1-12 months 0

0 of the 64,000 rows fail a check. The file is clean at the row level, and each row is in scope.

2b. Columns: which values exist before the email?

A test compares groups that were the same before the treatment. Thus the split axis for a column is its time against the email. A column that exists before the email describes the customer. A column that exists after the email is an outcome: the email can change it. An outcome never goes into a model as a feature. Otherwise the model learns the result of the email from the result itself.

Columns: the role of each raw column against the time of the email 
# Purpose: Give each raw column its role: pre-test feature, test group or outcome (Step 2b).
# Input:   `d`.
# Output:  `COL_ROLE` (named vector, raw column -> role; Appendix A uses it). Table of the roles.

COL_ROLE <- c(recency = "Pre-test feature", history_segment = "Pre-test feature", history = "Pre-test feature",
              mens = "Pre-test feature", womens = "Pre-test feature", zip_code = "Pre-test feature",
              newbie = "Pre-test feature", channel = "Pre-test feature", segment = "Test group",
              visit = "Outcome", conversion = "Outcome", spend = "Outcome")
# Check: the roles cover each raw column one time.
stopifnot(setequal(names(COL_ROLE), c("recency", "history_segment", "history", "mens", "womens", "zip_code",
                                      "newbie", "channel", "segment", "visit", "conversion", "spend")),
          all(names(COL_ROLE) %in% names(d)))
role_tab <- data.frame(Role = c("Pre-test feature", "Test group", "Outcome"),
                       Time = c("Before the email", "At the email", "In the two weeks after the email"),
                       Use = c("Balance check (2d), segments (4c), uplift models (4d)",
                               "The treatment: no email, men's email or women's email",
                               "Metrics of the test. Never a feature."))
role_tab$Columns <- sapply(role_tab$Role, function(r) paste(names(COL_ROLE)[COL_ROLE == r], collapse = ", "))
N$n_pre <- sum(COL_ROLE == "Pre-test feature")
N$n_out <- sum(COL_ROLE == "Outcome")
N$n_raw_cols <- length(COL_ROLE)
kable(role_tab[, c("Role", "Columns", "Time", "Use")], row.names = FALSE)
Role Columns Time Use
Pre-test feature recency, history_segment, history, mens, womens, zip_code, newbie, channel Before the email Balance check (2d), segments (4c), uplift models (4d)
Test group segment At the email The treatment: no email, men’s email or women’s email

The file has 8 pre-test features, one test group and 3 outcomes. The email can change the outcomes, but it cannot change the pre-test features. Thus a difference of a pre-test feature between the groups can come only from the random assignment. Step 2d uses this fact for the balance check.

2c. Values: the spend cap, the outcomes, the coded features and empty cells

The split axis for a value is the reason that it needs attention. A value can be extreme, two outcomes can disagree, a raw value can need a code, or a cell can be empty. The code checks each group.

Values: spend cap, spend against conversion, coded features and empty cells 
# Purpose: Check the values of Step 2c: the spend cap, the agreement of the outcomes, the coded features
#          and the empty cells.
# Input:   `d` (with the coded features of the load chunk).
# Output:  Table `value_checks`. Table `coded`. N values for the text.

# Extreme value: the largest spend repeats. We read this as a cap of the data source.
spend_max <- max(d$spend)
at_cap <- d$spend == spend_max
N$cap <- usd(spend_max, 0)
N$n_cap <- num(sum(at_cap))
N$n_buyers <- num(sum(d$spend > 0))
N$cap_usd_share <- pct(sum(d$spend[at_cap]) / sum(d$spend))
N$spend_2nd <- usd(max(d$spend[!at_cap]), 2)
N$buyer_median <- usd(median(d$spend[d$spend > 0]), 0)

# Outcomes that must agree: spend > $0 if and only if conversion = 1. A conversion needs a visit.
n_spend_noconv <- sum((d$spend > 0) != (d$conversion == 1))
n_conv_novisit <- sum(d$conversion == 1 & d$visit == 0)
# Coded values: the history bucket must hold the history in dollars. Parse "$100 - $200" and "$1,000 +".
h_txt <- sub("^\\d\\) ", "", d$history_segment)  # Remove the bucket number "1) " to "7) "
bounds <- lapply(regmatches(h_txt, gregexpr("[0-9][0-9,]*", h_txt)), function(x) as.numeric(gsub(",", "", x)))
h_lo <- sapply(bounds, `[`, 1)
h_hi <- sapply(bounds, function(b) if (length(b) > 1) b[2] else Inf)  # "$1,000 +" has no upper bound
n_hseg_bad <- sum(d$history < h_lo | d$history >= h_hi)
# Each customer bought men's products, women's products or both. "Neither" must not exist.
n_no_product <- sum(d$mens == 0 & d$womens == 0)
# Empty cells in all raw columns.
n_na <- sum(is.na(d[, names(COL_ROLE)]))

value_checks <- data.frame(
  Group = c("Extreme value", "Outcomes that must agree", "Outcomes that must agree",
            "Coded values", "Coded values", "Empty cells"),
  Check = c(paste0("Buyers with spend at the largest value (", N$cap, ")"),
            "Spend > $0 without a conversion, or a conversion with $0",
            "Conversion without a visit",
            "History outside its history bucket",
            "Customer with neither men's nor women's products",
            paste("Empty cells in the", length(COL_ROLE), "raw columns")),
  Rows = num(c(sum(at_cap), n_spend_noconv, n_conv_novisit, n_hseg_bad, n_no_product, n_na)))
N$n_spend_noconv <- num(n_spend_noconv)
N$n_conv_novisit <- num(n_conv_novisit)
N$n_hseg_bad <- num(n_hseg_bad)
N$n_no_product <- num(n_no_product)
N$n_na <- num(n_na)
kable(value_checks, row.names = FALSE, align = "llr")
Group Check Rows
Extreme value Buyers with spend at the largest value ($499) 12
Outcomes that must agree Spend > $0 without a conversion, or a conversion with $0 0
Outcomes that must agree Conversion without a visit 0
Coded values History outside its history bucket 0
Coded values Customer with neither men’s nor women’s products 0
Empty cells Empty cells in the 12 raw columns 0

What we do with each group:

Group Example in this data What we do
Extreme value from a cap 12 of the 578 buyers have exactly $499. The next largest spend is $482.31. These buyers hold 8.9% of all spend dollars. Keep the value. The cap is the same in each group, so it does not change the comparison. The effect is an effect on spend up to the cap.
Two outcomes that must agree 0 rows have spend without a conversion, or a conversion without spend. 0 rows have a conversion without a visit. No change is necessary. Visit, conversion and spend tell one consistent story for each customer.
Coded values 0 customers have a history outside their history bucket. 0 customers have neither men’s nor women’s products. Use the coded features of the table below.
Empty cells 0 empty cells in the 12 raw columns. No imputation is necessary.

Why we do not cap the spend again. The median buyer spends $81, so the cap affects only a few large orders. A second cap at a lower value (winsorization) makes the variance smaller. But it also changes the outcome that the profit calculation uses. The cap of the data source is the same in all three groups, so the comparison stays fair.

The load chunk of Step 1 makes five coded features from the raw columns. The table shows each one with its levels.

Coded features: source, rule and levels 
# Purpose: Show the coded features of the load chunk and check that each one has a value for each row.

coded <- data.frame(
  Feature = c("arm", "buyer", "hseg", "zip", "channel", "lhist"),
  Source = c("segment", "mens, womens", "history_segment", "zip_code", "channel", "history"),
  Rule = c("Test group: control, mens, womens",

coded$Levels <- sapply(coded$Feature, function(f) {

  else paste0("from ", formatC(min(x), format = "f", digits = 2), " to ", formatC(max(x), format = "f", digits = 2))
})
# Check: each coded feature has a value for each row.
stopifnot(!anyNA(d[, coded$Feature]))
N$lhist_lo <- formatC(min(d$lhist), format = "f", digits = 2)
N$hist_min <- usd(min(d$history))

2d. Randomization check: do the groups differ only by the email?

This check gives the evidence for branch 1 (validity) of the framework in Step 3a. If the groups are different before the email, a difference of the outcomes can come from the customers and not from the email. The check has two parts:

  • Balance. The standardized difference of each pre-test feature between each email group and the control group. The rule is: each absolute value is less than 0.05.
  • Sample ratio. The number of customers in the three groups against an equal split. The rule is: the chi-square p-value is more than 0.01. A smaller p-value shows a problem in the assignment, for example lost rows in one group.

Technical note. Let x be a feature, a an email group and c the control group. The standardized difference is (mean(x in a) − mean(x in c)) / sd(x in all rows). It does not depend on the sample size, unlike a p-value. The code makes one column for each level of zip_code and channel (model.matrix). The sample ratio check is a chi-square goodness-of-fit test of the three group sizes against equal shares.

Randomization check: standardized difference of each feature and the sample ratio check 
# Purpose: Check the random assignment: the evidence of branch 1 (validity).
# Input:   `d`.
# Output:  `feat` (pre-test features, one column for each level), `bal` (balance table),
#          N$smd_max, N$srm_p and the rule results.

feat <- data.frame(model.matrix(~ recency + history + mens + womens + newbie + zip + channel - 1, d))
smd <- function(a) sapply(feat, function(x) (mean(x[d$arm == a]) - mean(x[d$arm == "control"])) / sd(x))
bal <- data.frame(Feature = names(feat),
                  `Mean, control` = sapply(feat, function(x) mean(x[d$arm == "control"])),
                  `Std. difference, men's` = smd("mens"),
                  `Std. difference, women's` = smd("womens"), check.names = FALSE)
smd_max <- max(abs(bal[, 3:4]))
srm_p <- chisq.test(table(d$arm))$p.value  # Equal shares are the default of chisq.test
N$smd_max <- formatC(smd_max, format = "f", digits = 3)
N$srm_p <- formatC(srm_p, format = "f", digits = 2)
N$smd_feature <- bal$Feature[which.max(pmax(abs(bal[, 3]), abs(bal[, 4])))]
# The rules of branch 1, set before the rerun.
N$smd_pass <- smd_max < 0.05
N$srm_pass <- srm_p > 0.01
N$valid_txt <- if (N$smd_pass && N$srm_pass) "passes both rules" else "fails a rule"
kable(bal, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)
Feature Mean, control Std. difference, men’s Std. difference, women’s
recency 5.750 0.007 0.005
history 240.883 0.008 0.006
mens 0.553 -0.005 -0.009
womens 0.548 0.008 0.005
newbie 0.502 -0.001 0.003
zipRural 0.147 0.014 0.004
zipSurburban 0.452 -0.012 -0.001
zipUrban 0.401 0.002 -0.002
channelPhone 0.438 -0.008 0.009
channelWeb 0.440 0.011 -0.005

The largest absolute standardized difference is 0.014 (zipRural). The rule needs less than 0.05. The group sizes agree with an equal split: the chi-square p-value is 0.90, and the rule needs more than 0.01. Thus the validity branch passes both rules. A difference of the mean outcomes between the groups gives the causal effect of the email.

2e. Baseline: what does the control group do without an email?

The groups are the same before the email. Thus the control group shows what all customers do without an email. Each effect in this notebook is a difference against this baseline. The baseline also shows why spend is a noisy metric.

The code measures four values for the control group. They are the visit rate, the conversion rate, the mean spend and the share with $0 spend.

Baseline: visit, conversion and spend of the control group

N$base_n <- num(base0$customers)

N$base_spend <- usd(base0$spend)

How to read: each bar is the share of the 21,306 control customers who reach a stage in the two weeks of the test. The control group got no email.

So what: 99.4% of the customers without an email spend $0, and the mean spend is only $0.65. The few buyers spend $114 each, so a small number of orders sets the mean. The standard deviation of the spend is about 18 times its mean. Thus the spend effect of an email has a wide confidence interval, and the test needs many customers (Step 3c).

Business note. The test file has 64,000 valid customers, no empty cells and one consistent outcome for each customer. The random assignment works: the largest standardized difference is 0.014, and the sample ratio p-value is 0.90. Without an email, a campaign of 100,000 customers gives about $65,279 of spend in two weeks. Each email must add to this baseline more than its cost. Step 3 now fixes the rules of the test and checks that the test is large enough to find such an effect.

Step 3. Split data: the test design

Step 2 gave clean data for 64,000 customers in three groups, and it showed that the groups look the same before the test. It also showed that 99.1% of the customers spend $0 in the two weeks. Before we measure an effect, we must agree on two things. What does “the email works” mean, and is the test large enough to show it?

Purpose. This step fixes the rules of the test, the use of the data and the primary metric. It supports this decision: use the test result for the campaign, or run a larger test first.

Steps 3 to 7 use the same small set of tools, for example the power, the bootstrap and the Qini curve. The code keeps them in the file case03_helpers.R, so that the story stays short. The appendix shows the full file. The next cell loads the tools and the rules of the evaluation framework.

Tools: load case03_helpers.R and the rules of the evaluation framework 
# Purpose: Load the helper functions that Steps 3–7 use, and record the rules of section 3a.
# Input:   case03_helpers.R, chart_style.R, the constants of the setup chunk.
# Output:  The functions of case03_helpers.R, `CS` and the chart functions, `RULES`.

source("chart_style.R")    # Chart style (deck style guide). A second source is safe.
source("case03_helpers.R")

# The rules of the evaluation framework (section 3a). We set them before the rerun.
RULES <- list(
  b1_smd = 0.05,          # Branch 1: largest absolute standardized difference less than 0.05
  b1_srm_p = 0.01,        # Branch 1: p-value of the sample-ratio check more than 0.01
  b3_adj_dev = 0.10,      # Branch 3: each adjusted effect within 10% of the unadjusted effect
  b5_model_gain = 0.20,   # Branch 5: an ML uplift model needs a 20% higher mean Qini area ...
  b5_model_pos = 9,       # ... and a Qini area more than 0 in 9 or more of the repeats
  b5_policy_level = 0.90  # Branch 5: the 90% interval of the gain of a targeting rule must be above 0
)

3a. What the test must measure

A test has many metrics. A reader can ask: “Why these metrics, and why not others?” Thus we start from the question that each metric answers.

The framework splits the risks of a campaign decision in two groups. The first group is statistical: the test can be wrong in its design, too small to show the effect, or right only with one method. The second group is business: the effect can be real but make no money. Or a smaller list of customers can make more money than “send to all”. Each failure belongs to one branch only. A policy that passes all five branches is ready for the rollout.

We set these rules before the rerun of this version, and we do not change them after a result. If a result fails a rule, the notebook reports the failure and what it means for the decision.

Branch Question Metric Rule
1. Validity Do the groups differ only by the email? Largest absolute standardized difference of the pre-test features; sample-ratio chi-square p-value Less than 0.05; p-value more than 0.01
2. Effect Does the men’s email change spend, and is the test large enough? Welch 95% CI of the spend effect; customers in each group vs. customers needed for 80% power at the observed effect The CI excludes 0; the test has at least the customers needed
3. Robustness Does the effect hold with other methods? Bootstrap 95% CI; effect with CUPED and with regression adjustment The bootstrap CI excludes 0; each adjusted effect is within 10% of the unadjusted effect
4. Business value Does the recommended policy make money? Incremental profit for 100,000 customers at the base margin and contact cost (as-01, as-02), with the 95% CI of the effect Profit more than 0, and the lower end of its 95% CI more than 0
5. Targeting Does a targeting rule or an uplift model beat “send to all”? Gain of each targeting rule vs. send-to-all with its 90% bootstrap interval at the base cost. Qini area of the ML uplift models vs. rank by history. Model rule: an ML uplift model replaces “rank by history” only if two conditions are true. Its mean Qini area is 20% or more higher. Its Qini area is more than 0 in at least 9 of 10 repeats. Policy rule: a targeting rule replaces “send to all” only if the 90% interval of its gain is above 0 at the base cost. The recommended policy passes if it follows these two rules.

The notebook uses each branch in these sections:

  • Branch 1: Step 2d (the randomization check), Step 3b and Step 6a.
  • Branch 2: Step 3c (the primary metric and the power), Step 4a and Step 6b.
  • Branch 3: Step 4a (the bootstrap, CUPED and the regression adjustment) and Step 6c.
  • Branch 4: Step 4a (the profit of each email), Step 6d and Step 7b.
  • Branch 5: Step 4d (the uplift method), Step 5, Step 6e and Step 7a.

Branches 2 and 4 are different. An effect can be real but too small to pay for the email. The CI of branch 2 says that the effect is more than $0. The rule of branch 4 says that the effect is more than the breakeven effect. Thus the notebook checks both.

Technical note. How each metric works:

  • Standardized difference. For each pre-test feature: (mean in the email group − mean in the control group) / standard deviation in all customers. It does not depend on the unit or on the sample size. A value less than 0.05 is a small difference.
  • Sample-ratio check. A chi-square test of the group sizes against the planned split (one third in each group). A small p-value shows a problem in the assignment, for example a group that lost customers.
  • Welch 95% CI. Effect = mean of the email group − mean of the control group. The standard error is √(s₁²/n₁ + s₀²/n₀), and the CI is the effect ± t × standard error. The Welch test does not need equal variances in the two groups.
  • Power and MDE. For n customers in each group and a standard deviation σ, MDE ≈ (z₀.₉₇₅ + z₀.₈₀) × σ × √(2/n) at 5% significance and 80% power. The code uses the exact t-test version (power.t.test). The inverse gives the customers needed for an effect: n ≈ 2 × σ² × (z₀.₉₇₅ + z₀.₈₀)² / effect².
  • Qini area. Rank the customers by the predicted uplift. Take the top share g of the list. The Qini curve gives (mean spend of the email group − mean spend of the control group, in the top g) × g. A random order gives a straight line from 0 to the effect of “send to all”. The Qini area is the mean distance between the curve and this line, at g = 5%, 10%, …, 100%. A higher area means a better order. An area of 0 or less means no better than a random order.

3b. How we split the data

A model project splits the data into a training set and a test set. A randomized test needs a different split. The question here is not “Does a model predict well?”. The question is “What does the email cause?”. Thus the data has two uses, and each use needs its own split:

Use Question Split Who makes it
Effect (Steps 4a–4c) What does the email cause, on average and in each segment? Random assignment into three groups: no email, men’s email, women’s email The data source, before the test
Uplift (Steps 4d and 5) Which customers get the most from the email? 5-fold cross-fit inside the men’s email and the control group This notebook

Random assignment. The data source put each customer at random into one of the three groups. The control group then shows what the email groups do without an email. Thus a difference of means gives the causal effect, and no model must learn from the data. Branch 1 checks that the random assignment worked.

Cross-fit for the uplift. An uplift model learns from the same customers that it then puts in order. A model that scores the customers of its own training data finds noise and calls it uplift. Then the Qini curve looks good, but the order fails on new customers.

The fix is a cross-fit: cut the customers into five folds at random. For each fold, the model learns from the other four folds and gives an uplift to the customers of this fold. Thus each customer gets an uplift from a model that did not see that customer. We repeat this with 10 different random folds, because one cut of the folds can give a lucky result.

A single hold-out set (for example 70/30) is a simpler option. But less than 1% of the customers buy, so a test set of 30% has few buyers, and its Qini curve is noisy. With a cross-fit, each customer is in the test data one time. Rank by history needs no cross-fit, because it learns nothing from the test data.

Parameters: one third of the customers in each group (the planned split of the data source), 5 folds and 10 repeats for the uplift.

Test design: group sizes, sample-ratio check, balance and the folds of the cross-fit 
# Purpose: Show the two splits of section 3b and the evidence of branch 1 (validity).
# Input:   `d` (with `arm`), `feat` (pre-test features, Step 2d), `SEED`, `RULES`.
# Output:  Table of the groups; N values of branch 1 (`d3_smd`, `d3_srm_p`, `d3_b1`) and of the folds.

# Random assignment: group sizes against the planned split of one third each.
grp <- table(d$arm)
smd_all <- sapply(c("mens", "womens"), function(a) sapply(feat, std_diff, arm = d$arm, a = a))
b1_smd <- max(abs(smd_all))
b1_srm <- srm_p(d$arm)
N$d3_smd <- formatC(b1_smd, format = "f", digits = 3)
N$d3_srm_p <- formatC(b1_srm, format = "f", digits = 2)
N$d3_b1 <- if (b1_smd < RULES$b1_smd && b1_srm > RULES$b1_srm_p) "passes" else "fails"

# Cross-fit: five folds of the men's email + control customers. Each fold is one fifth of them.
n_mc <- sum(d$arm != "womens")
N$d3_n_mc <- num(n_mc)
N$d3_n_fold <- num(n_mc / 5)
N$d3_buy_fold <- num(sum(d$conversion[d$arm != "womens"]) / 5)

kable(data.frame(
  Group = c("No email (control)", "Men's email", "Women's email"),
  Customers = num(as.vector(grp)),
  `Share of customers` = pct(as.vector(grp) / sum(grp), 2),
  `Planned share` = pct(rep(1 / 3, 3), 2),
  `Largest standardized difference against control` = c("", formatC(apply(abs(smd_all), 2, max), format = "f", digits = 3)),
  check.names = FALSE), row.names = FALSE, align = "lrrrr")
Group Customers Share of customers Planned share Largest standardized difference against control
No email (control) 21,306 33.29% 33.33%
Men’s email 21,307 33.29% 33.33% 0.014
Women’s email 21,387 33.42% 33.33% 0.009

How to read: each row is one group. The last column gives the largest standardized difference of the pre-test features against the control group.

So what: the shares agree with the planned split (p-value 0.90), and the largest standardized difference is 0.014. Branch 1 passes, so a difference of means gives the effect of the email.

For the uplift, the men’s email and the control group have 42,613 customers. Each fold has about 8,523 customers and about 78 buyers. This low number of buyers is the main limit of the uplift models in Step 4d.

3c. The primary metric and the power

Which metric decides the test?

Why this question matters. The primary metric decides if the email “works”. A metric that is easy to move but far from the money can approve an email that loses money. A metric that is close to the money but noisy can miss a profitable email. The test must also be large enough for the metric: if not, an effect of zero and a small effect look the same.

Ways to do it. The split axis is the place of the metric on the path from the email to the profit. The four places are a visit, a purchase, the dollars of the purchase, and the value after the test window. These four places cover all metrics of an email test, and each metric belongs to one of them.

Place on the path Metric Advantage Main risk Status
Engagement Email open or click; website visit Many customers act, so the test has the most power. An email can increase visits without more spend. The data has no opens or clicks. Visit: possible. Test it. Opens and clicks: screened out (not in the data).
Purchase Conversion (the customer buys) Closer to the money than a visit. Less than 1% of customers buy, so the test has less power. It ignores the size of each purchase. Possible. Test it.
Dollars Spend in the two weeks Gives dollars. The profit is margin × spend − contact cost, so the profit needs spend. Most customers spend $0 and a few spend a lot, so the noise is large. Possible. Test it.
After the window Spend over 12 months, or the customer lifetime value Shows a long effect or fatigue. The data stops after two weeks (as-03). Screened out (not in the data)

Evidence. For each metric, the code calculates the MDE of this test at 5% significance and 80% power. It compares the MDE with the observed effect of each email. It also gives the customers in each group that the test needs to find each observed effect (branch 2).

Evidence: MDE of each metric against the observed effect 
# Purpose: Compare the power of visit, conversion and spend for this test (dec-01, branch 2).
# Input:   `d`, `ALPHA`, `POWER`, mde_metric() (case03_helpers.R).
# Output:  `n_arm` (customers in the smallest group), `mde` (matrix: one column for each metric),
#          N values of the MDE and of the customers needed.

n_arm <- min(table(d$arm))
mde <- sapply(c(visit = "visit", conversion = "conversion", spend = "spend"),
              function(y) mde_metric(d[[y]], d$arm, n_arm))
mde <- rbind(mde, need = mde["need_w", ])  # Old row name: customers needed for the women's effect

N$mde_spend <- usd(mde["mde", "spend"])
N$eff_w_spend <- usd(mde["womens", "spend"])
N$eff_m_spend <- usd(mde["mens", "spend"])
N$need_w_spend <- num(mde["need_w", "spend"])
N$need_m_spend <- num(mde["need_m", "spend"])
N$need_ratio <- formatC(n_arm / mde["need_w", "spend"], format = "f", digits = 1)
N$need_ratio_m <- formatC(n_arm / mde["need_m", "spend"], format = "f", digits = 1)
N$d3_n_arm <- num(n_arm)
N$mde_conv <- pct(mde["mde", "conversion"], 2)
N$base_conv <- pct(mde["base", "conversion"], 2)
N$mde_conv_rel <- pct(mde["mde", "conversion"] / mde["base", "conversion"], 0)
N$mde_spend_rel <- pct(mde["mde", "spend"] / mde["base", "spend"], 0)
N$n_above_mde <- sum(mde[c("mens", "womens"), ] > rbind(mde["mde", ], mde["mde", ]))
N$d3_b2_power <- if (n_arm >= mde["need_m", "spend"]) "has" else "does not have"

f_metric <- function(x, y) if (y == "spend") usd(x, 3) else pct(x, 2)
kable(data.frame(
  Metric = c("Visit", "Conversion", "Spend"),
  `Control mean` = mapply(f_metric, mde["base", ], colnames(mde)),
  MDE = mapply(f_metric, mde["mde", ], colnames(mde)),
  `Effect, men's` = mapply(f_metric, mde["mens", ], colnames(mde)),
  `Effect, women's` = mapply(f_metric, mde["womens", ], colnames(mde)),
  `Customers needed, men's effect` = num(mde["need_m", ]),
  `Customers needed, women's effect` = num(mde["need_w", ]),
  check.names = FALSE), row.names = FALSE, align = "lrrrrrr")
Metric Control mean MDE Effect, men’s Effect, women’s Customers needed, men’s effect Customers needed, women’s effect
Visit 10.62% 0.96% 7.66% 4.52% 333 954
Conversion 0.57% 0.26% 0.68% 0.31% 3,032 14,505
Spend $0.653 $0.408 $0.770 $0.424 5,987 19,696

How to read: the MDE is the smallest effect that this test finds in 80% of tests. An observed effect above the MDE is large enough for this test. The last two columns give the customers that each group needs to find the observed effect.

So what: of the 6 effects (2 emails × 3 metrics), 6 are larger than the MDE. For spend, the women’s effect is only a little above the MDE.

Decision. Spend is the primary metric. Visit and conversion are secondary metrics: they help to explain the spend result.

Why. Three reasons, from the most important:

  1. The decision is about profit, and profit needs dollars. The profit of each email is margin × change in spend − contact cost. A visit or a conversion has no dollar value without a second assumption: the spend of each buyer.
  2. The test is large enough for spend. The MDE of spend is $0.41. The men’s email gives $0.77, and the women’s email gives $0.42. To find the men’s effect, the test needs 5,987 customers in each group. It has 21,306, or 3.6 times this number. Thus the test has the customers that branch 2 needs.
  3. The power is tight for the women’s email. To find the women’s effect, the test needs 19,696 customers in each group, so it has only 1.1 times this number. Thus a smaller effect than the women’s effect is not clear in this test.

Spend has the least power of the three metrics. For spend, the MDE is 63% of the control mean. For conversion, it is 45% of the control mean (0.26% on a base of 0.57%). We accept the lower power, because only spend gives the dollars.

What would change the decision. If a test has fewer customers, for example a test in one segment, spend does not have sufficient power. Then use conversion as the primary metric, and calculate the dollars with the mean spend of a buyer.

Business note. The data source made a fair split: the three groups look the same before the test. The primary metric is spend, because the campaign decision needs dollars. The test can find an effect of $0.41 for each customer, and the men’s email gives $0.77. Step 4 measures the effect of each email and checks it with other methods.

Step 4. Build models

Step 3 fixed the rules of the test and made spend the primary metric. The test can find an effect of $0.41 for each customer, and the first look gives $0.77 for the men’s email. That first look is only a difference of two means.

This step answers four questions in order. How large is the effect of each email, with which method (4a)? Which version do we send (4b)? Does the effect change by segment (4c)? Which method puts the customers in order of uplift (4d)?

Purpose. This step measures the effect of each email and builds the tools that select the version and the customers. It supports this decision: send an email or not, which version, and to which customers.

4a. Average effect

The average effect is the base of all later decisions. If the effect is not real, no version and no list of customers can make money. Two choices set the result: the method that compares the spend of two groups, and the use of the pre-test data.

Which method measures the change in mean spend?

Why this question matters. The profit of the campaign is margin × change in mean spend × customers − contact cost. Thus the method must give the change in mean spend in dollars, with an interval that we can trust. Spend has a long right tail: 99.1% of the customers spend $0, and a few spend up to $499. A method that is wrong for this shape can give a false interval.

Ways to do it. The split axis is what the method compares between the two groups: the mean, the rank of each customer, or a model of the outcome. These three groups cover the usual methods, and each method belongs to one of them.

What it compares Method Advantage Main risk Status
The mean Welch t-test Simple. All reviewers know it. Gives the change in dollars. With a long tail and a small sample, the interval can be wrong. Possible. Test it.
The mean Bootstrap of the difference of means Gives the change in dollars. Needs no normal distribution. More computation. It needs a seed to repeat the result. Possible. Test it.
The rank Mann-Whitney test Not sensitive to large values. It tests if one group usually spends more. It gives no change in dollars. Possible. Test it as a check.
A model of the outcome Two-part model (conversion × spend of a buyer), Tobit model, or a model of log(spend) Shows where the effect comes from. In a randomized test, the two-part model gives the same mean with more parts. Tobit needs a normal distribution. A log cannot use $0 and changes the question. Screened out

Evidence. The code calculates the three possible methods for the two emails. The bootstrap uses 2,000 samples with the seed of the setup chunk.

Evidence: three methods on the real spend 
# Purpose: Compare the Welch t-test, the Mann-Whitney test and the bootstrap on the spend (dec-02, branch 3).
# Input:   `d`, `SEED`, welch() and boot_diff() (case03_helpers.R).
# Output:  Table `dec02`, `boot_ci` (bootstrap 95% CI of each email, numbers), N values of the bootstrap.

B <- 2000
y0 <- d$spend[d$arm == "control"]
boot_ci <- matrix(NA_real_, 2, 2, dimnames = list(c("mens", "womens"), c("lo", "hi")))
dec02 <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("mens", "womens"), function(a) {
  y1 <- d$spend[d$arm == a]
  w <- welch(y1, y0)
  wt <- wilcox.test(y1, y0)
  bd <- boot_diff(y1, y0, B, SEED)
  boot_ci[a, ] <<- quantile(bd, c(0.025, 0.975))  # Keep the numbers for Step 6 (branch 3)
  data.frame(Email = rep(ifelse(a == "mens", "Men's", "Women's"), 3),
             Method = c("A. Welch t-test", "B. Mann-Whitney", "C. Bootstrap"),
             `Change in mean spend` = c(usd(w[["eff"]], 3), "not measured", usd(w[["eff"]], 3)),
             `95% CI` = c(ci_txt(w[["lo"]], w[["hi"]]), "not measured", ci_txt(boot_ci[a, 1], boot_ci[a, 2])),
             `p-value` = c(fmt_p(w[["p"]]), fmt_p(wt$p.value), fmt_p(2 * min(mean(bd <= 0), mean(bd >= 0)))),
             check.names = FALSE)
}))
N$boot_ci_m <- ci_txt(boot_ci["mens", 1], boot_ci["mens", 2])
N$boot_ci_w <- ci_txt(boot_ci["womens", 1], boot_ci["womens", 2])
N$n_arm_min <- num(min(table(d$arm)))
w_m <- welch(d$spend[d$arm == "mens"], y0)
N$welch_ci_m <- ci_txt(w_m[["lo"]], w_m[["hi"]])
kable(dec02, row.names = FALSE)
Email Method Change in mean spend 95% CI p-value
Men’s A. Welch t-test $0.770 [$0.49, $1.05] < 0.001
Men’s B. Mann-Whitney not measured not measured < 0.001
Men’s C. Bootstrap $0.770 [$0.48, $1.06] < 0.001
Women’s A. Welch t-test $0.424 [$0.17, $0.68] 0.001
Women’s B. Mann-Whitney not measured not measured < 0.001
Women’s C. Bootstrap $0.424 [$0.17, $0.67] 0.002

How to read: each email has three rows, one for each method. The Mann-Whitney test gives only a p-value.

So what: the Welch t-test and the bootstrap give almost the same interval for each email.

Decision. The Welch t-test. The bootstrap is a check (branch 3).

Why. The business decision uses total dollars, so the method must measure the change in mean spend. For the men’s email, the Welch interval is [$0.49, $1.05], and the bootstrap interval is [$0.48, $1.06]. Each group has 21,306 or more customers, so the mean is close to a normal distribution, even with the long tail. The Welch t-test is simpler to explain and to repeat. The Mann-Whitney test gives no dollar value, so it cannot go into the profit calculation.

What would change the decision. If a group has fewer than about 5,000 customers, or the top 1% of customers give most of the spend, use the bootstrap.

Can the pre-test data make the interval smaller?

Why this question matters. A smaller interval gives a clearer decision with the same customers. In a later test, it can also give the same power with fewer customers, and thus a lower cost of the test. Each method that removes noise also adds a model that a reviewer must check.

Ways to do it. The split axis is how much pre-test data adjusts the outcome. The four groups are no data, one feature, all features in a linear model, and an ML prediction.

Pre-test data Method Advantage Main risk Status
None Difference of means Simple. No model. The interval can be wider than necessary. Possible. Test it.
One feature CUPED with history A standard method. It removes the part of the spend that history predicts. It helps only if history predicts the spend in the test window. Possible. Test it.
All features, linear Regression adjustment (or post-stratification by segment, the same idea with cells) Uses all the pre-test data. More complex. A reviewer must check the model. Possible. Test it.
All features, ML model CUPAC: an ML prediction of the spend is the covariate Can find curves and interactions. A model to train and to approve. It helps only if the linear methods help. Screened out if the linear methods give no gain

Evidence. The code adjusts each metric of each email with the possible methods. The table gives the effect and the width of the 95% CI against no adjustment. A width of 100% means no gain. The effects also give branch 3: each adjusted effect must be within 10% of the unadjusted effect.

Evidence: CUPED and regression adjustment 
# Purpose: Compare no adjustment, CUPED and the regression adjustment for each metric (dec-03, branch 3).
# Input:   `d`, cuped() (case03_helpers.R), `RULES`.
# Output:  Table `dec03`, `adj_eff` (the spend effects of the three options, numbers), N values.

dec03 <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("visit", "conversion", "spend"), function(y) do.call(rbind, lapply(c("mens", "womens"), function(a) {
  s <- d[d$arm %in% c("control", a), ]
  s$t <- as.integer(s$arm == a)
  s$y_cuped <- cuped(s[[y]], s$history)
  fits <- list(A = lm(as.formula(paste(y, "~ t")), s),
               B = lm(y_cuped ~ t, s),
               C = lm(as.formula(paste(y, "~ t + lhist + recency + mens + womens + zip + newbie + channel")), s))
  se <- sapply(fits, function(f) summary(f)$coefficients["t", 2])
  data.frame(Metric = y, Email = ifelse(a == "mens", "Men's", "Women's"),
             `Effect, A` = coef(fits$A)["t"], `Effect, B` = coef(fits$B)["t"], `Effect, C` = coef(fits$C)["t"],
             `CI width B / A` = pct(se["B"] / se["A"]), `CI width C / A` = pct(se["C"] / se["A"]),
             r_hist = cor(s[[y]], s$history), gain = 1 - min(se) / se["A"], check.names = FALSE)
}))))
N$r_hist_spend <- formatC(max(dec03$r_hist[dec03$Metric == "spend"]), format = "f", digits = 3)
N$cuped_best <- pct(max(dec03$gain[dec03$Metric == "spend"]), 2)
N$cuped_visit <- pct(max(dec03$gain[dec03$Metric == "visit"]), 1)

# Branch 3: distance of each adjusted spend effect from the unadjusted effect.
adj_eff <- dec03[dec03$Metric == "spend", c("Email", "Effect, A", "Effect, B", "Effect, C")]
rownames(adj_eff) <- c("mens", "womens")
adj_dev <- abs(adj_eff[, c("Effect, B", "Effect, C")] / adj_eff[, "Effect, A"] - 1)
N$cuped_m <- usd(adj_eff["mens", "Effect, B"], 3)
N$reg_m <- usd(adj_eff["mens", "Effect, C"], 3)
N$ate_m_a <- usd(adj_eff["mens", "Effect, A"], 3)
N$adj_dev_m <- pct(max(adj_dev["mens", ]), 1)

dec03$r_hist <- NULL
dec03$gain <- NULL
kable(dec03, digits = 4, row.names = FALSE)
Metric Email Effect, A Effect, B Effect, C CI width B / A CI width C / A
visit Men’s 0.0766 0.0764 0.0762 99.8% 98.6%
visit Women’s 0.0452 0.0451 0.0454 99.8% 98.7%
conversion Men’s 0.0068 0.0068 0.0068 100.0% 99.9%
conversion Women’s 0.0031 0.0031 0.0031 100.0% 99.9%
spend Men’s 0.7698 0.7674 0.7692 100.0% 100.0%
spend Women’s 0.4244 0.4227 0.4268 100.0% 100.0%

How to read: option A has no adjustment, option B uses CUPED with history, and option C uses the regression adjustment. The last two columns give the width of the interval of B and C against A.

So what: the adjustments do not change the effects, and they make the interval of spend almost no smaller.

Decision. No adjustment. CUPED and the regression adjustment stay as a check (branch 3).

Why. The correlation of history with the spend in the test window is only 0.021. Thus CUPED and the regression make the interval of spend at most 0.04% smaller. For visits, the gain is at most 1.4%. The effects stay the same: for the men’s email, $0.770 with no adjustment, $0.767 with CUPED and $0.769 with the regression. The largest distance is 0.3%.

A simple method is better for the same result, and an ML adjustment cannot help when the linear methods find nothing.

What would change the decision. If the outcome repeats each month, CUPED can make the interval much smaller. For example, the monthly spend on a card is similar from one month to the next. In a card test, use CUPED with the spend of the three months before the test.

The effect of each email

The table gives the effect of each email on the three metrics, with the Welch t-test. The chart then compares the spend effect with the breakeven effect: contact cost / margin. If the effect is below the breakeven effect, the email loses money.

Effect of each email, with the Welch t-test 
# Purpose: The effect of each email on visit, conversion and spend (Welch t-test, dec-02).
# Input:   `d`, `MARGIN`, `COST`, welch() and breakeven() (case03_helpers.R).
# Output:  `ate` (all effects), `ATE`, `ATE_LO`, `ATE_HI` (spend effect of each email and its 95% CI), N values.

ate <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("visit", "conversion", "spend"), function(y) do.call(rbind, lapply(c("mens", "womens"), function(a) {
  y1 <- d[[y]][d$arm == a]; y0 <- d[[y]][d$arm == "control"]
  w <- welch(y1, y0)
  data.frame(metric = y, arm = a, eff = w[["eff"]], lo = w[["lo"]], hi = w[["hi"]],
             rel = w[["eff"]] / mean(y0), p = w[["p"]])
}))))
ATE <- setNames(ate$eff[ate$metric == "spend"], c("mens", "womens"))
ATE_LO <- setNames(ate$lo[ate$metric == "spend"], c("mens", "womens"))
ATE_HI <- setNames(ate$hi[ate$metric == "spend"], c("mens", "womens"))
N$ate_m <- usd(ATE["mens"]); N$ci_m <- ci_txt(ATE_LO["mens"], ATE_HI["mens"])
N$ate_w <- usd(ATE["womens"]); N$ci_w <- ci_txt(ATE_LO["womens"], ATE_HI["womens"])
N$rel_m <- pct(ate$rel[ate$metric == "spend" & ate$arm == "mens"], 0)
N$prof_m <- usd(MARGIN * ATE["mens"] - COST, 3)
N$prof_w <- usd(MARGIN * ATE["womens"] - COST, 3)
N$roi_m <- formatC(MARGIN * ATE["mens"] / COST, format = "f", digits = 1)
N$breakeven_eff <- usd(breakeven())
N$ate_lo_m <- usd(ATE_LO["mens"]); N$ate_lo_w <- usd(ATE_LO["womens"])
N$w_lo_vs_be <- if (ATE_LO["womens"] > breakeven()) "above" else "below"
N$m_lo_vs_be <- if (ATE_LO["mens"] > breakeven()) "above" else "below"
N$d4_b2_ci <- if (ATE_LO["mens"] > 0) "excludes" else "includes"

kable(data.frame(
  Metric = c("Visit", "Visit", "Conversion", "Conversion", "Spend", "Spend"),
  Email = rep(c("Men's", "Women's"), 3),
  Effect = ifelse(ate$metric == "spend", usd(ate$eff, 3), paste(formatC(100 * ate$eff, format = "f", digits = 2), "points")),
  `95% CI` = ifelse(ate$metric == "spend", ci_txt(ate$lo, ate$hi), paste0("[", formatC(100 * ate$lo, format = "f", digits = 2), ", ", formatC(100 * ate$hi, format = "f", digits = 2), "]")),
  `Change against control` = paste0("+", pct(ate$rel, 0)),
  `p-value` = fmt_p(ate$p), check.names = FALSE), row.names = FALSE, align = "llrrrr")
Metric Email Effect 95% CI Change against control p-value
Visit Men’s 7.66 points [7.00, 8.32] +72% < 0.001
Visit Women’s 4.52 points [3.89, 5.16] +43% < 0.001
Conversion Men’s 0.68 points [0.50, 0.86] +119% < 0.001
Conversion Women’s 0.31 points [0.15, 0.47] +54% < 0.001
Spend Men’s $0.770 [$0.49, $1.05] +118% < 0.001
Spend Women’s $0.424 [$0.17, $0.68] +65% 0.001
Chart: spend effect of each email with the 95% CI and the breakeven effect 
# Purpose: Show the spend effect of each email against $0 and against the breakeven effect.
# Input:   `ATE`, `ATE_LO`, `ATE_HI`, breakeven(), `CS` and the chart functions (chart_style.R).
# Output:  Chart only.

yy <- c(mens = 2, womens = 1)
pcol <- c(mens = CS$blue, womens = CS$gray)
cs_setup(mar = c(3.6, 7.5, 0.6, 1.5))
plot(ATE, yy, xlim = c(0, max(ATE_HI) * 1.45), ylim = c(0.5, 2.6), pch = 19, cex = 1.4, col = pcol,
     yaxt = "n", xaxt = "n", xlab = "Change in mean spend for each customer, against no email", ylab = "")
segments(ATE_LO, yy, ATE_HI, yy, col = pcol, lwd = 3)

axis(2, at = yy, labels = c("Men's email", "Women's email"), tick = FALSE, col.axis = CS$ink)

# Direct labels to the right of each interval: the effect and its 95% CI.
text(ATE_HI, yy, paste0(usd(ATE), "  ", ci_txt(ATE_LO, ATE_HI)), pos = 4, cex = 0.8, col = pcol, font = c(2, 1))
cs_title(paste0("The men's email adds ", N$ate_m, " of spend for each customer, ", N$roi_m, " times the breakeven"),

How to read: each point is the change in mean spend of one email, against the control group. The line is the 95% CI. The dashed line is the breakeven effect at a 30% margin (as-01) and a $0.10 contact cost (as-02).

So what: the lower end of the men’s interval is $0.49, above the breakeven effect of $0.33. The lower end of the women’s interval is $0.17, below the breakeven effect.

Both emails increase visits, conversions and spend. The men’s email increases the mean spend by $0.77 for each customer (95% CI [$0.49, $1.05]), or 118% more than the control group. The Welch CI excludes $0, as branch 2 asks. The women’s email increases the mean spend by $0.42 (95% CI [$0.17, $0.68]).

At a 30% margin and a $0.10 contact cost, each men’s email gives $0.131 of profit. Each women’s email gives $0.027. The ROI of the men’s email is 2.3. Thus both emails make money on average, and the men’s email makes more. Section 4b examines if a mix of the two versions makes more than the men’s email alone.

4b. Email version

Section 4a showed that both emails increase spend. The men’s email adds $0.77 for each customer, and the women’s email adds $0.42. But the mean effect of a version mixes customers who buy men’s products, women’s products or both. The next question is: do we send one version to all customers, or the version that matches the products of each customer?

Which email version do we send?

Why this question matters. The version sets the size of the effect for each customer, and thus the profit of the campaign. A second version doubles the creative work and makes the campaign harder to run. It earns its place only if it adds spend for some customers.

Ways to do it. The split axis is: does the version depend on the customer? If not, one version goes to all customers. If yes, a known feature or a model selects the version. A fifth way sends both versions to the same customer. Each way then goes through one filter: can this test measure its effect?

Group Option Advantage Main risk Screen
One version for all A. Men’s email to all customers One email. Simple to run. The largest mean effect. Customers who buy only women’s products can prefer the women’s email. Test
One version for all B. Women’s email to all customers One email. A smaller mean effect. Test
Version by a known feature C. Match the version to the product history Each customer gets the products that they buy. Two emails. It helps only if the women’s email is better for some customers. Test
Version by a model D. A model predicts the effect of each version for each customer and selects the larger one Uses all features. The choice depends on the difference of two noisy uplift estimates. Less than 1% of customers convert. Screened out: Section 4d tests uplift models for one email. A model for the difference of two emails has more noise.
Both versions E. Send both emails to the same customer No choice is necessary. Two contact costs. Fatigue. Screened out: the test has no group with both emails, so the data cannot measure the effect.

Evidence. The table gives the spend effect of each version in each product history, with its Welch 95% CI. The last two columns compare the two versions directly. Then the code calculates the mean effect of option C. It adds the effect of the matched version in each product history, with the share of the customers as the weight.

Evidence: spend effect of each version by product history, and the mean effect of option C 
# Purpose: Compare the two versions in each product history, and option C against option A (dec-04).
# Input:   `d`, `ATE` (Section 4a).
# Output:  Table `dec04`. `eff_c` (mean effect of option C). N values for the text.

dec04 <- do.call(rbind, lapply(levels(d$buyer), function(b) {
  s <- d[d$buyer == b, ]
  # Welch t-test of each email against the control group in this product history.
  r <- sapply(c("mens", "womens"), function(a) {
    tt <- t.test(s$spend[s$arm == a], s$spend[s$arm == "control"])
    c(-diff(tt$estimate), tt$conf.int)
  })
  # Direct comparison of the two versions.
  dw <- t.test(s$spend[s$arm == "mens"], s$spend[s$arm == "womens"])
  data.frame(`Product history` = b, Customers = num(nrow(s)),
             `Effect, men's` = usd(r[1, "mens"]), `95% CI, men's` = ci_txt(r[2, "mens"], r[3, "mens"]),
             `Effect, women's` = usd(r[1, "womens"]), `95% CI, women's` = ci_txt(r[2, "womens"], r[3, "womens"]),
             `Men's minus women's` = usd(-diff(dw$estimate)), `p-value` = fmt_p(dw$p.value),
             check.names = FALSE)
}))
