# Option C: men's email to "mens only" and "both", women's email to "womens only".
eff_c <- sum(sapply(levels(d$buyer), function(b) {
  a <- if (b == "womens only") "womens" else "mens"
  mean(d$buyer == b) * (mean(d$spend[d$buyer == b & d$arm == a]) - mean(d$spend[d$buyer == b & d$arm == "control"]))
}))
N$eff_c <- usd(eff_c, 3)
N$ate_m3 <- usd(ATE["mens"], 3)
N$eff_c_gain <- unname(usd(eff_c - ATE["mens"], 3))
N$eff_c_gain_100k <- unname(usd(CAMPAIGN * MARGIN * (eff_c - ATE["mens"]), 0))
N$w_only_m <- dec04$`Effect, men's`[dec04$`Product history` == "womens only"]
N$w_only_w <- dec04$`Effect, women's`[dec04$`Product history` == "womens only"]
N$m_only_w <- dec04$`Effect, women's`[dec04$`Product history` == "mens only"]
N$m_only_w_ci <- dec04$`95% CI, women's`[dec04$`Product history` == "mens only"]
N$both_m <- dec04$`Effect, men's`[dec04$`Product history` == "both"]
N$both_w <- dec04$`Effect, women's`[dec04$`Product history` == "both"]

Decision. Option A: send the men’s email to all customers.

Why. The men’s email increases spend in each product history. For the customers who buy only men’s products, the women’s email has no clear effect: $0.28, with a 95% CI of [-$0.12, $0.68]. For the customers who buy both product types, the men’s email gives $1.82 and the women’s email $0.16.

The women’s email works as well as the men’s email only for the customers who buy only women’s products: $0.63 against $0.62. Thus option C changes the version only where the two versions are equal. Option C gives a mean effect of $0.775, and option A gives $0.770. The difference of $0.005 adds only $152 of margin for 100,000 customers, but it needs a second email.

What would change the decision. If Marketing makes a new women’s email with a larger effect for women’s buyers, test option C again. The test then needs a group for each version in that product history.

4c. Segment effects

Section 4b selected the men’s email. From this section, the notebook uses only the men’s email and the control group. The mean effect can hide a segment where the email loses money. The next question is: does the effect of the men’s email change by segment, and how do we report it without false results?

How do we report the effect in each segment?

Why this question matters. Marketing wants to know where the email pays for itself. Five features give many segments. If we test each segment at 5%, some segments show an effect by chance. A false segment effect can stop the email for customers where it makes money, or send it where it loses money.

Ways to do it. The split axis is: how does the report control the false results? It can use no control, correct each p-value, first test if the effect changes at all, or make the segment estimates smaller toward the mean. Each way then goes through one filter: can a reviewer check it without a new model?

Group Option Advantage Main risk Screen
No control A. Effect of each segment, p < 0.05 Simple. With many segments, some segments show an effect by chance. Test
Correct each p-value B. Effect of each segment, with the Holm correction Controls the probability of one or more false results. Less power for each segment. Test
Test the change first C. Interaction test for each feature. Then option B for the features with an interaction. Examines only the features where the effect really changes. Two steps. Test
Estimates toward the mean D. A hierarchical model that pulls each segment effect toward the mean effect Uses all segments together. Fewer extreme results. It needs a prior and a model review. The result depends on the prior. Screened out: Section 4d tests a model that finds the customers with a large uplift. Each customer gets an uplift from a model that did not see that customer.

Evidence. The first table gives the interaction test for each feature, with the Holm correction over the features. The last row tests a straight-line change of the effect with the history in dollars. The second table repeats options A and B on 50 placebo data sets. In each placebo data set, the code puts the treatment flag in a random order. Thus the true effect is zero in each segment, and each segment effect that a test finds is false.

Technical note. The interaction test for a feature v compares two linear models with an F-test: spend ~ t + v against spend ~ t × v. The second model gives one effect of the email for each level of v. A small p-value shows that the effect changes with v.

The Holm correction sorts the k p-values from small to large. It multiplies the j-th p-value by (k − j + 1) and keeps the order. It keeps the probability of one or more false results at 5% or less. The chart below uses a Bonferroni width for each interval: the Welch standard error times the normal quantile at 1 − 0.05 / (2k). This width is a safe bound for the Holm intervals.

Evidence: interaction tests and a placebo test 
# Purpose: Test if the effect changes by segment, and measure the false results of options A and B (dec-05).
# Input:   `d`, `SEED`, `ALPHA`.
# Output:  `m` (men's email and control, with `t`), `seg_vars`, `inter` (interaction p-values),
#          `placebo`. N values for the text.

m <- d[d$arm != "womens", ]
m$t <- as.integer(m$arm == "mens")  # 1 = men's email, 0 = control
seg_vars <- c(`History bucket` = "hseg", `Product history` = "buyer", `New customer` = "newbie",
              Channel = "channel", `Area type` = "zip")
# F-test of the interaction for each feature.
inter <- sapply(seg_vars, function(v) {
  f0 <- lm(as.formula(paste("spend ~ t + factor(", v, ")")), m)
  f1 <- lm(as.formula(paste("spend ~ t * factor(", v, ")")), m)
  anova(f0, f1)[2, "Pr(>F)"]
})
lin <- summary(lm(spend ~ t * history, m))$coefficients
inter <- c(inter, `History (straight line)` = lin["t:history", 4])
kable(data.frame(Feature = names(inter), `Interaction p-value` = fmt_p(inter),
                 `Holm p-value` = fmt_p(p.adjust(inter, "holm")), check.names = FALSE), row.names = FALSE)
Feature Interaction p-value Holm p-value
History bucket 0.426 1.000
Product history 0.049 0.294
New customer 0.188 0.754
Channel 0.346 1.000
Area type 0.977 1.000
History (straight line) 0.063 0.313
Evidence: interaction tests and a placebo test 
# Placebo: a random order of the treatment flag. Each segment effect that a test finds is false.
seg_tests <- function(dat) {
  unlist(lapply(seg_vars, function(v) sapply(split(dat, dat[[v]]), function(s) t.test(s$spend[s$t == 1], s$spend[s$t == 0])$p.value)))
}
n_seg <- length(seg_tests(m))
set.seed(SEED)
placebo <- replicate(50, {
  p <- m
  p$t <- sample(p$t)
  ps <- seg_tests(p)
  c(raw = sum(ps < ALPHA), holm = sum(p.adjust(ps, "holm") < ALPHA))
})
kable(data.frame(Option = c("A. p < 0.05", "B. Holm correction"),
                 `Mean number of false segment effects` = paste0(formatC(rowMeans(placebo), format = "f", digits = 2), " of ", n_seg),
                 `Placebo tests with one or more false results` = pct(rowMeans(placebo > 0), 0), check.names = FALSE), row.names = FALSE)
Option Mean number of false segment effects Placebo tests with one or more false results
A. p < 0.05 0.92 of 18 62%
B. Holm correction 0.02 of 18 2%
Evidence: interaction tests and a placebo test 
N$n_seg_tests <- n_seg
N$placebo_any <- pct(mean(placebo["raw", ] > 0), 0)
N$placebo_holm <- pct(mean(placebo["holm", ] > 0), 0)
N$n_inter <- sum(p.adjust(inter, "holm") < ALPHA)
N$min_raw <- names(inter)[which.min(inter)]
N$min_raw_p <- fmt_p(min(inter))
N$min_holm_p <- fmt_p(min(p.adjust(inter, "holm")))
N$lin_slope <- usd(100 * lin["t:history", 1])

Decision. Option C: the interaction test first, then the effect of each segment with the Holm correction. Report the segment effects as a description, not as a reason to target.

Why. The five features give 18 segments. The placebo data has no real effect, but option A finds one or more false segment effects in 62% of the runs.

With the Holm correction, this share is 2%. In this test, 0 features have an interaction after the Holm correction. The smallest raw p-value is 0.049 (Product history), and its Holm p-value is 0.294. Thus the data gives only weak evidence that the effect changes by segment.

The straight-line test points in one direction: each $100 of history adds about $0.11 to the effect. Section 4d uses this signal: it puts the customers in order by history.

What would change the decision. If the business names one or two segments before the test, test only these segments. Then the correction is not necessary.

The chart shows the effect of the men’s email in each history bucket and each product history. Each interval has the Holm-adjusted width of the technical note above. Two reference lines help to read it. The first is the mean effect of Section 4a. The second is the breakeven effect: the contact cost divided by the margin (as-01, as-02). Above the breakeven effect, the email pays for itself.

Chart: spend effect of the men’s email by segment, with Holm-adjusted 95% intervals 
# Purpose: Show the segment effects of dec-05 against the mean effect and the breakeven effect.
# Input:   `m`, `ATE`, `ALPHA`, `COST` (as-02), `MARGIN` (as-01), `CS` and the functions of chart_style.R.
# Output:  `seg` (one row for each segment). Chart. N values for the text.

if (!exists("CS")) source("chart_style.R")  # The setup chunk sources it. This line keeps a part test alive.
seg <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("hseg", "buyer"), function(v) do.call(rbind, lapply(levels(m[[v]]), function(lv) {
  s <- m[m[[v]] == lv, ]
  tt <- t.test(s$spend[s$t == 1], s$spend[s$t == 0])
  data.frame(var = v, level = lv, n = nrow(s), eff = -diff(tt$estimate), se = tt$stderr, p = tt$p.value)
}))))
k <- nrow(seg)
z <- qnorm(1 - ALPHA / (2 * k))  # Bonferroni width. It is a safe bound for the Holm intervals.
seg$lo <- seg$eff - z * seg$se
seg$hi <- seg$eff + z * seg$se
seg$p_holm <- p.adjust(seg$p, "holm")
be_seg <- COST / MARGIN
N$breakeven_eff <- usd(be_seg)
N$n_seg_above <- sum(seg$eff > be_seg)
N$k_seg <- k
N$n_seg_holm <- sum(seg$p_holm < ALPHA & seg$eff > 0)
N$n_seg_lo_above <- sum(seg$lo > be_seg)
# History of $350 or more against less: the pattern that Section 4d uses.
hi_h <- m$history >= 350
N$eff_hist_hi <- usd(mean(m$spend[hi_h & m$t == 1]) - mean(m$spend[hi_h & m$t == 0]))
N$eff_hist_lo <- usd(mean(m$spend[!hi_h & m$t == 1]) - mean(m$spend[!hi_h & m$t == 0]))

# Labels: the segment and its number of customers.
buyer_lab <- c(`mens only` = "Men's products only", `womens only` = "Women's products only", both = "Both product types")
lab <- ifelse(seg$var == "hseg", paste("History", seg$level), buyer_lab[seg$level])
lab <- paste0(lab, "  (", num(seg$n), ")")
yy <- rev(seq_len(k))
pcol <- ifelse(seg$p_holm < ALPHA, CS$blue, CS$gray)

cs_setup(mar = c(3.6, 13, 1.6, 1.5))
plot(NA, xlim = range(c(seg$lo, seg$hi, 0)), ylim = c(0.5, k + 0.5), axes = FALSE,
     xlab = "Change in mean spend for each customer ($)", ylab = "")
axis(1, at = axTicks(1), labels = usd(axTicks(1), 0))  # usd() writes a plain minus sign
axis(2, at = yy, labels = lab, tick = FALSE, col.axis = CS$ink, cex.axis = 0.8)
abline(v = 0, col = CS$light_gray)
abline(h = sum(seg$var == "buyer") + 0.5, col = CS$light_gray, lty = 3)  # Line between the two features
# Reference lines with direct labels at the top: the mean effect and the breakeven effect.
abline(v = ATE["mens"], col = CS$navy, lty = 2, lwd = 1.2)
abline(v = be_seg, col = CS$muted, lty = 3, lwd = 1.2)
text(ATE["mens"], k + 0.9, paste0(" Mean effect ", N$ate_m), adj = c(0, 0.5), xpd = NA, col = CS$navy, cex = 0.75)
text(be_seg, k + 0.9, paste0("Breakeven ", N$breakeven_eff, " "), adj = c(1, 0.5), xpd = NA, col = CS$muted, cex = 0.75)
# Intervals and point effects. Blue: Holm p < 0.05. Gray: the others.
segments(seg$lo, yy, seg$hi, yy, col = pcol, lwd = 2.5)
points(seg$eff, yy, pch = 19, col = pcol, cex = 1.1)
cs_title(paste0("The effect beats the ", N$breakeven_eff, " breakeven in ", N$n_seg_above, " of ",
                N$k_seg, " segments, with wide intervals"),
         "Spend effect of the men's email, Holm-adjusted 95% intervals. Blue: Holm p < 0.05; gray: the others")

How to read: each row is one segment, with its number of customers in brackets. The dot is the spend effect of the men’s email, and the line is its Holm-adjusted 95% interval. A blue line has a Holm p-value less than 0.05.

So what: the point effect is above the breakeven effect of $0.33 in 10 of 10 segments. But only 2 segments have a Holm p-value less than 0.05, and 0 intervals are fully above the breakeven effect. Thus one feature at a time cannot show a segment where the email loses money. The effect is $1.40 for customers with $350 or more of history and $0.59 for the others. Section 4d tests if an order by history, or a model, finds the customers with the largest uplift.

4d. Uplift method

Section 4c found only weak evidence that the effect changes with one feature at a time. A combination of features can still find customers with a larger uplift. If the contact cost is high, the order of the customers by uplift decides who gets the email. Thus the last question of Step 4 is: which method puts the customers in this order?

Which method puts the customers in order of uplift?

Why this question matters. A targeting rule sends the email to the top of a list. If the list has the wrong order, the rule removes customers who buy because of the email, and it keeps customers who do not. A complex model also needs a model review and a monthly check. Thus a model must give a clearly better order than a simple rule.

Ways to do it. The split axis is where the order comes from. It can come from one pre-test feature, a table of segments, a model of the outcome in each group, or a model of the uplift. These four groups cover the usual uplift methods, and each method belongs to one of them.

Where the order comes from Method Advantage Main risk Status
One pre-test feature A. Rank by history (no model) Simple. No model to approve. Customers who spent more in the past can buy more. It ranks by the value of the customer, not directly by the uplift. Possible. Test it as the baseline.
A table of segments B. Segment table: history bucket × product history Easy to read. Each cell has few buyers, so each estimate is noisy. Possible. Test it.
A model of the outcome in each group C. T-learner: one logistic regression of the conversion in each group Uses all features. A standard method. The uplift is the difference of two noisy predictions. Possible. Test it.
A model of the outcome in each group S-learner or X-learner The S-learner uses one model. The X-learner can help when the groups have different sizes. Here the groups have the same size. A linear S-learner with no interaction gives the same uplift to all customers. Screened out
A model of the uplift D. Uplift tree on the transformed outcome One model. The tree gives rules that a person can read. The transformed outcome has a large variance for spend. Possible. Test it.
A model of the uplift Causal forest or uplift random forest Strong on large data with many buyers. Needs packages outside base R and rpart. With so few buyers, a forest of trees also fits noise. Screened out

The rule before the evidence (branch 5). We set the model rule in section 3a, before the rerun. An ML uplift model (C or D) replaces rank by history only if two conditions are true. Its mean Qini area is 20% or more higher than the area of rank by history. Its Qini area is more than 0 in at least 9 of 10 repeats. The segment table also uses estimates from the test data, so we apply the same bar to it.

Technical note. Settings of the methods. Each method uses only the men’s email and the control group.

  • Cross-fit. 5 folds, repeated 10 times with the seeds SEED + 1 to SEED + 10. Rank by history needs no folds, so its area is the same in each repeat.
  • B. Segment table. For each cell of history bucket × product history in the training folds: mean spend of the email group − mean spend of the control group. A cell with no customers in the training folds gets an uplift of 0.
  • C. T-learner. In each group, a logistic regression of the conversion on recency, log(history), product history, area type, new customer and channel. The uplift = (mean spend of a buyer × probability to buy) in the email group − the same in the control group.
  • D. Uplift tree. The transformed outcome z = spend × (t − p) / (p × (1 − p)), with p the share of the email group. Its mean is the uplift. A regression tree on z (rpart) with at most 3 levels, at least 3,000 customers in each leaf and no cost-complexity limit (cp = 0).
  • Qini area. At the top 5%, 10%, …, 100% of the list (section 3a). A tie in the score gets a random order.

Evidence. For each repeat, the code gives each customer a cross-fitted uplift from each method. It then draws the Qini curve of each method and calculates its Qini area. The table gives the area over the 10 repeats and applies the model rule.

Evidence: four uplift methods with a 5-fold cross-fit, 10 repeats, and the model rule 
# Purpose: Compare four uplift methods by the Qini area and apply the model rule of branch 5 (dec-06).
# Input:   `m` (men's email + control, Step 4c), `SEED`, `RULES`, uplift_oof(), qini(), qini_area()
#          (case03_helpers.R).
# Output:  `p_t`, `GRID`, `preds`, `curves`, `area` (one row for each repeat), `OPT6`, table, N values.

p_t <- mean(m$t)            # Share of the email group
GRID <- seq(0.05, 1, 0.05)  # Top shares of the list for the Qini curve

REPS <- 10
preds <- lapply(seq_len(REPS), function(r) uplift_oof(SEED + r))
curves <- lapply(preds, function(p) { set.seed(SEED); sapply(colnames(p), function(cn) qini(p[, cn], m$spend, m$t)) })
area <- t(sapply(curves, qini_area))
OPT6 <- c(A = "A. Rank by history", B = "B. Segment table", C = "C. T-learner", D = "D. Uplift tree")

# The model rule of branch 5, set before the evidence.
gain6 <- colMeans(area) / mean(area[, "A"]) - 1     # Mean Qini area against rank by history (relative)
pos6 <- colSums(area > 0)                           # Repeats with a Qini area more than 0
pass6 <- gain6 >= RULES$b5_model_gain & pos6 >= RULES$b5_model_pos
pass6["A"] <- NA                                    # The baseline
cand <- names(which(pass6[c("B", "C", "D")]))
chosen6 <- if (length(cand)) cand[which.max(colMeans(area)[cand])] else "A"

kable(data.frame(Option = OPT6,
                 `Mean Qini area` = usd(colMeans(area), 3),
                 `Lowest of 10 repeats` = usd(apply(area, 2, min), 3),
                 `Highest of 10 repeats` = usd(apply(area, 2, max), 3),
                 `Repeats with area > 0` = paste(pos6, "of", REPS),
                 `Mean area against A` = c("baseline", paste0(ifelse(gain6[-1] > 0, "+", ""), pct(gain6[-1], 0))),
                 `Model rule` = c("baseline", ifelse(pass6[-1], "passes", "fails")),
                 check.names = FALSE), row.names = FALSE, align = "lrrrrrl")
Option Mean Qini area Lowest of 10 repeats Highest of 10 repeats Repeats with area > 0 Mean area against A Model rule
A. Rank by history $0.083 $0.083 $0.083 10 of 10 baseline baseline
B. Segment table $0.068 $0.017 $0.136 10 of 10 -18% fails
C. T-learner -$0.029 -$0.076 $0.017 3 of 10 -135% fails
D. Uplift tree -$0.019 -$0.043 -$0.000 0 of 10 -123% fails
Evidence: four uplift methods with a 5-fold cross-fit, 10 repeats, and the model rule 
best6 <- names(which.max(colMeans(area)))
N$best6 <- OPT6[best6]
N$chosen6 <- OPT6[chosen6]
N$b5_model <- if (chosen6 == "A") "keeps" else "replaces"
N$n_pass6 <- length(cand)
N$area_a <- usd(mean(area[, "A"]), 3)
N$area_b <- usd(mean(area[, "B"]), 3)
N$area_b_range <- ci_txt(min(area[, "B"]), max(area[, "B"]), function(x) usd(x, 3))
N$area_cd <- paste0(usd(mean(area[, "C"]), 3), " and ", usd(mean(area[, "D"]), 3))
N$gain_b <- pct(gain6[["B"]], 0); N$gain_c <- pct(gain6[["C"]], 0); N$gain_d <- pct(gain6[["D"]], 0)
N$pos_b <- pos6[["B"]]; N$pos_c <- pos6[["C"]]; N$pos_d <- pos6[["D"]]
Chart: Qini curves of the four methods, first repeat 
# Purpose: Show the Qini curves of the first repeat against the line of a random order (dec-06).
# Input:   `curves`, `GRID`, `OPT6`, `CS` and the chart functions (chart_style.R).
# Output:  Chart only.

cv <- rbind(0, curves[[1]])
xs <- c(0, GRID) * 100
col6 <- c(A = CS$navy, B = CS$cyan, C = CS$gray, D = CS$gray)
lwd6 <- c(A = 2.8, B = 1.8, C = 1.5, D = 1.5)
cs_setup(mar = c(3.6, 5.4, 0.6, 1.5))
plot(xs, cv[, "A"], type = "n", ylim = range(0, cv), xlim = c(0, 100), xaxt = "n", yaxt = "n",
     xlab = "Share of customers that get the email, in the order of each method", ylab = "")
title(ylab = "Incremental spend for each customer", line = 3.6)  # More room for the dollar labels
axis(1, at = seq(0, 100, 20), labels = paste0(seq(0, 100, 20), "%"))
cs_dollar_axis(2)
lines(c(0, 100), c(0, cv[nrow(cv), "A"]), lty = 2, col = CS$light_gray, lwd = 1.5)
for (o in c("D", "C", "B", "A")) lines(xs, cv[, o], col = col6[o], lwd = lwd6[o])
# Direct labels in the empty space next to each curve: A and B above the curves, C and D below.
lab <- data.frame(o = c("A", "B", "C", "D"), x = c(25, 70, 65, 85),
                  ax = c(1.05, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5), ay = c(-0.6, -0.9, 1.8, 1.8))
for (j in seq_len(nrow(lab))) {
  o <- lab$o[j]; i <- which.min(abs(xs - lab$x[j]))
  text(xs[i], cv[i, o], OPT6[o], adj = c(lab$ax[j], lab$ay[j]), cex = 0.78,
       col = if (o == "A") CS$navy else if (o == "B") CS$cyan else CS$muted, font = if (o == "A") 2 else 1)
}
cs_title(paste0("Rank by history gives the largest Qini area: ", N$area_a, " for each customer"),
         "Qini curves of the first repeat of the 5-fold cross-fit; dashed line: random order")

How to read: each line starts at 0 and adds customers in the order of one method. The height is the incremental spend for each customer of the campaign. The dashed line is a random order. A curve above the dashed line puts the customers with a large uplift first.

So what: rank by history (navy) stays above the random order at each share. The T-learner and the uplift tree (gray) cross the random order, and their mean areas over 10 repeats are below 0.

Decision. Rank by history. The model rule keeps rank by history: 0 of the three methods with estimates passes the rule.

Why. Three reasons, from the most important:

  1. No model passes the rule. The T-learner has a mean area -135% against rank by history, with an area more than 0 in 3 of 10 repeats. The uplift tree has -123%, with 0 of 10. The two models are not better than a random order (-$0.029 and -$0.019). Less than 1% of the customers buy, so the models with more features fit noise.
  2. The segment table is not stable. Its mean area is $0.068 (-18% against rank by history), and it changes from repeat to repeat ([$0.017, $0.136]). One cut of the folds can make it look better or worse than history.
  3. Rank by history is simple and stable. It has the largest mean area, $0.083. It needs no model, so Marketing can use it without a model review.

What would change the decision. If a test has many more buyers, an ML model can find a pattern that history cannot show. Repeat this comparison with each new test and the same rule. Keep rank by history as the baseline.

Business note. The men’s email increases the mean spend by $0.77 for each customer (95% CI [$0.49, $1.05]). This is 2.3 times the breakeven effect. The best order of the customers by uplift is the simplest one: rank by history. No ML model passes the rule of branch 5. Step 5 gives each customer an uplift from this order.

Step 5. Make predictions

Step 4 selected the men’s email and rank by history as the order of the customers. A targeting rule needs more than an order: it needs the uplift in dollars of each part of the list. Only then can we compare the uplift with the breakeven effect of $0.33. This step answers: what uplift does each customer get, and how sure are we?

Purpose. This step gives each customer an uplift on spend from the history quartile of the customer. It supports this decision: the list of customers for the email if the contact cost goes up (Step 7a).

The prediction for a customer is the uplift of the history quartile of that customer. We use quartiles, because each quartile has about one quarter of the customers and enough buyers for an interval. Smaller groups give intervals that are too wide for a decision.

The code gives two estimates for each quartile:

  • The uplift of the quartile. The mean spend of the email group − the mean spend of the control group, with the Welch 95% CI. All customers of the quartile give this estimate.
  • The cross-fitted uplift. Each customer gets the uplift of the quartile from the other four folds (5-fold cross-fit). Thus the estimate of a customer never uses that customer. Step 7a uses this estimate in the breakeven rule. The range of the cross-fitted uplift over the five folds shows how much the data of one fold moves the estimate.
Uplift on spend by history quartile, with the cross-fitted uplift 
# Purpose: The uplift on spend of each history quartile and the cross-fitted uplift of each customer (Step 5).
# Input:   `m`, `MARGIN`, `COST`, `SEED`, group_effect(), xfit_group() and breakeven() (case03_helpers.R).
# Output:  `qs` (quartile cuts), `m$hq` (history quartile), `uq` (uplift of each quartile with its 95% CI),
#          `uq_cf` (cross-fitted uplift of each customer), N values.

qs <- quantile(m$history, c(0.25, 0.50, 0.75))
m$hq <- cut(m$history, c(-Inf, qs, Inf), labels = c("Q1 (lowest)", "Q2", "Q3", "Q4 (highest)"))
uq <- group_effect(m, m$hq)
names(uq)[names(uq) == "level"] <- "q"
uq$lo_h <- as.vector(tapply(m$history, m$hq, min))
uq$hi_h <- as.vector(tapply(m$history, m$hq, max))
uq <- uq[, c("q", "n", "lo_h", "hi_h", "eff", "lo", "hi")]

# Cross-fitted uplift: the same folds as Step 7a (seed SEED + 1).
uq_cf <- xfit_group(m, m$hq, SEED + 1)
cf_mean <- tapply(uq_cf, m$hq, mean)
cf_fold <- tapply(seq_along(uq_cf), m$hq, function(i) range(uq_cf[i]))

kable(data.frame(`History quartile` = uq$q, `History range` = paste(usd(uq$lo_h, 0), "to", usd(uq$hi_h, 0)),
                 Customers = num(uq$n), `Uplift on spend` = usd(uq$eff), `95% CI` = ci_txt(uq$lo, uq$hi),
                 `Cross-fitted uplift, mean` = usd(cf_mean),
                 `Cross-fitted uplift, range of 5 folds` = sapply(cf_fold, function(r) ci_txt(r[1], r[2])),
                 `Profit for each email at $0.10` = usd(MARGIN * uq$eff - COST), check.names = FALSE),
      row.names = FALSE, align = "llrrrrrr")
History quartile History range Customers Uplift on spend 95% CI Cross-fitted uplift, mean Cross-fitted uplift, range of 5 folds Profit for each email at $0.10
Q1 (lowest) $30 to $64 10,654 $0.63 [$0.07, $1.19] $0.63 [$0.26, $0.90] $0.09
Q2 $65 to $157 10,653 $0.40 [-$0.03, $0.84] $0.40 [$0.22, $0.54] $0.02
Q3 $157 to $325 10,653 $0.65 [$0.09, $1.22] $0.65 [$0.49, $0.85] $0.10
Q4 (highest) $325 to $3,346 10,653 $1.39 [$0.70, $2.08] $1.39 [$0.99, $1.60] $0.32
Uplift on spend by history quartile, with the cross-fitted uplift 
N$q4_eff <- usd(uq$eff[4]); N$q4_cut <- usd(qs[3], 0)
N$q4_ci <- ci_txt(uq$lo[4], uq$hi[4])
N$q13 <- paste(usd(min(uq$eff[1:3])), "to", usd(max(uq$eff[1:3])))
N$q_min_profit <- usd(min(MARGIN * uq$eff - COST), 3)
N$q_n <- num(min(uq$n))
N$n_q_above <- sum(uq$eff > breakeven())
N$n_q_lo_above <- sum(uq$lo > breakeven())
N$q_lo_min <- usd(min(uq$lo))
N$cf_range <- paste(usd(min(sapply(cf_fold, min))), "to", usd(max(sapply(cf_fold, max))))
N$q4_cf_range <- ci_txt(cf_fold[[4]][1], cf_fold[[4]][2])
N$q4_ratio <- formatC(uq$eff[4] / mean(uq$eff[1:3]), format = "f", digits = 1)
# Does the top quartile stay above the other quartiles in each fold?
q4_top <- cf_fold[[4]][1] > max(sapply(cf_fold[1:3], max))
N$q4_order <- if (q4_top) "stays on top in each fold" else "does not stay on top in each fold"
Chart: uplift on spend by history quartile, with the 95% CI and the breakeven effect 
# Purpose: Show the uplift of each history quartile against the breakeven effect (Step 5).
# Input:   `uq`, breakeven(), `CS` and the chart functions (chart_style.R).
# Output:  Chart only.

xq <- seq_len(nrow(uq))
qcol <- ifelse(xq == 4, CS$blue, CS$navy)
cs_setup(mar = c(3.6, 5.4, 0.6, 7))
plot(xq, uq$eff, ylim = range(0, uq$lo, uq$hi), xlim = c(0.6, 4.4), pch = 19, cex = 1.3, col = qcol,
     xaxt = "n", yaxt = "n", xlab = "History quartile (spend in the 12 months before the test)", ylab = "")
title(ylab = "Uplift on spend for each customer", line = 3.6)  # More room for the dollar labels
segments(xq, uq$lo, xq, uq$hi, col = qcol, lwd = 3)
axis(1, at = xq, labels = paste0(uq$q, "\n", usd(uq$lo_h, 0), " to ", usd(uq$hi_h, 0)), padj = 0.5, cex.axis = 0.75)
cs_dollar_axis(2)
abline(h = 0, col = CS$light_gray)
abline(h = breakeven(), lty = 2, col = CS$gray)
cs_label_end(4.4, breakeven(), paste0("Breakeven ", usd(breakeven())), col = CS$muted)
text(xq, uq$eff, usd(uq$eff), pos = 4, offset = 0.7, cex = 0.8, col = qcol, font = ifelse(xq == 4, 2, 1))
cs_title(paste0("The top history quartile adds ", N$q4_eff, " of spend; the other quartiles ", N$q13),
         "Uplift of the men's email on spend for each customer, with the Welch 95% CI")

How to read: each point is the uplift of one history quartile, with its 95% CI. The dashed line is the breakeven effect at a $0.10 contact cost. A quartile above the line makes money with each email.

So what: the point estimate is above the breakeven effect in 4 of 4 quartiles. The interval is fully above it in only 1 of 4 quartiles, so the uplift of a quartile is not certain.

The uplift is $0.40 to $0.65 in the three lower quartiles. In the top quartile (history more than $325), it is $1.39 (95% CI [$0.70, $2.08]). At a contact cost of $0.10, each quartile is profitable, but the lowest profit is only $0.020 for each email.

The cross-fitted uplift of a customer goes from $0.22 to $1.60. In the top quartile, the range is [$0.99, $1.60]. Thus the estimate of a quartile moves with the fold, and the top quartile stays on top in each fold.

Business note. Each customer now has an uplift from the history quartile. The top quartile gives $1.39 for each customer, 2.5 times the mean of the other quartiles. Thus the top quartile is the first group to keep if the contact cost goes up. Step 6 checks the recommended policy against the five branches of section 3a. Step 7a then compares “send to all” with the rules that use this uplift.

Step 6. Evaluate

Steps 4 and 5 gave the evidence one piece at a time. The men’s email increases spend, it is the better version, and each history quartile is profitable at the base contact cost. Now we must judge the recommended policy as a whole: send the men’s email to all customers. This step uses the five branches of the evaluation framework of Step 3a, one at a time.

Purpose. This step answers: is the policy “men’s email to all customers” valid, large enough, robust, profitable and better than a targeting rule? It supports this decision: approve the policy for the launch with a holdout.

The table repeats the five rules of Step 3a. We set these rules before the rerun of this version, and we do not change them after a result. If a result fails a rule, this step reports the failure and what it means.

Branch Question Rule
1. Validity Do the groups differ only by the email? The largest absolute standardized difference is less than 0.05. The p-value of the sample-ratio check is more than 0.01.
2. Effect Does the men’s email change spend, and is the test large enough? The Welch 95% CI excludes 0. Each group has at least the customers for 80% power at the observed effect.
3. Robustness Does the effect hold with other methods? The bootstrap 95% CI excludes 0. The CUPED effect and the regression effect are each within 10% of the unadjusted effect.
4. Business value Does the recommended policy make money? The profit for 100,000 customers is more than 0, and the lower end of its 95% CI is more than 0.
5. Targeting Does a targeting rule or an uplift model beat “send to all”? The policy follows the model rule and the policy rule of Step 3a.

6a. Branch 1: validity

The question: do the three groups differ only by the email? The data source put each customer into a group at random. A random split gives groups that are equal on average, but a fault in the split can make them different. If the groups differ before the email, the difference of the means is not the effect of the email.

Two checks answer the question, because they find different faults:

  • Standardized difference. It compares the mean of each pre-test feature in each email group with the control group. It finds a group with different customers.
  • Sample-ratio check. It compares the number of customers in each group with an equal split. It finds a group that lost or gained customers.

Step 2d gives the full table of the standardized differences. This section applies the rule of Step 3a to it.

Branch 1: largest standardized difference and the sample-ratio check 
# Purpose: Measure branch 1 (validity) of the evaluation framework of Step 3a.
# Input:   `feat`, `d` (contract C2), `RULES` (Step 3a).
# Output:  `RULES` (if Step 3a did not make it), `e1_smd`, `e1_srm`, `b1_pass`, N$e1_*.

# The chart style of the notebook. The setup chunk loads it. This guard keeps the part usable alone.
if (!exists("CS")) source("chart_style.R")

# The rules of the evaluation framework: `RULES` of Step 3a. The fallback has the same values (the brief of
# round 2), for a run without the chunk of Step 3a. We set the rules before the rerun.
if (!exists("RULES")) {
  RULES <- list(
    b1_smd = 0.05,          # Branch 1: largest absolute standardized difference less than 0.05
    b1_srm_p = 0.01,        # Branch 1: p-value of the sample-ratio check more than 0.01
    b3_adj_dev = 0.10,      # Branch 3: each adjusted effect within 10% of the unadjusted effect
    b5_model_gain = 0.20,   # Branch 5: an ML uplift model needs a 20% higher mean Qini area ...
    b5_model_pos = 9,       # ... and a Qini area more than 0 in 9 or more of the repeats
    b5_policy_level = 0.90  # Branch 5: the 90% interval of the gain of a targeting rule must be above 0
  )
}

# Standardized difference of each pre-test feature: (mean of the email group - mean of control) / sd.
smd_arm <- function(a) sapply(feat, function(x) (mean(x[d$arm == a]) - mean(x[d$arm == "control"])) / sd(x))
smd_all <- cbind(mens = smd_arm("mens"), womens = smd_arm("womens"))
e1_smd <- max(abs(smd_all))
e1_smd_feat <- rownames(smd_all)[which.max(apply(abs(smd_all), 1, max))]
# Sample-ratio check: chi-square test of the group sizes against an equal split.
e1_srm <- chisq.test(table(d$arm))$p.value

b1_pass <- e1_smd < RULES$b1_smd && e1_srm > RULES$b1_srm_p
N$e1_smd <- formatC(e1_smd, format = "f", digits = 3)
N$e1_smd_feat <- e1_smd_feat
N$e1_srm <- formatC(e1_srm, format = "f", digits = 2)
N$e1_n_feat <- ncol(feat)
N$b1_verdict <- if (b1_pass) "The policy passes branch 1." else "The policy fails branch 1."

kable(data.frame(
  Check = c("Largest absolute standardized difference (both emails against control)", "Sample-ratio check: chi-square p-value"),
  Result = c(N$e1_smd, N$e1_srm),
  Rule = c("Less than 0.05", "More than 0.01"), check.names = FALSE), row.names = FALSE, align = "lrl")
Check Result Rule
Largest absolute standardized difference (both emails against control) 0.014 Less than 0.05
Sample-ratio check: chi-square p-value 0.90 More than 0.01

The largest standardized difference of the 10 pre-test features is 0.014 (zipRural), against the limit of 0.05. The p-value of the sample-ratio check is 0.90, against the limit of 0.01. The policy passes branch 1. Thus a difference of the means gives the causal effect of the email.

6b. Branch 2: effect

The question: does the men’s email change spend, and is the test large enough to trust the answer? A test with too few customers can find an effect by chance, and its estimate is often too large. Thus the rule has two parts:

  • The Welch 95% CI of the spend effect excludes 0.
  • Each group has at least the customers that a test needs for 80% power at the observed effect, at 5% significance.
Branch 2: Welch CI of the spend effect and the customers for 80% power 
# Purpose: Measure branch 2 (effect): the Welch CI and the size of the test at the observed effect.
# Input:   `d`, `ATE`, `ATE_LO`, `ATE_HI` (contract C3), `ALPHA`, `POWER`.
# Output:  `e2_need`, `e2_have`, `e2_power`, `b2_pass`, N$e2_*.

# Pooled standard deviation of spend in the three groups (the same as the power of Step 3c).
s_pool <- sqrt(mean(tapply(d$spend, d$arm, var)))
e2_have <- min(table(d$arm))
e2_need <- power.t.test(delta = ATE[["mens"]], sd = s_pool, sig.level = ALPHA, power = POWER)$n
# Power of this test at the observed effect.
e2_power <- power.t.test(n = e2_have, delta = ATE[["mens"]], sd = s_pool, sig.level = ALPHA)$power

b2_pass <- ATE_LO[["mens"]] > 0 && e2_have >= e2_need
N$e2_ci <- ci_txt(ATE_LO[["mens"]], ATE_HI[["mens"]])
N$e2_ate <- usd(ATE[["mens"]])
N$e2_need <- num(ceiling(e2_need))
N$e2_have <- num(e2_have)
N$e2_ratio <- formatC(e2_have / e2_need, format = "f", digits = 1)
N$e2_power <- pct(e2_power, 0)
N$b2_verdict <- if (b2_pass) "The policy passes branch 2." else "The policy fails branch 2."

kable(data.frame(
  Check = c("Spend effect of the men's email, Welch 95% CI", "Customers in the smallest group",
            "Customers for 80% power at the observed effect", "Power of this test at the observed effect"),
  Result = c(paste(N$e2_ate, N$e2_ci), N$e2_have, N$e2_need, N$e2_power),
  Rule = c("The CI excludes 0", "At least the customers for 80% power", "", ""), check.names = FALSE),
  row.names = FALSE, align = "lrl")
Check Result Rule
Spend effect of the men’s email, Welch 95% CI $0.77 [$0.49, $1.05] The CI excludes 0
Customers in the smallest group 21,306 At least the customers for 80% power
Customers for 80% power at the observed effect 5,988
Power of this test at the observed effect 100%

The men’s email increases the mean spend by $0.77 for each customer (95% CI [$0.49, $1.05]). The CI excludes 0. At this effect, a test needs 5,988 customers in each group for 80% power. The smallest group has 21,306, or 3.6 times this number, and the power is 100%. The policy passes branch 2.

6c. Branch 3: robustness

The question: does the effect hold if we use other methods? The Welch CI assumes that the mean of the spend has a normal distribution. Spend has a long right tail, so a reviewer can doubt this. The pre-test data can also change the estimate. Thus the rule uses three other methods:

  • Bootstrap. It needs no normal distribution. The code repeats the bootstrap of Step 4a with the same seed and 2,000 samples, so the CI is the same.
  • CUPED with history. It removes the part of the spend that history predicts.
  • Regression adjustment. It adds all pre-test features to a linear regression.

The two adjusted effects come from the evidence of the variance-reduction decision in Step 4a.

Branch 3: bootstrap CI and the adjusted effects against the unadjusted effect 
# Purpose: Measure branch 3 (robustness): bootstrap CI, CUPED effect and regression effect of the men's email.
# Input:   `d`, `dec03` (contract C3), `SEED`, `ATE`.
# Output:  `e3_boot`, `e3_adj` (effects A, B and C), `b3_pass`, N$e3_*.

# Bootstrap: the same code and seed as dec-02, so the interval is the interval of Step 4a.
y1 <- d$spend[d$arm == "mens"]
y0 <- d$spend[d$arm == "control"]
set.seed(SEED)
bd <- replicate(2000, mean(y1[sample.int(length(y1), replace = TRUE)]) - mean(y0[sample.int(length(y0), replace = TRUE)]))
e3_boot <- quantile(bd, c(0.025, 0.975))

# Effects A (no adjustment), B (CUPED) and C (regression) for spend, men's email, from dec03.
# If dec03 has other column names, fit the three models again with the method of dec-03.
cols3 <- c("Metric", "Email", "Effect, A", "Effect, B", "Effect, C")
if (all(cols3 %in% names(dec03))) {
  r3 <- dec03[dec03$Metric == "spend" & dec03$Email == "Men's", ]
  e3_adj <- c(A = r3[["Effect, A"]], B = r3[["Effect, B"]], C = r3[["Effect, C"]])
} else {
  s3 <- d[d$arm %in% c("control", "mens"), ]
  s3$t <- as.integer(s3$arm == "mens")
  theta <- cov(s3$spend, s3$history) / var(s3$history)
  s3$y_cuped <- s3$spend - theta * (s3$history - mean(s3$history))
  e3_adj <- c(A = coef(lm(spend ~ t, s3))[["t"]], B = coef(lm(y_cuped ~ t, s3))[["t"]],
              C = coef(lm(spend ~ t + lhist + recency + mens + womens + zip + newbie + channel, s3))[["t"]])
}
e3_dev <- abs(e3_adj[c("B", "C")] / e3_adj[["A"]] - 1)  # Relative change against the unadjusted effect

b3_pass <- e3_boot[[1]] > 0 && all(e3_dev <= RULES$b3_adj_dev)
N$e3_boot <- ci_txt(e3_boot[[1]], e3_boot[[2]])
N$e3_cuped <- usd(e3_adj[["B"]], 3)
N$e3_reg <- usd(e3_adj[["C"]], 3)
N$e3_unadj <- usd(e3_adj[["A"]], 3)
N$e3_dev_max <- pct(max(e3_dev), 1)
N$b3_verdict <- if (b3_pass) "The policy passes branch 3." else "The policy fails branch 3."

kable(data.frame(
  Method = c("Welch t-test (no adjustment)", "Bootstrap, 2,000 samples", "CUPED with history", "Regression adjustment, all features"),
  `Effect on spend` = c(N$e3_unadj, N$e3_unadj, N$e3_cuped, N$e3_reg),
  `95% CI` = c(N$e2_ci, N$e3_boot, "", ""),
  `Change against no adjustment` = c("", "", pct(e3_dev[["B"]], 1), pct(e3_dev[["C"]], 1)),
  Rule = c("", "The CI excludes 0", "Within 10%", "Within 10%"), check.names = FALSE),
  row.names = FALSE, align = "lrrrl")
Method Effect on spend 95% CI Change against no adjustment Rule
Welch t-test (no adjustment) $0.770 [$0.49, $1.05]
Bootstrap, 2,000 samples $0.770 [$0.48, $1.06] The CI excludes 0
CUPED with history $0.767 0.3% Within 10%
Regression adjustment, all features $0.769 0.1% Within 10%

The bootstrap 95% CI is [$0.48, $1.06], almost the same as the Welch CI, and it excludes 0. The CUPED effect is $0.767, and the regression effect is $0.769. The unadjusted effect is $0.770. The largest change is 0.3%, against the limit of 10%. The policy passes branch 3.

6d. Branch 4: business value

The question: does the recommended policy make money, also at the low end of the effect? A positive effect is not sufficient. Each email has a contact cost, so the effect must be more than the breakeven effect. The rule uses the base margin of 30% (as-01) and the base contact cost of $0.10 (as-02), for one campaign of 100,000 customers (as-04).

Technical note. For a campaign of n customers, with margin m, contact cost c and spend effect u, the incremental profit is n × (m × u − c). The profit is a straight line in u. Thus the 95% CI of the profit comes directly from the Welch 95% CI of u. The breakeven effect is c / m.

Branch 4: incremental profit of the men’s email to all, with its 95% CI 
# Purpose: Measure branch 4 (business value) at the base margin and contact cost (as-01, as-02, as-04).
# Input:   `ATE`, `ATE_LO`, `ATE_HI`, `MARGIN`, `COST`, `CAMPAIGN`.
# Output:  `e4_prof` (profit, lower end, upper end), `b4_pass`, N$e4_*.

# Profit = customers x (margin x effect - contact cost). The CI of the effect gives the CI of the profit.
e4_prof <- CAMPAIGN * (MARGIN * c(est = ATE[["mens"]], lo = ATE_LO[["mens"]], hi = ATE_HI[["mens"]]) - COST)
b4_pass <- e4_prof[["est"]] > 0 && e4_prof[["lo"]] > 0
N$e4_prof <- usd(e4_prof[["est"]], 0)
N$e4_ci <- ci_txt(e4_prof[["lo"]], e4_prof[["hi"]], function(x) usd(x, 0))
N$e4_be <- usd(COST / MARGIN)
N$e4_lo_eff <- usd(ATE_LO[["mens"]])
N$e4_cost <- usd(COST)
N$e4_margin <- pct(MARGIN, 0)
N$e4_campaign <- num(CAMPAIGN)
N$b4_verdict <- if (b4_pass) "The policy passes branch 4." else "The policy fails branch 4."

kable(data.frame(
  Check = c("Incremental profit for 100,000 customers", "95% CI of the profit", "Breakeven effect (contact cost / margin)",
            "Lower end of the 95% CI of the effect"),
  Result = c(N$e4_prof, N$e4_ci, N$e4_be, N$e4_lo_eff),
  Rule = c("More than 0", "Lower end more than 0", "", "More than the breakeven effect"), check.names = FALSE),
  row.names = FALSE, align = "lrl")
Check Result Rule
Incremental profit for 100,000 customers $13,095 More than 0
95% CI of the profit [$4,554, $21,635] Lower end more than 0
Breakeven effect (contact cost / margin) $0.33
Lower end of the 95% CI of the effect $0.49 More than the breakeven effect

At a margin of 30% and a contact cost of $0.10, the men’s email to all gives $13,095 for 100,000 customers. The 95% CI of the profit is [$4,554, $21,635]. The lower end of the effect, $0.49, is above the breakeven effect of $0.33. The policy passes branch 4. The margin and the contact cost are assumptions, so Step 7c changes them.

6e. Branch 5: targeting

The question: can a smaller list of customers make more money than “send to all”? Step 5 showed that the top history quartile has the largest uplift. If the contact cost is high, an email to the low quartiles can lose money. The rule of Step 3a has two parts:

  • Model rule. An ML uplift model replaces “rank by history” only if two conditions are true. Its mean Qini area is 20% or more higher, and its area is more than 0 in at least 9 of 10 repeats. The evidence comes from Step 4d.
  • Policy rule. A targeting rule replaces “send to all” only if the 90% interval of its gain is above 0 at the base contact cost.

The recommended policy passes if it follows both rules. The policy rule compares two targeting rules with “send to all”:

  • Top 25% by history. The email goes only to the top history quartile.
  • Breakeven rule by history quartile. The email goes to a quartile only if the margin on its cross-fitted uplift is more than the contact cost.

The code calculates the profit of each rule for six contact costs, from $0.05 to $0.30. Branch 5 uses only the base cost. Step 7a uses the full table to select the targeting rule for other costs. Thus this table is also the evidence for that decision.

Technical note. The profit of a rule for each customer in the campaign is s × (m × û − c). Here s is the share of customers that the rule selects. The value û is the mean spend of the treated customers minus the mean spend of the control customers in that selection.

The breakeven rule uses the cross-fitted uplift of each history quartile, with 5 folds. Thus each customer gets an uplift from folds that do not contain that customer. The 90% interval of the gain comes from 500 bootstrap samples of the customers. Each rule and each cost use the same samples, so the code compares the rules on the same data.

Branch 5 and the evidence for the targeting rule: profit of each rule at six contact costs 
# Purpose: Measure branch 5 (targeting): the model rule (Qini area, dec-06) and the policy rule (gain against
#          "send to all", 90% bootstrap interval). The table is also the evidence for dec-07 (Step 7a).
# Input:   `m` with `t`, `spend`, `hq` (contracts C4, C5), `area`, `MARGIN`, `COST`, `CAMPAIGN`, `SEED`.
# Output:  Contract C6: `policy_profit`, `u_q`, `all_sel`, `top_q`, `dec07`, `k100`. Also `boot_idx`,
#          `b5_model`, `b5_policy`, `b5_pass`, N$b5_*. Existing N names of dec-07 (a_base, cost_sig and others).

# Helper of case03_helpers.R. The definition below is the same, for a run without that file.
if (!exists("policy_profit")) {
  policy_profit <- function(sel, y, t, cost, margin = MARGIN) {
    # Profit for each customer in the campaign. Customers outside the selection get no email.
    share <- mean(sel)
    if (share == 0) return(0)
    eff <- mean(y[sel & t == 1]) - mean(y[sel & t == 0])
    share * (margin * eff - cost)
  }
}

# --- Model rule (dec-06 evidence): ML models against rank by history ---
# Columns of `area`: A rank by history, B segment table, C T-learner, D uplift tree (Step 4d).
area_mean <- colMeans(area)
b5_model <- data.frame(
  model = c("B", "C", "D"),
  gain = area_mean[c("B", "C", "D")] / area_mean[["A"]] - 1,
  pos = colSums(area[, c("B", "C", "D")] > 0))
b5_model$replaces <- b5_model$gain >= RULES$b5_model_gain & b5_model$pos >= RULES$b5_model_pos
ml_models <- c("C", "D")  # The T-learner and the uplift tree are the ML models. B is a table of means.
model_ok <- !any(b5_model$replaces[b5_model$model %in% ml_models])

# --- Policy rule: targeting rules against "send to all" ---
# Cross-fitted uplift of each history quartile (5 folds)
set.seed(SEED + 1)
fold <- sample(rep(1:5, length.out = nrow(m)))
u_q <- numeric(nrow(m))
for (k in 1:5) {
  tr <- m[fold != k, ]; te <- fold == k
  uu <- tapply(tr$spend[tr$t == 1], tr$hq[tr$t == 1], mean) - tapply(tr$spend[tr$t == 0], tr$hq[tr$t == 0], mean)
  u_q[te] <- uu[as.character(m$hq[te])]
}

COSTS <- c(0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.20, 0.25, 0.30)
all_sel <- rep(TRUE, nrow(m))
top_q <- m$hq == "Q4 (highest)"
# The same 500 bootstrap samples for each rule and each cost: the gains are paired.
set.seed(SEED)
boot_idx <- replicate(500, sample.int(nrow(m), replace = TRUE), simplify = FALSE)
boot_gain <- function(sel, cst) {
  # 90% bootstrap interval of the gain of a rule against "send to all", for each customer.
  g <- sapply(boot_idx, function(i) policy_profit(sel[i], m$spend[i], m$t[i], cst) - policy_profit(all_sel[i], m$spend[i], m$t[i], cst))
  quantile(g, c((1 - RULES$b5_policy_level) / 2, (1 + RULES$b5_policy_level) / 2))
}

dec07 <- do.call(rbind, lapply(COSTS, function(cst) {
  sel_c <- MARGIN * u_q > cst
  ib <- boot_gain(top_q, cst); ic <- boot_gain(sel_c, cst)
  data.frame(cost = cst, a = policy_profit(all_sel, m$spend, m$t, cst), b = policy_profit(top_q, m$spend, m$t, cst),
             c = policy_profit(sel_c, m$spend, m$t, cst), share_c = mean(sel_c),
             b_lo = ib[[1]], b_hi = ib[[2]], c_lo = ic[[1]], c_hi = ic[[2]])
}))
k100 <- function(x) usd(CAMPAIGN * x, 0)  # Profit for each customer -> profit for one campaign
iv <- function(lo, hi) ci_txt(CAMPAIGN * lo, CAMPAIGN * hi, function(x) usd(x, 0))

# Branch 5 at the base contact cost (as-02)
base <- dec07[dec07$cost == COST, ]
b5_policy <- c(top = base$b_lo > 0, rule = base$c_lo > 0)  # TRUE: the rule replaces "send to all"
b5_pass <- model_ok && !any(b5_policy)

# Existing N names of the dec-07 evidence (the decision text of Step 7a and the summary use them)
N$a_base <- k100(base$a)
N$b_base <- k100(base$b)
N$c_share_base <- pct(base$share_c, 0)
N$c_base_gain <- k100(base$c - base$a)
sig_b <- dec07$cost[dec07$b_lo > 0]
N$has_sig <- length(sig_b) > 0
N$cost_sig <- if (N$has_sig) usd(min(sig_b)) else "more than $0.30"
N$b_gain_030 <- k100(dec07$b[dec07$cost == 0.30] - dec07$a[dec07$cost == 0.30])
N$c_vs_b_030 <- if (dec07$c[dec07$cost == 0.30] < dec07$b[dec07$cost == 0.30]) "less" else "more"
N$cost_zero_all <- usd(MARGIN * ATE[["mens"]])

# New N names of branch 5
fmt_gain <- function(g) paste0(ifelse(g >= 0, "+", ""), pct(g, 0))
N$b5_area_a <- usd(area_mean[["A"]], 3)
best_ml <- ml_models[which.max(area_mean[ml_models])]  # The ML model with the largest mean Qini area
N$b5_best_ml <- c(C = "the T-learner", D = "the uplift tree")[[best_ml]]
N$b5_best_ml_gain <- fmt_gain(b5_model$gain[b5_model$model == best_ml])
N$b5_best_ml_pos <- b5_model$pos[b5_model$model == best_ml]
N$b5_seg_gain <- fmt_gain(b5_model$gain[b5_model$model == "B"])
N$b5_seg_pos <- b5_model$pos[b5_model$model == "B"]
N$b5_top_iv <- iv(base$b_lo, base$b_hi)
N$b5_rule_iv <- iv(base$c_lo, base$c_hi)
N$b5_model_txt <- if (model_ok) "No ML model passes the model rule, so rank by history stays." else
  "An ML model passes the model rule, so it must replace rank by history."
N$b5_policy_txt <- if (!any(b5_policy)) "No targeting rule passes the policy rule at the base cost, so \"send to all\" stays." else
  "A targeting rule passes the policy rule at the base cost, so it must replace \"send to all\"."
N$b5_verdict <- if (b5_pass) "The policy passes branch 5." else "The policy fails branch 5."

# Table 1: the model rule
kable(data.frame(
  Option = c("B. Segment table", "C. T-learner", "D. Uplift tree"),
  `ML model` = c("No", "Yes", "Yes"),
  `Mean Qini area` = usd(area_mean[c("B", "C", "D")], 3),
  `Change against rank by history` = fmt_gain(b5_model$gain),
  `Repeats with area > 0` = paste(b5_model$pos, "of", nrow(area)),
  `Replaces rank by history` = ifelse(b5_model$replaces, "Yes", "No"), check.names = FALSE),
  row.names = FALSE, align = "llrrrl",
  caption = paste0("Model rule. Rank by history has a mean Qini area of ", N$b5_area_a, "."))
Model rule. Rank by history has a mean Qini area of $0.083.

C. T-learner Yes -$0.029 -135% 3 of 10 No
D. Uplift tree Yes -$0.019 -123% 0 of 10 No
Branch 5 and the evidence for the targeting rule: profit of each rule at six contact costs 
# Table 2: the policy rule, for each contact cost (Step 7a uses the full table)
kable(data.frame(`Contact cost` = usd(dec07$cost),
                 `A. Send to all` = k100(dec07$a),
                 `B. Top 25%` = k100(dec07$b),
                 `B minus A, 90% interval` = iv(dec07$b_lo, dec07$b_hi),
                 `C. Breakeven rule` = k100(dec07$c),
                 `C sends to` = pct(dec07$share_c, 0),
                 `C minus A, 90% interval` = iv(dec07$c_lo, dec07$c_hi), check.names = FALSE),
      row.names = FALSE, align = "rrrrrrr",
      caption = "Policy rule. Profit for 100,000 customers. Branch 5 uses the row of the base contact cost ($0.10).")

Model rule. Rank by history has a mean Qini area of $0.083. The best ML model is the uplift tree, with a change of -123% against the limit of +20%. Its area is more than 0 in 0 of 10 repeats. No ML model passes the model rule, so rank by history stays. The segment table is not an ML model. For information, its change is -18%, with an area more than 0 in 10 of 10 repeats.

Policy rule. At the base contact cost, “send to all” gives $13,095 for 100,000 customers. The top 25% gives $7,924, and the 90% interval of its gain is [-$11,245, $11]. The breakeven rule sends to 90% of the customers, and the interval of its gain is [-$6,383, -$1,621]. No targeting rule passes the policy rule at the base cost, so “send to all” stays.

The policy passes branch 5. The result depends on the contact cost. The gain of the top 25% is above 0 with 90% confidence from a contact cost of $0.25. Step 7a uses this result for the targeting rule.

6f. Summary of the evaluation

The table collects one result for each branch, with the rule of Step 3a.

Summary: the recommended policy against the rule of each branch 
# Purpose: Collect the result of the recommended policy (men's email to all) for each branch (6a–6e).
# Input:   Results of sections 6a–6e.
# Output:  Table `evaluation`, N$n_pass, N$fail_list.

evaluation <- data.frame(
  Branch = c("1. Validity", "2. Effect", "3. Robustness", "4. Business value", "5. Targeting"),
  Metric = c("Largest absolute standardized difference; sample-ratio p-value",
             "Welch 95% CI of the spend effect; customers in each group / customers for 80% power",
             "Bootstrap 95% CI; largest change of the CUPED and the regression effect",
             "Profit for 100,000 customers, with its 95% CI",
             "Best ML model against rank by history (Qini area); 90% interval of the gain of the top 25% at $0.10"),
  Result = c(paste0(N$e1_smd, "; ", N$e1_srm),
             paste0(N$e2_ci, "; ", N$e2_have, " / ", N$e2_need),
             paste0(N$e3_boot, "; ", N$e3_dev_max),
             paste0(N$e4_prof, " ", N$e4_ci),
             paste0(N$b5_best_ml_gain, ", ", N$b5_best_ml_pos, " of 10; ", N$b5_top_iv)),
  Rule = c("Less than 0.05; more than 0.01",
           "Excludes 0; at least the customers for 80% power",
           "Excludes 0; within 10%",
           "More than 0; lower end more than 0",
           "+20% or more and 9 of 10; interval above 0 (then targeting replaces send to all)"),
  Pass = ifelse(c(b1_pass, b2_pass, b3_pass, b4_pass, b5_pass), "Yes", "No"))
failed <- tolower(sub("^\\d\\. ", "", evaluation$Branch[evaluation$Pass == "No"]))
N$n_pass <- sum(evaluation$Pass == "Yes")
N$fail_list <- if (length(failed)) paste(failed, collapse = ", ") else "none"
kable(evaluation, row.names = FALSE, align = "lllll")

2. Effect Welch 95% CI of the spend effect; customers in each group / customers for 80% power [$0.49, $1.05]; 21,306 / 5,988 Excludes 0; at least the customers for 80% power Yes
3. Robustness Bootstrap 95% CI; largest change of the CUPED and the regression effect [$0.48, $1.06]; 0.3% Excludes 0; within 10% Yes

The recommended policy passes 5 of the 5 branches. The branches that fail are: none.

Two results need attention, also when a branch passes:

  • Power (branch 2). The test has 3.6 times the customers for 80% power at the effect of the men’s email. A test of one segment has fewer customers, so it cannot find an effect of this size.
  • Contact cost (branches 4 and 5). Both results use the base contact cost of $0.10 (as-02). The data does not give this cost. At $0.25 or more, the top 25% by history beats “send to all”.

Business note. The men’s email to all customers passes 5 of the 5 branches of the evaluation framework. It gives $13,095 for each campaign of 100,000 customers (95% CI [$4,554, $21,635]). At the base contact cost, no targeting rule and no ML model beats “send to all”. The full contact cost decides the targeting rule, and the data does not give it. Step 7 changes this result into a policy for each contact cost, a dollar value and a rollout plan.

Step 7. Implementation

Step 6 showed that the men’s email to all customers passes 5 of the 5 branches of the evaluation framework. At the base contact cost, no targeting rule beats “send to all”. But the contact cost is an assumption (as-02), and the data does not give it. A result on test data is not yet a policy.

This step answers four questions. Which rule selects the customers at each contact cost? How much money does the policy make? Does the choice hold for other margins and costs? How do we confirm the result after the launch?

Purpose. This step changes the evaluation into a targeting rule, a dollar value and a rollout plan. It supports this decision: launch the men’s email to all customers with a holdout, and the contact cost at which the list becomes shorter.

7a. From result to policy

A test gives the effect of the email. A policy says which customers get the email. The breakeven rule links the two. It sends the email to a customer only if the incremental margin is more than the contact cost. At a margin of 30% and a contact cost of $0.10, the breakeven effect is $0.33 of spend for each customer.

Technical note. The breakeven rule sends the email to a customer if m × û(q) > c. Here m is the margin (as-01) and c is the contact cost (as-02). The value û(q) is the cross-fitted uplift of the history quartile q of the customer (Step 5). A rule with a fixed list, for example the top 25% by history, does not use c. Its profit falls more slowly with c, because it sends fewer emails.

Which rule selects the customers for the email?

Why this question matters. The contact cost decides if an email to a customer with a small uplift pays for itself. If the list is too long, the emails to customers with a small uplift lose money. If the list is too short, the policy loses the profit of customers who buy because of the email.

Ways to do it. A rule can select the customers with four kinds of information. Each kind adds information to the kind before it:

Information that the rule uses Rule Advantage Main risk
None A. Send to all customers. (No email to any customer is the other rule with no information.) Simple. No estimate to trust. It gets all of the positive mean effect. It sends to customers where the email can lose money. “No email” loses the profit of branch 4, so we screen it out.
A fixed share by history B. Top 25% by history Simple. A quarter of the contact cost. It keeps the quartile with the largest uplift. The list does not change with the contact cost.
The uplift of each quartile and the contact cost C. Breakeven rule by history quartile It sends only where the margin is more than the cost. The list changes with the cost. It depends on four noisy estimates and on the contact cost.
The uplift of each customer from an ML model T-learner or uplift tree It can find customers that history does not show. No ML model beats rank by history (branch 5, Step 4d). We screen it out.

Evidence. The policy-rule table of Step 6e gives the profit of rules A, B and C for 100,000 customers at six contact costs. It also gives the 90% interval of the gain of B and C against A. The chart below shows the profit of each rule for each contact cost from $0 to $0.35. It also gives the contact cost at which rule B starts to give more than rule A.

Chart: profit for 100,000 customers against the contact cost, for the three rules 
# Purpose: Show the profit of each targeting rule against the contact cost (dec-07, as-02).
# Input:   `policy_profit`, `all_sel`, `top_q`, `u_q`, `m`, `MARGIN`, `COST`, `CAMPAIGN`, `N`, `CS`.
# Output:  Line chart, N$cost_cross (contact cost where the top 25% starts to beat "send to all").

cost_grid <- seq(0, 0.35, 0.01)
prof <- sapply(cost_grid, function(cst) c(all = policy_profit(all_sel, m$spend, m$t, cst),
                                          top = policy_profit(top_q, m$spend, m$t, cst),
                                          rule = policy_profit(MARGIN * u_q > cst, m$spend, m$t, cst)))
prof_k <- CAMPAIGN * prof / 1000  # $ thousand for one campaign

# Profit of a fixed list is a straight line in the cost: p(c) = p(0) - share x c. Thus the two lines cross at
# c = (p_all(0) - p_top(0)) / (1 - share of the top 25%).
cost_cross <- (policy_profit(all_sel, m$spend, m$t, 0) - policy_profit(top_q, m$spend, m$t, 0)) / (1 - mean(top_q))
N$cost_cross <- usd(cost_cross)

cs_setup(mar = c(3.6, 4.6, 0.6, 9.5))
plot(cost_grid, prof_k["all", ], type = "n", ylim = range(0, prof_k), xlim = c(0, 0.35),
     xlab = "Full contact cost of one email ($)", ylab = "Profit for 100,000 customers ($ thousand)")
abline(h = 0, col = CS$light_gray)
# The base contact cost (as-02) as a reference line
abline(v = COST, col = CS$gray, lty = 2)
text(COST, par("usr")[4], paste0(" Base cost ", usd(COST), " (as-02)"), adj = c(0, 1), cex = 0.75, col = CS$muted)
lines(cost_grid, prof_k["rule", ], col = CS$gray, lwd = 1.8)
lines(cost_grid, prof_k["top", ], col = CS$cyan, lwd = 2.2)
lines(cost_grid, prof_k["all", ], col = CS$navy, lwd = 2.5)
# The one point: the cost where the top 25% starts to give more than "send to all"
y_cross <- CAMPAIGN * policy_profit(top_q, m$spend, m$t, cost_cross) / 1000
points(cost_cross, y_cross, pch = 19, col = CS$blue, cex = 1.3)
text(cost_cross, y_cross, paste0("  Lines cross at ", N$cost_cross), adj = c(0, -0.8), cex = 0.8, col = CS$blue, font = 2)
# Direct labels at the line ends. Move labels apart if the ends are near each other.
n_end <- length(cost_grid)
ends <- prof_k[, n_end]
dy <- c(all = 0, top = 0, rule = 0)
if (abs(ends["top"] - ends["rule"]) < 0.06 * diff(range(prof_k))) dy[c("top", "rule")] <- if (ends["top"] >= ends["rule"]) c(0.7, -0.7) else c(-0.7, 0.7)
cs_label_end(0.35, ends["all"], "A. Send to all", col = CS$navy, bold = TRUE, dy = dy["all"])
cs_label_end(0.35, ends["top"], "B. Top 25% by history", col = CS$cyan, dy = dy["top"])
cs_label_end(0.35, ends["rule"], "C. Breakeven rule", col = CS$gray, dy = dy["rule"])
cs_title(paste0("Send to all earns the most until the contact cost passes ", N$cost_cross),
         "Profit for one campaign of 100,000 customers, men's email, margin 30% (as-01)")

How to read: each line is one rule. The x-axis is the full cost of one email, and the dashed line marks the base cost of $0.10. The blue point is the cost where the top 25% starts to give more than “send to all”.

So what: at the base cost, “send to all” gives the most profit, $13,095 for 100,000 customers. Above $0.17, the top 25% by history gives more, but the gain is reliable only from $0.25.

Decision. At the base contact cost of $0.10, rule A: send the men’s email to all customers. If the full contact cost is $0.25 or more, use rule B: send only to the top 25% by history.

Why. At $0.10, rule A gives $13,095 for 100,000 customers, and rule B gives $7,924. Each quartile is still profitable at this cost, so a shorter list loses money. Rule C gives -$3,885 against rule A, because the noise of the quartile estimates excludes some profitable customers.

Between $0.17 and $0.25, rule B gives more on the point estimate, but the 90% interval of its gain contains 0. From $0.25, the interval is above 0, so the policy rule of branch 5 lets rule B replace rule A. At $0.30, rule B gives $9,830 more than rule A, and rule C gives less than rule B.

What would change the decision. The contact cost decides the choice. If Marketing confirms a full cost of $0.25 or more, use rule B. A cost of this size is possible if the unsubscribe rate is high, or if the offer has a discount. If the contact cost is more than $0.23, “send to all” loses money. If a new test has many more buyers, compare the ML models again (Step 4d).

7b. Dollar impact

The dollar impact uses the decision of 7a at the base cost: the men’s email to all customers. The formula is: incremental profit = 100,000 × (0.30 × change in mean spend − $0.10). The table compares this policy with the women’s email to all and with no email.

Dollar impact for one campaign of 100,000 customers 
# Purpose: Give the dollar impact of each version for one campaign (as-01, as-02, as-04).
# Input:   `ATE`, `ATE_LO`, `ATE_HI`, `MARGIN`, `COST`, `CAMPAIGN`.
# Output:  Contract C6: `d_m`, `d_w` (profit for each customer). Table `imp`, N$imp_*.

d_w <- MARGIN * ATE[["womens"]] - COST
d_m <- MARGIN * ATE[["mens"]] - COST
ci_prof <- function(a) ci_txt(CAMPAIGN * (MARGIN * ATE_LO[[a]] - COST), CAMPAIGN * (MARGIN * ATE_HI[[a]] - COST), function(x) usd(x, 0))
imp <- data.frame(
  Policy = c("No email", "Women's email to all", "Men's email to all (recommended)"),
  `Emails sent` = num(CAMPAIGN * c(0, 1, 1)),
  `Incremental spend` = usd(CAMPAIGN * c(0, ATE[["womens"]], ATE[["mens"]]), 0),
  `Incremental margin` = usd(CAMPAIGN * MARGIN * c(0, ATE[["womens"]], ATE[["mens"]]), 0),
  `Contact cost` = usd(CAMPAIGN * COST * c(0, 1, 1), 0),
  `Incremental profit` = usd(CAMPAIGN * c(0, d_w, d_m), 0),
  `95% CI of the profit` = c("", ci_prof("womens"), ci_prof("mens")),
  check.names = FALSE)
kable(imp, row.names = FALSE, align = "lrrrrrr")
Policy Emails sent Incremental spend Incremental margin Contact cost Incremental profit 95% CI of the profit
No email 0 $0 $0 $0 $0
Women’s email to all 100,000 $42,441 $12,732 $10,000 $2,732 [-$4,931, $10,396]
Men’s email to all (recommended) 100,000 $76,983 $23,095 $10,000 $13,095 [$4,554, $21,635]
Dollar impact for one campaign of 100,000 customers 
N$imp_m <- usd(CAMPAIGN * d_m, 0)
N$imp_diff <- usd(CAMPAIGN * (d_m - d_w), 0)
N$imp_m_lo <- usd(CAMPAIGN * (MARGIN * ATE_LO[["mens"]] - COST), 0)
N$imp_m_hi <- usd(CAMPAIGN * (MARGIN * ATE_HI[["mens"]] - COST), 0)
N$imp_roi <- formatC(MARGIN * ATE[["mens"]] / COST, format = "f", digits = 1)

The men’s email to all gives $13,095 for each campaign of 100,000 customers. The 95% CI of the effect gives a range of $4,554 to $21,635. Each $1 of contact cost gives 2.3 dollars of incremental margin. The men’s email gives $10,362 more than the women’s email. At the base cost, the version is the lever. The targeting rule adds money only at a high contact cost.

7c. Sensitivity check

The margin (as-01) and the contact cost (as-02) are assumptions. The check changes both and gives the profit of the two simple rules. The “Indicated choice” column uses a simple rule: the top 25% must give 25% more profit than “send to all”. This margin protects the choice against the noise of the estimate.

Sensitivity: profit of each rule by margin and contact cost 
# Purpose: Show how the margin (as-01) and the contact cost (as-02) change the choice of dec-07.
# Input:   `policy_profit`, `all_sel`, `top_q`, `m`, `k100`.
# Output:  Contract C6: `grid` (profit and indicated choice for each combination). N$n_all, N$n_grid, N$n_top.

grid <- expand.grid(cost = c(0.05, 0.10, 0.20, 0.30), margin = c(0.20, 0.30, 0.40))
grid$all <- mapply(function(mg, cst) policy_profit(all_sel, m$spend, m$t, cst, mg), grid$margin, grid$cost)
grid$top <- mapply(function(mg, cst) policy_profit(top_q, m$spend, m$t, cst, mg), grid$margin, grid$cost)
# The top 25% must give 25% more than "send to all", as a protection against noise.
grid$choice <- ifelse(pmax(grid$all, grid$top) <= 0, "No email",
                      ifelse(grid$top - grid$all > 0.25 * abs(grid$all), "Top 25% by history", "Send to all"))
kable(data.frame(Margin = pct(grid$margin, 0), `Contact cost` = usd(grid$cost),
                 `Profit, send to all` = k100(grid$all), `Profit, top 25%` = k100(grid$top),
                 `Indicated choice` = grid$choice, check.names = FALSE),
      row.names = FALSE, align = "rrrrl")
