Assumption check. The contact cost (as-02) has the largest effect on the choice. “Send to all” is the choice in 7 of 12 combinations. It is the choice in each combination with a contact cost of $0.10 or less. The top 25% is the choice in 4 combinations, all with a high cost or a low margin. “No email” is the choice in 1 combinations. Confirm the full contact cost with Marketing before the launch.

7d. Rollout

The test result covers two weeks (as-03). After the launch, the effect can become smaller, and customers can unsubscribe. A holdout is a random group of customers that gets no email after the launch. It shows the effect of the email over time, with the same causal logic as the test.

Which share of customers do we keep as a holdout after the launch?

Why this question matters. Each customer in the holdout gets no email, so the holdout costs profit. A holdout that is too small cannot show if the email still pays for itself. Then a fall of the effect stays hidden, and the campaign can lose money for months.

Ways to do it. The size of the holdout is one number. Thus the options are points on one scale: none, small, medium and large.

Option Advantage Disadvantage
A. No holdout No lost profit. We cannot see if the effect becomes smaller or if customers unsubscribe. We screen it out.
B. 5% holdout Small lost profit. Less power.
C. 10% holdout Good power to show that the email still pays for itself. More lost profit.
D. 20% holdout Most power. Twice the lost profit of option C.

Evidence. The holdout must show that the email still pays for itself. Thus the test asks: is the effect more than the breakeven effect of $0.33? The table gives the power of this test for one campaign of 100,000 customers, with a one-sided test at 5%. The lost profit is the profit that the holdout customers do not give.

Technical note. Let s be the standard deviation of spend in the test, n the customers of the campaign and h the share of the holdout. The standard error of the effect is se = s × √(1 / (n(1 − h)) + 1 / (nh)). The power to show an effect above the breakeven effect b, if the true effect is u, is Φ((u − b) / se − z₀.₉₅).

Evidence: power and lost profit of each holdout size 
# Purpose: Compare the power and the lost profit of each holdout size (dec-08).
# Input:   `m`, `COST`, `MARGIN`, `CAMPAIGN`, `ALPHA`, `ATE`, `d_m`.
# Output:  Contract C6: `sd_spend`. N$pow_*, N$lost_*, N$hw_10, N$hold_pct.

sd_spend <- sqrt(mean(tapply(m$spend, m$t, var)))
be <- COST / MARGIN
hold <- c(0.05, 0.10, 0.20)
se_h <- sapply(hold, function(h) sd_spend * sqrt(1 / (CAMPAIGN * (1 - h)) + 1 / (CAMPAIGN * h)))
# One-sided test: is the effect more than the breakeven effect?
pow <- function(true_eff) pnorm((true_eff - be) / se_h - qnorm(1 - ALPHA))
kable(data.frame(Option = c("B. 5%", "C. 10%", "D. 20%"),
                 `Holdout customers` = num(CAMPAIGN * hold),
                 `Half-width of the 95% CI` = usd(qnorm(1 - ALPHA / 2) * se_h),
                 `Power if the effect stays at the test result` = pct(pow(ATE[["mens"]]), 0),
                 `Power if the effect falls by 20%` = pct(pow(0.8 * ATE[["mens"]]), 0),
                 `Lost profit for each campaign` = usd(CAMPAIGN * hold * d_m, 0), check.names = FALSE),
      row.names = FALSE, align = "lrrrrr")
Option Holdout customers Half-width of the 95% CI Power if the effect stays at the test result Power if the effect falls by 20% Lost profit for each campaign
B. 5% 5,000 $0.43 64% 36% $655
C. 10% 10,000 $0.31 87% 56% $1,309
D. 20% 20,000 $0.23 98% 77% $2,619
Evidence: power and lost profit of each holdout size 
N$pow_10 <- pct(pow(ATE[["mens"]])[2], 0); N$pow_5 <- pct(pow(ATE[["mens"]])[1], 0); N$pow_20 <- pct(pow(ATE[["mens"]])[3], 0)
N$pow_10_fall <- pct(pow(0.8 * ATE[["mens"]])[2], 0)
N$lost_10 <- usd(CAMPAIGN * 0.10 * d_m, 0); N$lost_20 <- usd(CAMPAIGN * 0.20 * d_m, 0)
N$hw_10 <- usd(qnorm(1 - ALPHA / 2) * se_h[2])
N$hold_pct <- pct(hold[2], 0)  # The choice of dec-08 (option C)

Decision. Option C, a 10% holdout.

Why. If the effect stays at the test result, a 10% holdout shows that the email pays for itself with 87% power. A 5% holdout gives only 64%. A 20% holdout gives 98%, but it doubles the lost profit to $2,619. The lost profit of option C is $1,309 for each campaign. This is a small price to know if the email still makes money.

If the effect falls by 20%, the power of a 10% holdout is only 56% in one campaign. Thus the kill criteria below use two campaigns, not one.

What would change the decision. If a campaign has more than 200,000 customers, use 5%, because the holdout keeps the same number of customers. If the campaigns repeat each month, combine the holdouts of two or three campaigns.

Metrics and kill criteria

The holdout gives the primary metric for each campaign. The table gives the metrics, the limits and the action for each limit.

Metric Type Target or limit Action
Incremental spend for each customer (email group minus holdout) Primary More than $0.33 (the breakeven effect at $0.10) If it is less for two campaigns, stop “send to all”. Send only to the top 25% by history.
Conversion rate Secondary More than the holdout If the spend effect falls but conversion stays, examine the order size.
Unsubscribe rate Guardrail Less than 0.5 points more than the holdout. Confirm with Marketing. If it is more, update the contact cost (as-02). Then use the targeting rule of 7a again.
Complaints Guardrail No increase Stop the campaign.

Business note. At the base contact cost, send the men’s email to all customers. It gives $13,095 for each campaign of 100,000 customers (range $4,554 to $21,635). If the full contact cost is $0.25 or more, send only to the top 25% by history. Keep a 10% holdout. It costs $1,309 for each campaign.

If the effect stays below $0.33 for two campaigns, stop “send to all”. Part 2 shows how other teams can use the same method.

Part 2: Use in other teams

Steps 0 to 7 used one randomized test to answer one marketing question. The method has four parts: a random split, a primary metric with sufficient power, the effect in dollars, and a holdout after the launch. Case 01 left two questions that historical data cannot answer, because each loan got only one price and one collection treatment. Part 2 shows how the same method answers them.

Purpose. This part shows how the method of this notebook applies to two open questions of case 01. It supports these decisions: the design of a pricing test, and the design of a collections test.

The two questions come from the revised case 01. The next chunk records its facts, so that the text and the power calculation use the same values.

Facts from the revised case 01: rate increase for zero NPV, default rates, volumes, recoveries 
# Purpose: Record the facts of the revised case 01 that Part 2 uses (Part 2: Pricing, Part 2: Recoveries).
# Input:   None. The values come from case 01 (2015 loans of Lending Club, prices of 2015).
# Output:  `rate_up` (points of interest rate for zero NPV, by grade), `pricing` (grades A–C), `rec01`, N$p2_*.

# Increase of the interest rate (points) that makes the NPV of the 2015 loans equal to zero, by grade
rate_up <- c(A = 0.3, B = 0.1, C = 1.0, D = 2.7, E = 6.0, F = 12.9, G = 19.7)
# Grades A–C: the pricing test of case 01 (an increase of 1 point or less)
pricing <- data.frame(grade = c("A", "B", "C"), bad = c(0.054, 0.119, 0.195), loans_2015 = c(70107, 91672, 77363))
pricing$rate_up <- rate_up[pricing$grade]
# Recoveries (Part 2: Recoveries of case 01)
rec01 <- list(rate = 0.110, top20_balance = 0.455, top20_gbm = 0.462)

N$p2_up_ac <- paste(paste0(names(rate_up)[1:3], " +", formatC(rate_up[1:3], format = "f", digits = 1)), collapse = ", ")
N$p2_up_max_ac <- formatC(max(rate_up[1:3]), format = "f", digits = 1)
N$p2_up_dg <- paste0(formatC(min(rate_up[4:7]), format = "f", digits = 1), " to ", formatC(max(rate_up[4:7]), format = "f", digits = 1))
N$p2_rec <- pct(rec01$rate)
N$p2_top_bal <- pct(rec01$top20_balance)
N$p2_top_gbm <- pct(rec01$top20_gbm)
N$p2_two_pts_a <- pct(0.02 / pricing$bad[1], 0)

Pricing test for grades A to C (case 01, Part 2: Pricing)

The question. Case 01 shows that the 2015 loans lost money in every grade at 2015 prices. The increase of the interest rate for an NPV of zero is small in grades A to C: A +0.3, B +0.1, C +1.0 points. In grades D to G, it is 2.7 to 19.7 points. The market may not accept such an increase, so a cutoff is the better tool for D to G. Thus case 01 recommends a pricing test for grades A to C only.

Why a test. A price increase can change two things that the NPV calculation keeps fixed: the default rate and the volume. The historical data cannot measure this effect, because the price depends on the risk. A borrower with a higher price is also a riskier borrower. A random test gives each applicant the old price or the new price by chance, so the difference comes from the price.

The primary metric. The default rate decides if the higher price pays for itself, so it is the primary metric. The take-up rate of the offer is the second metric, because a higher price can reduce the volume.

The detectable change. The test must find a change of the default rate that matters for the NPV. The price changes by 1.0 points or less, so the change of the default rate is probably small. A fixed change of 2 points is 37% of the grade A rate. A test for 2 points can miss a real effect in grade A. Thus we use a relative change: 10% of the 2015 default rate of each grade. Confirm the detectable change with Risk.

Technical note. The code uses power.prop.test with the default rate of the grade as p₁ and 1.1 × p₁ as p₂, at 5% significance (two-sided) and 80% power. The test has two groups of equal size: the old price and the new price. The months of volume are 2 × (loans in each group) / (loans in 2015 / 12). This value assumes that all new loans of the grade go into the test.

Power for a pricing test of grades A–C: loans in each group to find a 10% change of the default rate 
# Purpose: Size the pricing test of case 01 for grades A–C (method of Step 3c).
# Input:   `pricing`, `ALPHA`, `POWER`.
# Output:  Table `pricing` with the loans in each group and the months of volume, N$p2_*.

REL_CHANGE <- 0.10  # Detectable change: 10% of the default rate of the grade (relative)
loans_needed <- function(p, rel) ceiling(power.prop.test(p1 = p, p2 = p * (1 + rel), sig.level = ALPHA, power = POWER)$n)
pricing$delta <- pricing$bad * REL_CHANGE
pricing$n <- sapply(pricing$bad, loans_needed, rel = REL_CHANGE)
pricing$months <- 2 * pricing$n / (pricing$loans_2015 / 12)
# For comparison: a larger change of 20% needs about a quarter of the loans.
pricing$n20 <- sapply(pricing$bad, loans_needed, rel = 0.20)
pricing$months20 <- 2 * pricing$n20 / (pricing$loans_2015 / 12)

kable(data.frame(Grade = pricing$grade,
                 `Rate increase for zero NPV (points)` = formatC(pricing$rate_up, format = "f", digits = 1),
                 `Default rate 2015` = pct(pricing$bad),
                 `Detectable change (points)` = formatC(100 * pricing$delta, format = "f", digits = 2),
                 `Loans in each group` = num(pricing$n),
                 `Loans in 2015` = num(pricing$loans_2015),
                 `Months of volume for two groups` = formatC(pricing$months, format = "f", digits = 1),
                 `Months for a 20% change` = formatC(pricing$months20, format = "f", digits = 1), check.names = FALSE),
      row.names = FALSE, align = "lrrrrrrr")
Grade Rate increase for zero NPV (points) Default rate 2015 Detectable change (points) Loans in each group Loans in 2015 Months of volume for two groups Months for a 20% change
A 0.3 5.4% 0.54 28,792 70,107 9.9 2.6
B 0.1 11.9% 1.19 12,120 91,672 3.2 0.8
C 1.0 19.5% 1.95 6,721 77,363 2.1 0.5
Power for a pricing test of grades A–C: loans in each group to find a 10% change of the default rate 
mo <- setNames(pricing$months, pricing$grade)
N$p2_months_a <- formatC(mo[["A"]], format = "f", digits = 1)
N$p2_months_b <- formatC(mo[["B"]], format = "f", digits = 1)
N$p2_months_c <- formatC(mo[["C"]], format = "f", digits = 1)
N$p2_months_a20 <- formatC(pricing$months20[pricing$grade == "A"], format = "f", digits = 1)
N$p2_n_a <- num(pricing$n[pricing$grade == "A"])
N$p2_delta_a <- formatC(100 * pricing$delta[pricing$grade == "A"], format = "f", digits = 2)

Grades B and C have sufficient volume for a test in 3.2 and 2.1 months. Grade A has the lowest default rate, so a 10% change is only 0.54 points. The test needs 28,792 loans in each group, or 9.9 months of volume. If Risk accepts a change of 20% for grade A, the test needs 2.6 months.

Two limits apply to the design:

  • The lifetime default rate comes late. We know it only after 36 months. Thus the test must use an early metric, for example the default rate at 12 months on book. This rate is lower than the lifetime rate, so the test needs more loans than the table shows.
  • One price change for each grade. A test of one increase in each grade gives one point on the price curve. To find the best price, a later test can use two or three increases.

Collections test (case 01, Part 2: Recoveries)

The question. Case 01 shows that the net recovery is about 11.0% of the principal in each segment. The top 20% of charged-off loans by balance holds 45.5% of the net recovery dollars, and a GBM holds 46.2%. Thus a model does not find better accounts than a rank by balance. The real lever is the choice between a sale of the debt and in-house collection. The data cannot measure this choice, because each loan got only one treatment.

The test design. The same method as this notebook applies. Each step of this notebook has a match in the collections test:

  1. Random split. Put the charged-off loans at random into two groups: sale of the debt, and in-house collection. Use a sample-ratio check and the standardized differences of Step 6a.
  2. Primary metric. The net dollars for each $1 of principal at the charge-off, after 12 months. For a sale, it is the sale price. For in-house collection, it is the net recovery minus the cost of the collection.
  3. Effect and power. Use the Welch CI of Step 6b. The net recovery has a long right tail, like spend, so check the result with the bootstrap of Step 6c.
  4. Targeting. Rank by balance is the baseline, as rank by history is the baseline in this notebook. If a model beats this baseline with the model rule of Step 6e, use the uplift method of Step 4d.
  5. Holdout. After the decision, keep a random share of the loans with the other treatment, as in Step 7d.

Case 02 uses the same champion/challenger logic for the fraud policy: a random 10% of the transactions goes to the new policy.

Business note. The method of this notebook answers the two open questions of case 01. A pricing test for grades A to C needs about 2.1 months of grade C volume and 9.9 months of grade A volume. A collections test compares a sale of the debt with in-house collection, on loans with a random treatment. The conclusion collects the results of all steps.

Conclusion

The notebook started with two questions from leadership: do we send the email to all customers, and which version do we send? Steps 0 to 7 answered them with one randomized test. Part 2 then showed how other teams can use the same method.

The answer

Send the men’s email to all customers. It increases the mean spend by $0.77 for each customer (95% CI [$0.49, $1.05]). For each campaign of 100,000 customers, it gives $13,095 of incremental profit, with a range of $4,554 to $21,635. It gives $10,362 more than the women’s email.

The policy passes 5 of the 5 branches of the evaluation framework. The branches that fail are: none. At the base contact cost of $0.10, no targeting rule and no ML uplift model beats “send to all”. A shorter list pays only if the full contact cost is $0.25 or more.

Recommendation

  1. Send the men’s email to all customers. At the base contact cost, it gives the most profit of all rules (Step 7a).
  2. Confirm the full contact cost before the launch. If Marketing confirms a cost of $0.25 or more, send only to the top 25% by history (Step 7a). If the cost is more than $0.23, “send to all” loses money.
  3. Keep a 10% holdout. It shows with 87% power that the email still pays for itself, and it costs $1,309 for each campaign (Step 7d).
  4. Stop “send to all” if the effect falls. If the incremental spend stays below $0.33 for two campaigns, send only to the top 25% by history (Step 7d).
  5. Use the same method for the open questions of case 01. A pricing test for grades A to C, and a test of a debt sale against in-house collection (Part 2).

What a reviewer should challenge

These limits can change the result most. Each one has a control.

Limitation Effect on the result Control, or what to do next
The contact cost of $0.10 is an assumption (as-02). The data does not give unsubscribes. The contact cost decides if a targeting rule beats “send to all”. The profit chart of Step 7a and the sensitivity check of Step 7c. Measure the unsubscribe rate as a guardrail and update the cost.
The margin of 30% is an assumption (as-01). The profit changes with the margin. At a low margin and a high cost, the top 25% is the better rule. The sensitivity check of Step 7c uses 20% and 40%. Finance confirms the margin.
The effect window is two weeks (as-03). The long-term effect is not known. It can be larger or smaller. Keep the 10% holdout for three months (Step 7d).
Less than 1% of customers convert. Each segment effect has a wide interval. The ML uplift models fit noise. Rank by history. Repeat the comparison with each new test, with the model rule of Step 3a.
The gain of the top 25% at the base cost is near the limit of the policy rule. A small change of the data or of the cost can change the targeting rule. The decision uses the 90% interval, not the point estimate. Confirm the cost before a high-cost campaign.
I examined the segment effects before I selected the uplift method, on the same data. The gain of a targeting rule can be too high. The cross-fitted uplift reduces this risk. A new test confirms the rule before a high-cost campaign.
The data is from one retailer in 2008 (as-05). The size of each effect is different for a card offer. The method stays the same. Repeat the analysis on the bank data.

Other limits have a small effect. The data source cut the spend at its largest value, so a few large orders can be larger in reality. The test has only one email version for each group, so it cannot show the best combination of versions.

Next steps

  1. Business case deck (6–8 slides): the men’s email to all customers, the breakeven contact cost and the 10% holdout.
  2. Confirm the contact cost (as-02) and the margin (as-01) with Marketing and Finance.
  3. Design the pricing test for grades A to C with case 01 (Part 2: Pricing). Add it to the pricing one-pager.
  4. Design the collections test (debt sale or in-house collection) with case 01 (Part 2: Recoveries). Add it to the collections one-pager.

Appendix A: data dictionary

The table gives each column of the Hillstrom file, then each feature that this notebook codes from them. The meaning of a raw column comes from the description of the MineThatData challenge (Hillstrom, 2008). The other parts of the table come from this notebook:

  • Role. The time of the value against the email (Step 2b): a pre-test feature, the test group or an outcome. A coded feature has the role of its source.
  • Type. The type of the value in R: a flag (0 or 1), a whole number, a number, a text or a category.
  • Values. The code calculates this column from the data. A flag gives the share of 1. A number gives the range and the mean. A category gives each level with its number of customers.
  • Use. The steps of this notebook that use the column.

The coded features t and hq exist only in the analysis set m (men’s email and control group, Section 4c). Their values come from m.

Data dictionary: meaning, role, type, values and use of each column

RAW <- names(COL_ROLE)
CODED <- c(arm = "segment", buyer = "mens, womens", hseg = "history_segment", zip = "zip_code",
           lhist = "history", t = "segment", hq = "history")

col_type <- function(x) {
  # Returns the type of a column in plain words.
  if (is.factor(x)) "Category"
  else if (is.character(x)) "Text"
  else if (all(x %in% c(0, 1))) "Flag (0 or 1)"
  else if (is.integer(x) || all(x == round(x))) "Whole number"
  else "Number"
}
col_values <- function(x) {
  # Returns the values of a column, calculated from the data.
  if (is.factor(x) || is.character(x)) {
    tb <- table(x)
    paste0(names(tb), ": ", num(as.vector(tb)), collapse = "; ")
  } else if (all(x %in% c(0, 1))) {
    paste0("Share of 1: ", pct(mean(x)))
  } else {
    dg <- if (all(x == round(x))) 0 else 2  # No decimals for whole numbers
    paste0("From ", num(min(x), dg), " to ", num(max(x), dg), "; mean ", num(mean(x), 2))
  }
}

rows <- c(RAW, names(CODED))
dictionary <- data.frame(
  Column = ifelse(rows %in% RAW, rows, paste0(rows, " (coded from ", CODED[rows], ")")),
  Meaning = MEANING[rows],
  Role = ifelse(rows %in% RAW, COL_ROLE[rows],
                ifelse(rows %in% c("arm", "t"), "Test group", "Pre-test feature")),
  Type = sapply(rows, function(r) col_type(if (r %in% c("t", "hq")) m[[r]] else d[[r]])),
  Values = sapply(rows, function(r) col_values(if (r %in% c("t", "hq")) m[[r]] else d[[r]])),
  Use = USE[rows], check.names = FALSE)
# Check: each row has a meaning and a use.

Reader guides: decisions, assumptions and glossary

This appendix holds the reference material of the notebook. Click a title to open it.

NoteHow to read this notebook
  • Read the text to follow the logic. Click Show code to see the code for a step.
  • The notebook follows the steps of a model project, from Step 0 to Step 7. Part 2 applies the same method to two questions of case 01.
  • Each step starts with a gray block. This block says what the step before showed, and the question of this step.
  • A blue block records a decision. It starts with a question. Then it gives the possible methods, the evidence, the decision and the reason.
  • A gray-blue block (Technical note) gives the method in detail for a data scientist. A business reader can skip it.
  • A green block is a business note. It gives the result of a step for a manager.
  • Appendix A gives the meaning of each column in the data.
  • The business case deck gives the recommendation for leadership: decks/03-test-and-learn.pdf.

Each team can read only the part that it needs.

Part Question Team
Step 0 What is the business problem? All
Steps 1–3 Did the randomization work? Is the test large enough to find the effect that matters? Marketing, all test owners
Step 4 Does the email increase spend? Which version do we send? Does the effect change by segment? Marketing
Steps 5–6 Which customers have the largest uplift? Is the policy good enough for the launch? Marketing, model risk
Step 7 Which customers get the email? What is the dollar value? How do we confirm the result after the launch? Marketing, Finance, CX and operations
Part 2 How does the method apply to a pricing test and a collections test? Product and pricing, collections

NoteDecision log

The decision blocks in the text show only the question. This log gives each decision an ID for a model risk review. Click the question to go to the decision.

ID Question Decision Step
dec-01 Which metric decides the test? Spend. Visit and conversion are secondary metrics. 3c
dec-02 Which method measures the change in mean spend? Welch t-test. The bootstrap is a check. 4a
dec-03 Can the pre-test data make the interval smaller? No adjustment. History does not predict the spend in the test window. 4a
dec-04 Which email version do we send? The men’s email to all customers. 4b
dec-05 How do we report the effect in each segment? Interaction test first. Then the effect of each segment with the Holm correction. The evidence for different effects is weak. 4c
dec-06 Which method puts the customers in order of uplift? Rank by history. The rule before the evidence: an ML model replaces it only if its Qini area is 20% or more higher. 4d
dec-07 Which rule selects the customers for the email? Send to all at the base contact cost. Send only to the top 25% by history if the contact cost is high. 7a
dec-08 Which share of customers do we keep as a holdout after the launch? 10% 7d

NoteAssumption register
ID Assumption Value Source Effect if the value is wrong
as-01 Contribution margin on incremental spend 30% Assumption: gross margin of an apparel retailer, minus the cost of delivery and returns. Confirm with Finance. Large. The profit of each email goes up or down with the margin. The sensitivity check of Step 7c uses 20% and 40%.
as-02 Full cost of one email $0.10 Assumption: the cost to send, plus the cost of creative work, plus the future value that we lose when a customer unsubscribes. The data does not give unsubscribes. Confirm with Marketing. Large. This value decides if targeting is better than “send to all”. Step 7a gives the contact cost at which the targeting rule changes.
as-03 Effect window Two weeks after the email The test design of the dataset The long-term effect is not known. It can be larger (more future purchases) or smaller (fatigue).
as-04 Size of one campaign 100,000 customers Assumption, for the dollar values No effect on the decision. The dollar values scale with the number of customers.
as-05 Proxy An email from a retailer to its customers is a proxy for a card offer to card customers The public data has no bank test The size of each effect is different for a bank. The method stays the same.

NoteGlossary

The words in this table are technical names. The notebook uses each name only with the meaning below.

Technical name Meaning in this notebook
A/B test A test that puts customers into groups at random. Each group gets a different treatment.
Randomized test A test where the data source, not the customer, selects the group of each customer at random. Thus a difference of means gives the causal effect. Same meaning as “A/B test”.
Treatment The action that the test examines. In this case, the men’s email or the women’s email.
Control group The customers that get no email.
Holdout The customers that get no email after the launch. They show the effect of the email over time.
Proxy Data from a similar decision that takes the place of the real data. Here, the email of a retailer takes the place of a card offer (as-05).
Visit The customer visited the website in the two weeks after the email.
Conversion The customer bought something in the two weeks after the email.
Spend The dollars that the customer spent in the two weeks after the email.
Spend cap The largest spend value in the data. The data source cut the larger values to this value.
History The dollars that the customer spent in the 12 months before the test.
Standardized difference The difference of the means of a pre-test feature in two groups, divided by the standard deviation of the feature. It shows if the groups are the same before the test.
Sample-ratio check A chi-square test of the group sizes against the planned split. A small p-value shows a problem in the assignment.
Average treatment effect (ATE) The mean outcome of a treatment group minus the mean outcome of the control group.
Significance level The probability of a false result “effect found” when the effect is zero. This notebook uses 5%.
Power The probability that the test finds an effect of a given size. This notebook uses 80%.
MDE Minimum detectable effect. The smallest effect that the test can find with the selected power and significance level.
Confidence interval (CI) A range that contains the true effect in 95% of tests.
Welch t-test A t-test that does not need equal variances in the two groups.
Bootstrap A method that samples the data again many times, with replacement, to estimate the uncertainty of a result.
CUPED Controlled experiment with pre-experiment data. A method that removes the part of the outcome that the pre-test data predicts.
Regression adjustment A linear regression of the outcome on the treatment and the customer features.
Uplift The change of an outcome that a treatment causes for a customer.
Segment effect The ATE in one group of customers, for example the customers with more than $500 of history.
Interaction test An F-test that compares a model with one effect for all customers against a model with one effect for each segment.
Holm correction A correction of the p-values when we test many segments. It keeps the probability of one or more false results at 5%.
Cross-fit A method that estimates the uplift of each customer with a model that did not see that customer. “Cross-fitted” has the same meaning.
Two-part model A model of spend in two parts: the probability of a purchase, and the spend of a buyer.
Tobit model A regression model for an outcome with many values at zero.
CUPAC A version of CUPED that uses the prediction of an ML model as the pre-test covariate.
S-learner An uplift model with one model for all customers. The treatment is one of its features.
X-learner An uplift model in two stages. It uses the T-learner and then corrects the uplift in each group.
Causal forest A random forest that estimates the uplift of each customer directly.
T-learner An uplift model with two models: one for the treatment group and one for the control group. The uplift is the difference of the two predictions.
Transformed outcome An outcome that has the same mean as the uplift. A normal regression model on it gives an uplift model.
ML uplift model An uplift model that learns from many features: here the T-learner and the uplift tree.
Qini curve The incremental spend from the top x% of customers, in the order of the predicted uplift.
Qini area The mean distance between the Qini curve of a model and the line of a random order. Higher is better.
Rank by history A targeting rule with no model: it sends the email first to the customers with the largest history.
Send to all The policy that sends the email to each customer in the campaign.
Targeting rule A rule that sends the email only to some customers, for example the top 25% by history.
Incremental margin The contribution margin multiplied by the incremental spend.
Contact cost The full cost of one email. See as-02.
Breakeven effect The uplift on spend at which the incremental margin equals the contact cost: contact cost / margin.
Breakeven rule A rule that sends the email to a customer if the incremental margin is more than the contact cost.
Decision layer The step that changes the effect into a policy and a dollar value, with the margin and the contact cost.
ROI Incremental margin divided by the total contact cost.
Evaluation framework The five branches (validity, effect, robustness, business value, targeting) with the rules that the result must pass (Step 3a).
Model rule The rule of branch 5 for the uplift method. An ML uplift model replaces rank by history only if its Qini area is 20% or more higher.
Policy rule The rule of branch 5 for the list of customers. A targeting rule replaces “send to all” only if the 90% interval of its gain is above 0.
Guardrail metric A metric that must not become worse, for example the unsubscribe rate.
Kill criteria The results that stop a rollout.
Champion/challenger test A test that sends a random share of the cases to a new policy and the rest to the current policy.
Business note A short result of a step for a manager.
Technical note Detail of a method for a data scientist. A business reader can skip it.

File case03_helpers.R

# Helper functions for case 03, Steps 3 to 7 (base R and rpart only).
#
# Purpose: One place for the tools of the evaluation framework (Step 3a): the checks of the test design,
#          the effect with its confidence interval, the power, the bootstrap, CUPED, the profit of a
#          policy, the uplift models with cross-fitting and the Qini curve.
# Input:   The notebook sources this file after the setup chunk. If an argument is not given, a function
#          uses the constants of the setup chunk (SEED, ALPHA, POWER, MARGIN, COST) and, for the uplift,
#          the data `m` (men's email + control, Step 4c) and `GRID` (Step 4d). R finds these names when
#          the function runs, so the notebook can define them after this file.
# Output:  Functions only. The file makes no data and prints nothing.
#
# The format helpers usd(), pct(), num(), ci_txt() and fmt_p() stay in the setup chunk for now.

# --- Branch 1 of the evaluation framework: validity ---

std_diff <- function(x, arm, a, ref = "control") {
  # Purpose: standardized difference of one pre-test feature between group `a` and the reference group.
  # Input:   x (numeric vector), arm (group of each customer), a and ref (group names).
  # Output:  (mean in a − mean in ref) / standard deviation of x in all customers.
  (mean(x[arm == a]) - mean(x[arm == ref])) / sd(x)
}

srm_p <- function(arm, p = NULL) {
  # Purpose: sample-ratio check. Do the group sizes agree with the planned split?
  # Input:   arm (group of each customer), p (planned share of each group; NULL = equal shares).
  # Output:  the p-value of the chi-square test of the counts against the planned shares.
  tab <- table(arm)
  if (is.null(p)) p <- rep(1 / length(tab), length(tab))
  chisq.test(tab, p = p)$p.value
}

# --- Branch 2: effect and power ---

welch <- function(y1, y0, level = 1 - ALPHA) {
  # Purpose: difference of means with the Welch t-test.
  # Input:   y1 (outcome of the treatment group), y0 (outcome of the control group).
  # Output:  named vector: eff (mean y1 − mean y0), lo and hi (confidence interval), p (p-value),
  #          se (standard error of the difference).
  tt <- t.test(y1, y0, conf.level = level)
  c(eff = unname(-diff(tt$estimate)), lo = tt$conf.int[1], hi = tt$conf.int[2], p = tt$p.value,
    se = unname(tt$stderr))
}

n_needed <- function(delta, sd, alpha = ALPHA, power = POWER) {
  # Purpose: customers in each group that a two-sample t-test needs to find an effect `delta`.
  # Output:  number of customers in each group (not rounded).
  power.t.test(delta = delta, sd = sd, sig.level = alpha, power = power)$n
}

mde_metric <- function(y, arm, n, alpha = ALPHA, power = POWER) {
  # Purpose: power and MDE of one metric for a test with `n` customers in each group (dec-01).
  # Input:   y (outcome of each customer), arm (factor: control, mens, womens), n (customers in each group).
  # Output:  named vector: base (control mean), sd (pooled standard deviation), mde, mens and womens
  #          (observed effects), need_m and need_w (customers in each group for 80% power at each
  #          observed effect).
  s <- sqrt(mean(tapply(y, arm, var)))  # Pooled standard deviation of the three groups
  mde <- power.t.test(n = n, sd = s, sig.level = alpha, power = power)$delta
  base <- mean(y[arm == "control"])
  eff <- sapply(c("mens", "womens"), function(a) mean(y[arm == a]) - base)
  c(base = base, sd = s, mde = mde, mens = eff[["mens"]], womens = eff[["womens"]],
    need_m = n_needed(eff[["mens"]], s, alpha, power), need_w = n_needed(eff[["womens"]], s, alpha, power))
}

# --- Branch 3: robustness ---

boot_diff <- function(y1, y0, B = 2000, seed = SEED) {
  # Purpose: bootstrap of the difference of means. Each sample draws each group again, with replacement.
  # Output:  vector of B bootstrap differences (mean y1 − mean y0).
  set.seed(seed)
  replicate(B, mean(y1[sample.int(length(y1), replace = TRUE)]) - mean(y0[sample.int(length(y0), replace = TRUE)]))
}

cuped <- function(y, x) {
  # Purpose: CUPED. Remove the part of the outcome y that the pre-test value x predicts.
  # Output:  adjusted outcome with the same mean as y.
  theta <- cov(y, x) / var(x)
  y - theta * (x - mean(x))
}

# --- Branch 4: business value ---

breakeven <- function(cost = COST, margin = MARGIN) {
  # Purpose: breakeven effect: the uplift on spend at which the incremental margin equals the contact cost.
  cost / margin
}

policy_profit <- function(sel, y, t, cost, margin = MARGIN) {
  # Purpose: profit for each customer in the campaign of a policy that emails only the selection.
  # Input:   sel (TRUE = gets the email), y (spend), t (1 = men's email, 0 = control), cost (contact cost).
  # Output:  share selected × (margin × uplift in the selection − cost). Customers outside the
  #          selection get no email, so they add no profit and no cost.
  share <- mean(sel)
  if (share == 0) return(0)
  eff <- mean(y[sel & t == 1]) - mean(y[sel & t == 0])
  share * (margin * eff - cost)
}

# --- Branch 5: targeting ---

uplift_oof <- function(seed, K = 5, dat = m,
                       f_conv = conversion ~ recency + lhist + mens + womens + zip + newbie + channel) {
  # Purpose: cross-fitted uplift on spend of each customer, for the four methods of dec-06.
  #          Each customer gets the uplift from a model that did not see that customer.
  # Input:   seed (sets the folds), K (number of folds), dat (men's email + control, with t = 1 for the email).
  # Output:  matrix with one row for each customer and one column for each method:
  #          A (history, no model), B (segment table), C (T-learner), D (uplift tree).
  set.seed(seed)
  p_t <- mean(dat$t)
  fold <- sample(rep(seq_len(K), length.out = nrow(dat)))
  pred <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow(dat), 4, dimnames = list(NULL, c("A", "B", "C", "D")))
  pred[, "A"] <- dat$history
  for (k in seq_len(K)) {
    tr <- dat[fold != k, ]; te <- fold == k
    # B. Segment table: mean spend of the email group minus mean spend of the control group in each cell
    cell_tr <- interaction(tr$hseg, tr$buyer); cell_te <- interaction(dat$hseg[te], dat$buyer[te])
    u <- tapply(tr$spend[tr$t == 1], cell_tr[tr$t == 1], mean) - tapply(tr$spend[tr$t == 0], cell_tr[tr$t == 0], mean)
    pred[te, "B"] <- u[as.character(cell_te)]
    # C. T-learner: conversion model in each group × mean spend of a buyer in each group
    g1 <- glm(f_conv, binomial, tr[tr$t == 1, ]); g0 <- glm(f_conv, binomial, tr[tr$t == 0, ])
    a1 <- mean(tr$spend[tr$t == 1 & tr$conversion == 1]); a0 <- mean(tr$spend[tr$t == 0 & tr$conversion == 1])
    pred[te, "C"] <- a1 * predict(g1, dat[te, ], type = "response") - a0 * predict(g0, dat[te, ], type = "response")
    # D. Tree on the transformed outcome: its mean in a leaf is the uplift of the leaf
    tr$z <- tr$spend * (tr$t - p_t) / (p_t * (1 - p_t))
    tree <- rpart(z ~ recency + history + mens + womens + zip + newbie + channel, tr,
                  control = rpart.control(cp = 0, minbucket = 3000, maxdepth = 3))
    pred[te, "D"] <- predict(tree, dat[te, ])
  }
  pred[is.na(pred)] <- 0  # A cell without customers in the training folds
  pred
}

qini <- function(score, y, t, grid = GRID) {
  # Purpose: Qini curve. Rank the customers by score (highest first) and take the top share g.
  # Output:  for each share g in grid: (mean y of the email group − mean y of the control group in the
  #          top g) × g. This is the incremental spend for each customer of the campaign.
  o <- order(-score, runif(length(score)))  # Random order for ties
  y <- y[o]; t <- t[o]; n <- length(y)
  sapply(grid, function(g) {
    i <- seq_len(ceiling(g * n))
    (sum(y[i][t[i] == 1]) / sum(t[i]) - sum(y[i][t[i] == 0]) / sum(1 - t[i])) * length(i) / n
  })
}

qini_area <- function(cv, grid = GRID) {
  # Purpose: Qini area of each column of a matrix of Qini curves.
  # Output:  mean distance between each curve and the line of a random order (from 0 to the last point).
  colMeans(cv - outer(grid, cv[length(grid), ]))
}

group_effect <- function(dat, g) {
  # Purpose: uplift on spend in each level of the grouping g, with the Welch 95% CI.
  # Input:   dat (with spend and t), g (factor with one value for each row of dat).
  # Output:  data frame: level, customers, eff, lo, hi.
  do.call(rbind, lapply(levels(g), function(l) {
    s <- dat[g == l, ]
    w <- welch(s$spend[s$t == 1], s$spend[s$t == 0])
    data.frame(level = l, n = nrow(s), eff = w[["eff"]], lo = w[["lo"]], hi = w[["hi"]])
  }))
}

xfit_group <- function(dat, g, seed, K = 5) {
  # Purpose: cross-fitted uplift on spend of each customer when the uplift depends only on a group g
  #          (for example the history quartile). Each customer gets the uplift of the group from the
  #          other K − 1 folds, so the estimate never uses that customer.
  # Input:   dat (with spend and t), g (factor with one value for each row of dat), seed (sets the folds).
  # Output:  vector with the cross-fitted uplift of each customer, and the attribute "fold".
  set.seed(seed)
  fold <- sample(rep(seq_len(K), length.out = nrow(dat)))
  u <- numeric(nrow(dat))
  for (k in seq_len(K)) {
    tr <- dat[fold != k, ]; gt <- g[fold != k]; te <- fold == k
    uu <- tapply(tr$spend[tr$t == 1], gt[tr$t == 1], mean) - tapply(tr$spend[tr$t == 0], gt[tr$t == 0], mean)
    u[te] <- uu[as.character(g[te])]
  }
  attr(u, "fold") <- fold
  u
}

# One chart style for the R notebook. It follows the deck style guide (project doc claude/deck-style-guide.md)
# and matches chart_style.py of cases 01 and 02.
#
# Rules:
# - One message per chart. The figure title is an action title: a full sentence with a number.
# - CS$navy for the main series, CS$blue for the one point, CS$gray for context, CS$cyan for a second series
#   only, CS$negative (red) only for losses.
# - No box, no gridlines, no legend box when a direct label at the line end works.
#
# Use a straight apostrophe (') in titles: the PNG device cannot draw the curly one in the serif font.
#
# Use (base R graphics only):
#   cs_setup()                                   # once per chart, before plot()
#   plot(x, y, type = "l", col = CS$navy, lwd = 2.5, ...)
#   cs_label_end(x_last, y_last, "Men's email", col = CS$navy, bold = TRUE)
#   cs_title("The men's email adds $0.77 of spend for each customer", "Mean spend, two weeks after the email")

CS <- list(
  navy = "#051C2C", blue = "#2251FF", cyan = "#0091D5", gray = "#8C8C8C",
  light_gray = "#D0D0D0", negative = "#C8102E", ink = "#1A1A1A", muted = "#6B6B6B"
)

cs_setup <- function(mar = c(3.6, 4.6, 0.6, 7), title_lines = 2) {
  # Purpose: set the margins and the colors of the axes. The outer top margin holds the action title.
  # mar[4] (right) leaves room for direct labels at the line ends.
  par(mar = mar, oma = c(0, 0, 1.2 * title_lines + 0.6, 0), bty = "l", las = 1,
      col.axis = CS$muted, col.lab = CS$ink, fg = CS$gray, family = "sans",
      cex.axis = 0.85, cex.lab = 0.9, mgp = c(2.2, 0.6, 0), tcl = -0.3)
  invisible(NULL)
}

cs_title <- function(title, subtitle = NULL) {
  # Purpose: write the action title (serif, bold) and an optional muted subtitle above the plot, left aligned.
  has_sub <- !is.null(subtitle)
  mtext(title, side = 3, outer = TRUE, line = if (has_sub) 1.3 else 0.3, adj = 0,
        font = 2, family = "serif", cex = 1.15, col = CS$ink)
  if (has_sub) mtext(subtitle, side = 3, outer = TRUE, line = 0.1, adj = 0, cex = 0.82, col = CS$muted)
  invisible(NULL)
}

cs_label_end <- function(x, y, label, col = CS$navy, bold = FALSE, dy = 0, cex = 0.8) {
  # Purpose: a direct label at the end of a line (use it instead of a legend). dy moves the label up (+) or down (-)
  # in lines of text, so labels of lines that end near each other do not overlap.
  usr <- par("usr")
  ystep <- dy * strheight("M", cex = cex) * 1.4
  text(x, y + ystep, paste0(" ", label), adj = c(0, 0.5), xpd = NA, col = col, font = if (bold) 2 else 1, cex = cex)
  invisible(usr)
}

cs_percent_axis <- function(side = 2, at = NULL, digits = 0) {
  # Purpose: an axis with percent labels for values on the 0–1 scale.
  if (is.null(at)) at <- axTicks(side)
  axis(side, at = at, labels = paste0(formatC(100 * at, format = "f", digits = digits), "%"))
}

cs_dollar_axis <- function(side = 2, at = NULL, digits = 2) {
  # Purpose: an axis with dollar labels.
  if (is.null(at)) at <- axTicks(side)
  axis(side, at = at, labels = ifelse(at < 0, paste0("-$", formatC(-at, format = "f", digits = digits)),
                                      paste0("$", formatC(at, format = "f", digits = digits))))
}

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| code-summary: "Setup: libraries, chart style, seed, paths, assumptions and format helpers"

# Purpose: Load the libraries and the chart style. Set the seed, the paths, the assumptions (as-01, as-02, as-04),
#          the test parameters and the format helpers.
# Input:   chart_style.R, the path of the raw data file.
# Output:  `N` (numbers for the text), `SEED`, `DATA_DIR`, `RAW_FILE`, `MARGIN`, `COST`, `CAMPAIGN`, `ALPHA`,
#          `POWER`, helpers `usd()`, `pct()`, `num()`, `ci_txt()`, `fmt_p()`, chart style `CS`.

library(knitr)
library(rpart)  # Recommended package. It comes with each R installation.
source("chart_style.R")  # One chart style for all notebooks (deck style guide): CS, cs_setup(), cs_title()

# Fixed seed: each run gives the same bootstrap samples, folds and placebo tests.
SEED <- 42
set.seed(SEED)

# Paths are relative to this notebook (cases/03-test-and-learn/).
DATA_DIR <- file.path("..", "..", "data")  # The raw data is not in the repository. See the README.
RAW_FILE <- file.path(DATA_DIR, "raw", "Kevin_Hillstrom_MineThatData_E-MailAnalytics_DataMiningChallenge_2008.03.20.csv")
# Stop early with a clear message if the data file is missing.
if (!file.exists(RAW_FILE)) stop("Download the Hillstrom data to ", RAW_FILE, ". See the README.")

# Assumptions (assumption register in the appendix) and test parameters.
MARGIN <- 0.30      # as-01: contribution margin on incremental spend
COST <- 0.10        # as-02: full cost of one email, $
CAMPAIGN <- 1e5     # as-04: customers in one campaign, for the dollar values
ALPHA <- 0.05       # Significance level of each test
POWER <- 0.80       # Power for the test design (Step 3c)

# Format helpers for the text and the tables. Each returns text.
usd <- function(x, d = 2) ifelse(x < 0, paste0("-$", formatC(-x, format = "f", digits = d, big.mark = ",")),
                                 paste0("$", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d, big.mark = ",")))
pct <- function(x, d = 1) paste0(formatC(100 * x, format = "f", digits = d), "%")
num <- function(x, d = 0) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d, big.mark = ",")
ci_txt <- function(lo, hi, f = usd) paste0("[", f(lo), ", ", f(hi), "]")
fmt_p <- function(p) ifelse(p < 0.001, "< 0.001", formatC(p, format = "f", digits = 3))


N <- list()  # Numbers for the text after each chunk.
# Assumption values that the text of Step 0 uses.
N$as_margin <- pct(MARGIN, 0)
N$as_cost <- usd(COST)
N$as_campaign <- num(CAMPAIGN)
N$as_alpha <- pct(ALPHA, 0)
N$as_power <- pct(POWER, 0)
N$as_breakeven <- usd(COST / MARGIN)  # Breakeven effect: the uplift on spend at which margin x uplift = contact cost

```

- A blue block is a decision. A green block is a business note. A grey block (**Technical note**) gives detail for data scientists. A business reader can skip it.

# Step 0. What and why {#step-0}

::: {.bridge}
This step gives the business problem, the question for leadership and the method that answers it with a randomized test. Each later step answers one part of the question.
:::

::: {.purpose}
**Purpose.** This step answers: *what must the campaign do for the business, and how does a test give a reliable answer?* It supports this decision: the email version, the customers that get it, and the holdout after the launch.
:::

## 0a. The business problem

**Situation.** A retailer sent an email to its customers who bought in the last year. The data source put each customer at random into one of three groups: the men's email, the women's email or no email. Then it measured visits, conversions and spend for two weeks. In this case, the email is a proxy for a card offer to card customers (as-05).

**Complication.** Each email has a contact cost: the cost to send, the creative work, and the future value that we lose when a customer unsubscribes (as-02). Most customers buy nothing in the test window, so the spend data is noisy. The mean effect can hide customers where the email loses money. Leadership asks two questions: "Which version do we send?" and "Do we send it to all customers?"

**Question.** Which email version do we send, and to which customers, for the most incremental profit?

**Resolution.** Measure the effect of each email on spend with the randomized test, and select the version. Then examine if the effect changes by segment, and if a targeting rule beats "send to all". A decision layer changes the effect into dollars with the margin (as-01) and the contact cost (as-02). A holdout after the launch confirms the result.

**Decision that this notebook supports.** The email version, the customers that get it, and the size of the holdout after the launch.

**Success metric.** The incremental profit for each customer in the campaign: the incremental margin minus the contact cost. At the base assumptions, the margin is `r N$as_margin` and the contact cost is `r N$as_cost`. Thus an email pays for itself if it adds more than `r N$as_breakeven` of spend (the breakeven effect).

## 0b. Method and data strategy

A technical reader asks one question first. Why does a difference of two group means give the causal effect of the email?

The answer is the random assignment. The data source, not the customer and not a model, selected the group of each customer. Thus, before the email, the three groups are the same on average. This is true for the features that we see and for the features that we do not see.

After the email, the only systematic difference between the groups is the email. Then a difference of means measures the effect of the email, with no model of customer behavior. Step 2d checks this condition with the data.

**From the effect to a policy.** The test gives one effect for each email. The business needs a policy: a version and a list of customers. We go from the effect to the policy in five moves. Each move uses the result of the move before it:

1. **Effect.** Does the email change spend, and is the test large enough to show the effect that matters? (Step 3, Step 4a)
2. **Version.** Which email gives the larger effect, also inside each product history? (Step 4b)
3. **Segments.** Does the effect of the selected email change by segment, after a correction for many tests? (Step 4c)
4. **Uplift.** Can a model or a simple rule rank the customers by their uplift? (Step 4d, Step 5)
5. **Decision layer.** At the margin and the contact cost, which rule selects the customers? How do we confirm it after the launch? (Step 6, Step 7)

If the effect is not real, the other moves have no base. If no segment and no model finds a reliable difference, the simple policy "send to all" stays.

::: {.assumption}
**The champion comes from the data. The dollar assumptions are ours.** Cases 01 and 02 must build their champion, because their data has no real policy. This case does not need to.

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| What is the champion here? | "No email": the control group of the test. The data source chose these customers at random, so they show what customers do with no email. |
| What does the data give? | A real randomized test: three groups, with visits, conversions and spend for two weeks. Each effect in this notebook is a difference between real groups. |
| What does the data not give? | The margin on extra spend (as-01), the full contact cost of one email (as-02), the effect after two weeks (as-03) and a bank customer (as-05). |
| Which assumptions do we add? | A margin of `r N$as_margin` (as-01), a contact cost of `r N$as_cost` (as-02) and a campaign of `r N$as_campaign` customers (as-04). They change the effect into dollars. |
| How can they be wrong? | A higher contact cost or a lower margin can make "send to all" lose money. Then a targeting rule becomes better. |
| How do we test them? | Step 7a gives the profit at contact costs from $0.05 to $0.30, and Step 7c at margins of 20%, 30% and 40%. Step 7a gives the contact costs at which the decision changes. |
| What does not depend on them? | The effect of each email, the choice of the version and the order of customers by history. These results use only the test data. |
:::

**Why "send to all" is the default.** A targeting rule must earn its place. We set the rules of the evaluation framework before the rerun of this version (Step 3a). An ML uplift model replaces a simple rank by history only if it is clearly better in repeated tests. A targeting rule replaces "send to all" only if the interval of its gain is above zero at the base contact cost.

**The proxy (as-05).** The data is an email test of a retailer, not a test of a bank. A card issuer has the same decision for a card offer: which offer, to which customers, at which contact cost. The size of each effect is different for a card offer, and the margin and the contact cost are different too. The method stays the same. Part 2 applies it to a pricing test and a collections test of case 01.

**The limits of the method.**

- The test window is two weeks (as-03). We do not know the long-term effect: more future purchases, or fatigue and unsubscribes.
- The data has no unsubscribes and no costs. The margin (as-01) and the contact cost (as-02) are assumptions. Step 7c repeats the result for other values.
- Few customers buy in the test window. Thus each segment effect has a wide interval, and a model with many features can fit noise.
- The segments and the uplift method come from the same test. Cross-fitted estimates decrease the risk of a result that is too good, but a new test must confirm a targeting rule.
- The data comes from one retailer in 2008. The dollar values are for this retailer.

::: {.tech-note}
**Technical note.** The method has these parts. Each later step gives the code.

- **Randomization check.** For each pre-test feature $x$, the standardized difference is $(\bar{x}_{\text{email}} - \bar{x}_{\text{control}}) / s_x$. A chi-square test compares the group sizes with an equal split (the sample-ratio check). Step 3a gives the limit of each check.
- **Average effect.** The effect is $\hat{\tau} = \bar{y}_1 - \bar{y}_0$, with the Welch standard error $\sqrt{s_1^2/n_1 + s_0^2/n_0}$. A bootstrap, CUPED and a regression adjustment check the same effect (Step 4a).
- **Power.** For $n$ customers in each group, the MDE is about $(z_{1-\alpha/2} + z_{1-\beta}) \, s \sqrt{2/n}$. The notebook uses a significance level of `r N$as_alpha` and a power of `r N$as_power` (Step 3c).
- **Segments.** An interaction F-test for each feature first. Then the effect of each segment, with the Holm correction (Step 4c).
- **Uplift.** A five-fold cross-fit gives each customer an uplift from a model that did not see that customer. The Qini area compares the order of each method with a random order, in repeated cross-fits (Step 4d).
- **Decision layer.** The breakeven effect is contact cost / margin. The breakeven rule sends the email if $\text{margin} \times \widehat{\text{uplift}} > \text{contact cost}$. For each customer in the campaign, the profit of a selection is $p \, (m \, \hat{\tau}_S - c)$. Here $p$ is the share of customers in the selection, $m$ the margin and $c$ the contact cost (Step 7a).
:::

## 0c. How the notebook answers the question

Each step answers one part of the question:

- [Step 1](#step-1). Which data gives a randomized test of an offer, and what does it contain?
- [Step 2](#step-2). Is the data clean, are the groups the same before the email, and what does a customer spend without an email?
- [Step 3](#step-3). Which rules must the result pass, how does the test split the customers, and which metric decides?
- [Step 4](#step-4). How large is the effect of each email? Which version do we send? Does the effect change by segment? Which method ranks the customers by uplift?
- [Step 5](#step-5). What is the cross-fitted uplift of each customer, by history quartile?
- [Step 6](#step-6). Does the recommended policy pass each rule of the evaluation framework?
- [Step 7](#step-7). Which customers get the email, what is it worth in dollars, and how do we confirm it after the launch?
- [Part 2](#part-2). How does the same method design a pricing test and a collections test for case 01?

::: {.business-note}
**Business note.** The question is a trade between the incremental margin of each email and its contact cost. A randomized test gives the effect without a model, so the core result is a measured fact, not a model estimate. A targeting rule must beat this simple result before we use it. Step 1 shows the data that gives this test.
:::

# Step 1. Get data {#step-1}

::: {.bridge}
Step 0 set the question and the method: measure the effect of each email with a randomized test, then build a policy in five moves. This step answers: which data gives this test, and what does it contain?
:::

::: {.purpose}
**Purpose.** This step gets the data and its meaning. It supports this decision: if the data can answer the business question.
:::

## 1a. Why this data

The data is the MineThatData email test of Kevin Hillstrom (2008). Source: the MineThatData blog, file `Kevin_Hillstrom_MineThatData_E-MailAnalytics_DataMiningChallenge_2008.03.20.csv`. The data is a fair proxy for a card offer, for five reasons:

- **A real randomized test.** The retailer put each customer at random into a group. Thus a difference of means gives the causal effect (Step 0b).
- **A choice like a card offer.** The test has two versions of one campaign and a control group with no contact. A card issuer has the same choice: which offer, or no offer.
- **Outcomes in dollars.** Spend gives the dollars that the decision layer needs. Visit and conversion help to explain the spend result.
- **Pre-test features.** History, recency, product history, channel and area type describe each customer before the email. Thus we can examine segments and uplift.
- **A public source.** Each reader can get the same file and repeat each result.

The data cannot show these things:

| What the data does not show | Why it matters | What the notebook does |
|---|---|---|
| Bank customers and a card offer | The size of each effect is different for a card offer. | The email is a proxy (as-05). The method stays the same. Part 2 applies it to two tests of case 01. |
| Unsubscribes and the cost of an email | The contact cost decides if targeting beats "send to all". | The contact cost is an assumption (as-02). Step 7c repeats the result for other costs. Step 7d watches the unsubscribe rate. |
| The margin of each purchase | The profit needs the margin. | The margin is an assumption (as-01). Step 7c repeats the result for other margins. |
| The long-term effect | The test window is two weeks (as-03). | A holdout after the launch (Step 7d). |
| Spend above a maximum value | The data source cut the largest spend values. | Step 2 examines the effect of this cap. |

## 1b. Key variables

The table gives all columns of the file. The treatment is `segment`, and the primary outcome is `spend` (Step 3c). [Appendix A](#data-dictionary) also gives the coded features that Step 1c and Step 2 make.

| Column | Meaning in plain words | Type | Use |
|---|---|---|---|
| **`segment` → `arm`** | **The test group of the customer: "Mens E-Mail", "Womens E-Mail" or "No E-Mail".** | **Text → category** | **Treatment** |
| **`spend`** | **The dollars that the customer spent in the two weeks after the email.** | **Number ($)** | **Primary outcome** |
| `visit` | 1 = the customer visited the website in the two weeks after the email. | 1/0 | Secondary outcome |
| `conversion` | 1 = the customer bought something in the two weeks after the email. | 1/0 | Secondary outcome |
| `history` | The dollars that the customer spent in the last year, before the test. | Number ($) | Pre-test feature. Rank by history (Step 4d). |
| `history_segment` | The same history in buckets, for example "1) $0 - $100". | Text → category | Pre-test feature (`hseg`). Segment effects (Step 4c). |
| `recency` | The number of months since the last purchase. | Number | Pre-test feature |
| `mens` | 1 = the customer bought men's products in the last year. | 1/0 | Pre-test feature. Product history (`buyer`). |
| `womens` | 1 = the customer bought women's products in the last year. | 1/0 | Pre-test feature. Product history (`buyer`). |
| `newbie` | 1 = a new customer in the last year. | 1/0 | Pre-test feature |
| `channel` | The channels where the customer bought in the last year: Phone, Web or Multichannel. | Category | Pre-test feature |
| `zip_code` | The area type of the address: Urban, Suburban or Rural. The file writes "Surburban". | Category | Pre-test feature (`zip`) |

The email cannot change a pre-test feature, so a pre-test feature is fair input for a segment or an uplift model. An outcome is never a feature. Step 2d also uses the pre-test features to check that the groups are the same before the email.

## 1c. Load the data and look at it

The file is small, so the code reads it in one step with base R. The load also makes the coded columns that the later steps use:

- `arm`: the test group, with the control group first. Thus each effect is "email minus control".
- `buyer`: the product history. It is "mens only", "womens only" or "both", from `mens` and `womens`.
- `hseg`: the history bucket, without the number at the start of the label.
- `zip` and `channel`: the area type and the channel as categories.
- `lhist`: the log of `history`. It decreases the effect of the largest histories in a regression.

```{r}
#| label: load-data
#| code-summary: "Load the data and make the coded columns"

# Purpose: Read the Hillstrom file and make the coded columns that Steps 2-7 use.
# Input:   RAW_FILE (setup chunk).
# Output:  `d` (one row for each customer, with `arm`, `buyer`, `hseg`, `zip`, `channel`, `lhist`),
#          `RAW_COLS` (the column names of the raw file), numbers for the text (`N`).

d <- read.csv(RAW_FILE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
RAW_COLS <- names(d)  # The 12 columns of the raw file, before the coded columns

# Test group. The control group is the first level, so each effect is "email minus control".
d$arm <- factor(d$segment, levels = c("No E-Mail", "Mens E-Mail", "Womens E-Mail"),
                labels = c("control", "mens", "womens"))
# Product history: men's products, women's products, or both, in the last year
d$buyer <- factor(ifelse(d$mens == 1 & d$womens == 1, "both", ifelse(d$mens == 1, "mens only", "womens only")),
                  levels = c("mens only", "womens only", "both"))
# History bucket: remove the number at the start ("1) "). The sort of the raw labels keeps the dollar order.
d$hseg <- factor(sub("^\\d\\) ", "", d$history_segment), levels = sub("^\\d\\) ", "", sort(unique(d$history_segment))))
d$zip <- factor(d$zip_code)
d$channel <- factor(d$channel)
d$lhist <- log(d$history)  # History is always more than $0, so the log is defined

N$rows <- num(nrow(d))
N$n_arm <- num(min(table(d$arm)))
N$spend_zero <- pct(mean(d$spend == 0))
N$spend_max <- usd(max(d$spend), 0)
N$conv_spend_ok <- all((d$spend > 0) == (d$conversion == 1))  # Spend > $0 if and only if a conversion
```

The next chunk shows the initial state of the data before any change: the size, the groups, the outcomes and the spend cap.

```{r}
#| label: initial-state
#| code-summary: "Initial state: size, groups, missing values, conversion and the spend cap"

# Purpose: Show the initial state of the data before any change: size, groups, outcomes and the spend cap.
# Input:   `d`, `RAW_COLS` (load-data chunk).
# Output:  Numbers for the text (`N`), table of the initial state.

n_grp <- table(d$arm)
N$s1_raw_cols <- num(length(RAW_COLS))
N$s1_cols <- num(ncol(d))
N$s1_n_ctrl <- num(n_grp[["control"]])
N$s1_n_mens <- num(n_grp[["mens"]])
N$s1_n_womens <- num(n_grp[["womens"]])
N$s1_missing <- num(sum(is.na(d[RAW_COLS])))
N$s1_buyers <- num(sum(d$conversion == 1))
N$s1_conv <- pct(mean(d$conversion), 2)
N$s1_visit <- pct(mean(d$visit), 1)
N$s1_cap_n <- num(sum(d$spend == max(d$spend)))  # Customers at the largest spend value

kable(data.frame(
  Fact = c("Rows (customers)", "Columns: raw file / after the load",
           "Customers in each group: no email / men's email / women's email", "Missing values (raw columns)",
           "Share with $0 spend in the test window", "Visit rate, all groups", "Conversion rate, all groups",
           "Buyers (conversion = 1)", "Largest spend (the spend cap)", "Customers at the spend cap",
           "Spend > $0 if and only if a conversion"),
  Value = c(N$rows, paste(N$s1_raw_cols, "/", N$s1_cols),
            paste(N$s1_n_ctrl, "/", N$s1_n_mens, "/", N$s1_n_womens), N$s1_missing,
            N$spend_zero, N$s1_visit, N$s1_conv, N$s1_buyers, N$spend_max, N$s1_cap_n,
            ifelse(N$conv_spend_ok, "Yes", "No"))),
  row.names = FALSE, align = "lr")
```

The data has `r N$rows` customers and `r N$s1_raw_cols` columns. The load adds the coded columns, so `d` has `r N$s1_cols` columns. The raw file has `r N$s1_missing` missing values. The three groups have `r N$s1_n_ctrl`, `r N$s1_n_mens` and `r N$s1_n_womens` customers. These sizes are near to an equal split, and Step 2d tests this with the sample-ratio check.

Of all customers, `r N$spend_zero` spend $0 in the test window. Only `r N$s1_buyers` customers buy something: a conversion rate of `r N$s1_conv`. The visit rate is `r N$s1_visit`. Thus spend is mostly zeros with a long right tail. Step 3 shows why this shape makes the test need many customers.

The largest spend is `r N$spend_max`, and `r N$s1_cap_n` customers have exactly this value. Thus the data source probably cut the spend at this value. Step 2 examines the effect of this cap. `r if (N$conv_spend_ok) "Each customer with spend more than $0 has a conversion, and each conversion has spend. Thus the two outcomes agree." else "Some customers have spend without a conversion, or a conversion without spend. Step 2 examines these rows."`

::: {.business-note}
**Business note.** The data is a real randomized test with outcomes in dollars, so it can answer the business question. It cannot show bank customers, the contact cost or the long-term effect, and the notebook says where each limit matters. Step 2 checks the data and the randomization, and it measures what a customer spends without an email.
:::

# Step 2. Clean and prepare data {#step-2}

::: {.bridge}
Step 1 showed that the Hillstrom file can answer the business question. It has one row for each customer, the test group of the customer and three outcomes over two weeks. But a test result is valid only if the groups were the same before the email. The spend data also has a cap and many customers with $0.

This step answers three questions. Which rows, columns and values can the analysis use? Do the groups differ only by the email? What do customers do without an email?
:::

::: {.purpose}
**Purpose.** This step makes sure that the test data can give a causal effect. It supports this decision: use the test result for the campaign decision, or run a new test.
:::

The data preparation follows one tree with three levels. Each level has one split axis. Each axis divides all cases into groups that do not overlap and that together cover all cases (MECE).

| Level | Split axis | Groups | What this data needs | Section |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Rows | Is the record a valid customer of the test? | Not valid · valid | Six technical checks. The test selected the customers, so each valid row is in scope. | 2a |
| Columns | When does the value exist, against the time of the email? | Before the email (pre-test feature) · the test group · after the email (outcome) | An outcome never goes into a model as a feature. The pre-test features show if the groups are the same (2d). | 2b |
| Values | Why is a value extreme, coded or empty? | Extreme value from a cap · two outcomes that must agree · coded values · empty cells | The spend cap. Spend against conversion. Five coded features. A check for missing values. | 2c |

Then Step 2d checks the random assignment: the evidence for branch 1 (validity) of the framework. Step 2e measures the baseline: what the control group does without an email.

## 2a. Rows: which customers can the analysis use?

The data source put each customer at random into one of three groups. Thus the analysis must keep all valid rows: a removed row can make the groups different. The code checks six conditions. A record is not valid if its test group is not one of the three groups, or if an outcome is not 0 or 1. It is also not valid if the spend is less than $0 or the history is $0 or less. The last check is a recency outside 1–12 months.

The data has no customer ID. Thus the code cannot find a customer who is in the file two times.

```{r}
#| label: clean-rows
#| code-summary: "Rows: six technical checks"

# Purpose: Check that each row is a valid customer of the test (Step 2a).
# Input:   `d` (from the load chunk of Step 1).
# Output:  Table `row_checks` (rows that fail each check). N values for the text.

# Each check gives TRUE for a row that is not valid.
row_checks <- list(
  `Test group not one of the three groups` = is.na(d$arm),
  `Visit not 0 or 1` = !d$visit %in% c(0, 1),
  `Conversion not 0 or 1` = !d$conversion %in% c(0, 1),
  `Spend less than $0` = d$spend < 0,
  `History of $0 or less` = d$history <= 0,
  `Recency outside 1-12 months` = !d$recency %in% 1:12
)
invalid <- Reduce(`|`, row_checks)
N$n_rows_raw <- num(nrow(d))
N$n_invalid <- num(sum(invalid))
# A random test keeps all valid rows. The code stops if a row fails, so that a later step cannot hide it.
if (any(invalid)) stop(sum(invalid), " rows fail a technical check. Examine them before you continue.")
kable(data.frame(Check = names(row_checks), `Rows that fail` = num(sapply(row_checks, sum)),
                 check.names = FALSE), row.names = FALSE, align = "lr")
```

`r N$n_invalid` of the `r N$n_rows_raw` rows fail a check. The file is clean at the row level, and each row is in scope.

## 2b. Columns: which values exist before the email?

A test compares groups that were the same before the treatment. Thus the split axis for a column is its time against the email. A column that exists before the email describes the customer. A column that exists after the email is an outcome: the email can change it. An outcome never goes into a model as a feature. Otherwise the model learns the result of the email from the result itself.

```{r}
#| label: column-roles
#| code-summary: "Columns: the role of each raw column against the time of the email"

# Purpose: Give each raw column its role: pre-test feature, test group or outcome (Step 2b).
# Input:   `d`.
# Output:  `COL_ROLE` (named vector, raw column -> role; Appendix A uses it). Table of the roles.

COL_ROLE <- c(recency = "Pre-test feature", history_segment = "Pre-test feature", history = "Pre-test feature",
              mens = "Pre-test feature", womens = "Pre-test feature", zip_code = "Pre-test feature",
              newbie = "Pre-test feature", channel = "Pre-test feature", segment = "Test group",
              visit = "Outcome", conversion = "Outcome", spend = "Outcome")
# Check: the roles cover each raw column one time.
stopifnot(setequal(names(COL_ROLE), c("recency", "history_segment", "history", "mens", "womens", "zip_code",
                                      "newbie", "channel", "segment", "visit", "conversion", "spend")),
          all(names(COL_ROLE) %in% names(d)))
role_tab <- data.frame(Role = c("Pre-test feature", "Test group", "Outcome"),
                       Time = c("Before the email", "At the email", "In the two weeks after the email"),
                       Use = c("Balance check (2d), segments (4c), uplift models (4d)",
                               "The treatment: no email, men's email or women's email",
                               "Metrics of the test. Never a feature."))
role_tab$Columns <- sapply(role_tab$Role, function(r) paste(names(COL_ROLE)[COL_ROLE == r], collapse = ", "))
N$n_pre <- sum(COL_ROLE == "Pre-test feature")
N$n_out <- sum(COL_ROLE == "Outcome")
N$n_raw_cols <- length(COL_ROLE)
kable(role_tab[, c("Role", "Columns", "Time", "Use")], row.names = FALSE)
```

The file has `r N$n_pre` pre-test features, one test group and `r N$n_out` outcomes. The email can change the outcomes, but it cannot change the pre-test features. Thus a difference of a pre-test feature between the groups can come only from the random assignment. Step 2d uses this fact for the balance check.

## 2c. Values: the spend cap, the outcomes, the coded features and empty cells

The split axis for a value is the reason that it needs attention. A value can be extreme, two outcomes can disagree, a raw value can need a code, or a cell can be empty. The code checks each group.

```{r}
#| label: clean-values
#| code-summary: "Values: spend cap, spend against conversion, coded features and empty cells"

# Purpose: Check the values of Step 2c: the spend cap, the agreement of the outcomes, the coded features
#          and the empty cells.
# Input:   `d` (with the coded features of the load chunk).
# Output:  Table `value_checks`. Table `coded`. N values for the text.

# Extreme value: the largest spend repeats. We read this as a cap of the data source.
spend_max <- max(d$spend)
at_cap <- d$spend == spend_max
N$cap <- usd(spend_max, 0)
N$n_cap <- num(sum(at_cap))
N$n_buyers <- num(sum(d$spend > 0))
N$cap_usd_share <- pct(sum(d$spend[at_cap]) / sum(d$spend))
N$spend_2nd <- usd(max(d$spend[!at_cap]), 2)
N$buyer_median <- usd(median(d$spend[d$spend > 0]), 0)

# Outcomes that must agree: spend > $0 if and only if conversion = 1. A conversion needs a visit.
n_spend_noconv <- sum((d$spend > 0) != (d$conversion == 1))
n_conv_novisit <- sum(d$conversion == 1 & d$visit == 0)
# Coded values: the history bucket must hold the history in dollars. Parse "$100 - $200" and "$1,000 +".
h_txt <- sub("^\\d\\) ", "", d$history_segment)  # Remove the bucket number "1) " to "7) "
bounds <- lapply(regmatches(h_txt, gregexpr("[0-9][0-9,]*", h_txt)), function(x) as.numeric(gsub(",", "", x)))
h_lo <- sapply(bounds, `[`, 1)
h_hi <- sapply(bounds, function(b) if (length(b) > 1) b[2] else Inf)  # "$1,000 +" has no upper bound
n_hseg_bad <- sum(d$history < h_lo | d$history >= h_hi)
# Each customer bought men's products, women's products or both. "Neither" must not exist.
n_no_product <- sum(d$mens == 0 & d$womens == 0)
# Empty cells in all raw columns.
n_na <- sum(is.na(d[, names(COL_ROLE)]))

value_checks <- data.frame(
  Group = c("Extreme value", "Outcomes that must agree", "Outcomes that must agree",
            "Coded values", "Coded values", "Empty cells"),
  Check = c(paste0("Buyers with spend at the largest value (", N$cap, ")"),
            "Spend > $0 without a conversion, or a conversion with $0",
            "Conversion without a visit",
            "History outside its history bucket",
            "Customer with neither men's nor women's products",
            paste("Empty cells in the", length(COL_ROLE), "raw columns")),
  Rows = num(c(sum(at_cap), n_spend_noconv, n_conv_novisit, n_hseg_bad, n_no_product, n_na)))
N$n_spend_noconv <- num(n_spend_noconv)
N$n_conv_novisit <- num(n_conv_novisit)
N$n_hseg_bad <- num(n_hseg_bad)
N$n_no_product <- num(n_no_product)
N$n_na <- num(n_na)
kable(value_checks, row.names = FALSE, align = "llr")
```

What we do with each group:

| Group | Example in this data | What we do |
|---|---|---|
| Extreme value from a cap | `r N$n_cap` of the `r N$n_buyers` buyers have exactly `r N$cap`. The next largest spend is `r N$spend_2nd`. These buyers hold `r N$cap_usd_share` of all spend dollars. | Keep the value. The cap is the same in each group, so it does not change the comparison. The effect is an effect on spend up to the cap. |
| Two outcomes that must agree | `r N$n_spend_noconv` rows have spend without a conversion, or a conversion without spend. `r N$n_conv_novisit` rows have a conversion without a visit. | No change is necessary. Visit, conversion and spend tell one consistent story for each customer. |
| Coded values | `r N$n_hseg_bad` customers have a history outside their history bucket. `r N$n_no_product` customers have neither men's nor women's products. | Use the coded features of the table below. |
| Empty cells | `r N$n_na` empty cells in the `r N$n_raw_cols` raw columns. | No imputation is necessary. |

**Why we do not cap the spend again.** The median buyer spends `r N$buyer_median`, so the cap affects only a few large orders. A second cap at a lower value (winsorization) makes the variance smaller. But it also changes the outcome that the profit calculation uses. The cap of the data source is the same in all three groups, so the comparison stays fair.

The load chunk of Step 1 makes five coded features from the raw columns. The table shows each one with its levels.

```{r}
#| label: coded-features
#| code-summary: "Coded features: source, rule and levels"

# Purpose: Show the coded features of the load chunk and check that each one has a value for each row.
# Input:   `d`.
# Output:  Table `coded`. N values for the text.

coded <- data.frame(
  Feature = c("arm", "buyer", "hseg", "zip", "channel", "lhist"),
  Source = c("segment", "mens, womens", "history_segment", "zip_code", "channel", "history"),
  Rule = c("Test group: control, mens, womens",
           "Product history: men's only, women's only, or both",
           "History bucket without the number prefix, in the order of the dollars",
           "Area type as a factor",
           "Purchase channel as a factor",
           "Natural log of the history, for the models with a straight line"))
coded$Levels <- sapply(coded$Feature, function(f) {
  x <- d[[f]]
  if (is.factor(x)) paste0(nlevels(x), ": ", paste(levels(x), collapse = ", "))
  else paste0("from ", formatC(min(x), format = "f", digits = 2), " to ", formatC(max(x), format = "f", digits = 2))
})
# Check: each coded feature has a value for each row.
stopifnot(!anyNA(d[, coded$Feature]))
N$lhist_lo <- formatC(min(d$lhist), format = "f", digits = 2)
N$hist_min <- usd(min(d$history))
kable(coded, row.names = FALSE)
```

The smallest history is `r N$hist_min`, so the log of the history (`lhist`) has no empty value. `buyer` has three levels that do not overlap, because no customer has neither product type.

## 2d. Randomization check: do the groups differ only by the email? {#randomization}

This check gives the evidence for branch 1 (validity) of the framework in Step 3a. If the groups are different before the email, a difference of the outcomes can come from the customers and not from the email. The check has two parts:

- **Balance.** The standardized difference of each pre-test feature between each email group and the control group. The rule is: each absolute value is less than 0.05.
- **Sample ratio.** The number of customers in the three groups against an equal split. The rule is: the chi-square p-value is more than 0.01. A smaller p-value shows a problem in the assignment, for example lost rows in one group.

::: {.tech-note}
**Technical note.** Let *x* be a feature, *a* an email group and *c* the control group. The standardized difference is (mean(*x* in *a*) − mean(*x* in *c*)) / sd(*x* in all rows). It does not depend on the sample size, unlike a p-value. The code makes one column for each level of `zip_code` and `channel` (`model.matrix`). The sample ratio check is a chi-square goodness-of-fit test of the three group sizes against equal shares.
:::

```{r}
#| label: randomization
#| code-summary: "Randomization check: standardized difference of each feature and the sample ratio check"
```
