```{r}
# Purpose: Check the random assignment: the evidence of branch 1 (validity).
# Input:   `d`.
# Output:  `feat` (pre-test features, one column for each level), `bal` (balance table),
#          N$smd_max, N$srm_p and the rule results.

feat <- data.frame(model.matrix(~ recency + history + mens + womens + newbie + zip + channel - 1, d))
smd <- function(a) sapply(feat, function(x) (mean(x[d$arm == a]) - mean(x[d$arm == "control"])) / sd(x))
bal <- data.frame(Feature = names(feat),
                  `Mean, control` = sapply(feat, function(x) mean(x[d$arm == "control"])),
                  `Std. difference, men's` = smd("mens"),
                  `Std. difference, women's` = smd("womens"), check.names = FALSE)
smd_max <- max(abs(bal[, 3:4]))
srm_p <- chisq.test(table(d$arm))$p.value  # Equal shares are the default of chisq.test
N$smd_max <- formatC(smd_max, format = "f", digits = 3)
N$srm_p <- formatC(srm_p, format = "f", digits = 2)
N$smd_feature <- bal$Feature[which.max(pmax(abs(bal[, 3]), abs(bal[, 4])))]
# The rules of branch 1, set before the rerun.
N$smd_pass <- smd_max < 0.05
N$srm_pass <- srm_p > 0.01
N$valid_txt <- if (N$smd_pass && N$srm_pass) "passes both rules" else "fails a rule"
kable(bal, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)
```

The largest absolute standardized difference is `r N$smd_max` (`r N$smd_feature`). The rule needs less than 0.05. The group sizes agree with an equal split: the chi-square p-value is `r N$srm_p`, and the rule needs more than 0.01. Thus the validity branch `r N$valid_txt`. A difference of the mean outcomes between the groups gives the causal effect of the email.

## 2e. Baseline: what does the control group do without an email?

::: {.bridge}
The groups are the same before the email. Thus the control group shows what all customers do without an email. Each effect in this notebook is a difference against this baseline. The baseline also shows why spend is a noisy metric.
:::

The code measures four values for the control group. They are the visit rate, the conversion rate, the mean spend and the share with $0 spend.

```{r}
#| label: baseline
#| code-summary: "Baseline: visit, conversion and spend of the control group"

# Purpose: Measure the outcomes of the control group without an email: the baseline of Step 2e.
# Input:   `d`, `CAMPAIGN` (as-04).
# Output:  `base0` (one row of baseline values). Table. N values for the text and the chart.

c0 <- d[d$arm == "control", ]
base0 <- data.frame(
  customers = nrow(c0), visit = mean(c0$visit), conversion = mean(c0$conversion),
  spend = mean(c0$spend), zero = mean(c0$spend == 0), buyer_spend = mean(c0$spend[c0$conversion == 1]))
N$base_n <- num(base0$customers)
N$base_visit <- pct(base0$visit, 1)
N$base_conv <- pct(base0$conversion, 2)
N$base_spend <- usd(base0$spend)
N$base_zero <- pct(base0$zero, 1)
N$base_buyer_spend <- usd(base0$buyer_spend, 0)
N$base_spend_100k <- usd(CAMPAIGN * base0$spend, 0)
N$base_cv <- formatC(sd(c0$spend) / mean(c0$spend), format = "f", digits = 0)
kable(data.frame(Customers = N$base_n, Visit = N$base_visit, Conversion = N$base_conv,
                 `Mean spend` = N$base_spend, `Share with $0 spend` = N$base_zero,
                 `Mean spend of a buyer` = N$base_buyer_spend, check.names = FALSE),
      row.names = FALSE, align = "rrrrrr")
rm(c0)
```

```{r}
#| label: baseline-chart
#| code-summary: "Chart: the path from customer to buyer in the control group"
#| fig-height: 3.2

# Purpose: Show the baseline that each email must beat: the share of control customers at each stage.
# Input:   `base0`, `N`, `CS` and the functions of chart_style.R.
# Output:  Bar chart.

if (!exists("CS")) source("chart_style.R")  # The setup chunk sources it. This line keeps a part test alive.
stage <- c("All customers", "Visit the website", "Buy (spend > $0)")
share <- c(1, base0$visit, base0$conversion)
cs_setup(mar = c(2, 9.5, 0.6, 5))
yy <- rev(seq_along(share))
# Bars: the share of customers at each stage. The stage with the spend in blue (the one point).
plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0.5, length(share) + 0.5), axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "")
rect(0, yy - 0.32, share, yy + 0.32, col = c(CS$gray, CS$navy, CS$blue), border = NA)
axis(2, at = yy, labels = stage, tick = FALSE, col.axis = CS$ink)
# Direct labels at the end of each bar instead of an x-axis.
text(share, yy, paste0(" ", mapply(pct, share, c(0, 1, 2))), adj = c(0, 0.5), xpd = NA,
     col = c(CS$muted, CS$navy, CS$blue), font = 2, cex = 0.85)
cs_title(paste0("Without an email, only ", N$base_conv, " of customers buy in two weeks"),
         paste0("Control group, ", N$base_n, " customers. Mean spend ", N$base_spend,
                " for each customer; ", N$base_buyer_spend, " for each buyer"))
```

**How to read:** each bar is the share of the `r N$base_n` control customers who reach a stage in the two weeks of the test. The control group got no email.

**So what:** `r N$base_zero` of the customers without an email spend $0, and the mean spend is only `r N$base_spend`. The few buyers spend `r N$base_buyer_spend` each, so a small number of orders sets the mean. The standard deviation of the spend is about `r N$base_cv` times its mean. Thus the spend effect of an email has a wide confidence interval, and the test needs many customers (Step 3c).

::: {.business-note}
**Business note.** The test file has `r N$n_rows_raw` valid customers, no empty cells and one consistent outcome for each customer. The random assignment works: the largest standardized difference is `r N$smd_max`, and the sample ratio p-value is `r N$srm_p`. Without an email, a campaign of 100,000 customers gives about `r N$base_spend_100k` of spend in two weeks. Each email must add to this baseline more than its cost. Step 3 now fixes the rules of the test and checks that the test is large enough to find such an effect.
:::

# Step 3. Split data: the test design {#step-3}

::: {.bridge}
Step 2 gave clean data for `r N$rows` customers in three groups, and it showed that the groups look the same before the test. It also showed that `r N$spend_zero` of the customers spend $0 in the two weeks. Before we measure an effect, we must agree on two things. What does "the email works" mean, and is the test large enough to show it?
:::

::: {.purpose}
**Purpose.** This step fixes the rules of the test, the use of the data and the primary metric. It supports this decision: use the test result for the campaign, or run a larger test first.
:::

Steps 3 to 7 use the same small set of tools, for example the power, the bootstrap and the Qini curve. The code keeps them in the file `case03_helpers.R`, so that the story stays short. The appendix shows the full file. The next cell loads the tools and the rules of the evaluation framework.

```{r}
#| label: helpers
#| code-summary: "Tools: load case03_helpers.R and the rules of the evaluation framework"

# Purpose: Load the helper functions that Steps 3–7 use, and record the rules of section 3a.
# Input:   case03_helpers.R, chart_style.R, the constants of the setup chunk.
# Output:  The functions of case03_helpers.R, `CS` and the chart functions, `RULES`.

source("chart_style.R")    # Chart style (deck style guide). A second source is safe.
source("case03_helpers.R")

# The rules of the evaluation framework (section 3a). We set them before the rerun.
RULES <- list(
  b1_smd = 0.05,          # Branch 1: largest absolute standardized difference less than 0.05
  b1_srm_p = 0.01,        # Branch 1: p-value of the sample-ratio check more than 0.01
  b3_adj_dev = 0.10,      # Branch 3: each adjusted effect within 10% of the unadjusted effect
  b5_model_gain = 0.20,   # Branch 5: an ML uplift model needs a 20% higher mean Qini area ...
  b5_model_pos = 9,       # ... and a Qini area more than 0 in 9 or more of the repeats
  b5_policy_level = 0.90  # Branch 5: the 90% interval of the gain of a targeting rule must be above 0
)
```

## 3a. What the test must measure

A test has many metrics. A reader can ask: "Why these metrics, and why not others?" Thus we start from the question that each metric answers.

The framework splits the risks of a campaign decision in two groups. The first group is statistical: the test can be wrong in its design, too small to show the effect, or right only with one method. The second group is business: the effect can be real but make no money. Or a smaller list of customers can make more money than "send to all". Each failure belongs to one branch only. A policy that passes all five branches is ready for the rollout.

We set these rules before the rerun of this version, and we do not change them after a result. If a result fails a rule, the notebook reports the failure and what it means for the decision.

| Branch | Question | Metric | Rule |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Validity | Do the groups differ only by the email? | Largest absolute standardized difference of the pre-test features; sample-ratio chi-square p-value | Less than 0.05; p-value more than 0.01 |
| 2. Effect | Does the men's email change spend, and is the test large enough? | Welch 95% CI of the spend effect; customers in each group vs. customers needed for 80% power at the observed effect | The CI excludes 0; the test has at least the customers needed |
| 3. Robustness | Does the effect hold with other methods? | Bootstrap 95% CI; effect with CUPED and with regression adjustment | The bootstrap CI excludes 0; each adjusted effect is within 10% of the unadjusted effect |
| 4. Business value | Does the recommended policy make money? | Incremental profit for 100,000 customers at the base margin and contact cost (as-01, as-02), with the 95% CI of the effect | Profit more than 0, and the lower end of its 95% CI more than 0 |
| 5. Targeting | Does a targeting rule or an uplift model beat "send to all"? | Gain of each targeting rule vs. send-to-all with its 90% bootstrap interval at the base cost. Qini area of the ML uplift models vs. rank by history. | **Model rule:** an ML uplift model replaces "rank by history" only if two conditions are true. Its mean Qini area is 20% or more higher. Its Qini area is more than 0 in at least 9 of 10 repeats. **Policy rule:** a targeting rule replaces "send to all" only if the 90% interval of its gain is above 0 at the base cost. The recommended policy passes if it follows these two rules. |

The notebook uses each branch in these sections:

- Branch 1: Step 2d (the randomization check), Step 3b and Step 6a.
- Branch 2: Step 3c (the primary metric and the power), Step 4a and Step 6b.
- Branch 3: Step 4a (the bootstrap, CUPED and the regression adjustment) and Step 6c.
- Branch 4: Step 4a (the profit of each email), Step 6d and Step 7b.
- Branch 5: Step 4d (the uplift method), Step 5, Step 6e and Step 7a.

Branches 2 and 4 are different. An effect can be real but too small to pay for the email. The CI of branch 2 says that the effect is more than $0. The rule of branch 4 says that the effect is more than the breakeven effect. Thus the notebook checks both.

::: {.tech-note}
**Technical note.** How each metric works:

- **Standardized difference.** For each pre-test feature: (mean in the email group − mean in the control group) / standard deviation in all customers. It does not depend on the unit or on the sample size. A value less than 0.05 is a small difference.
- **Sample-ratio check.** A chi-square test of the group sizes against the planned split (one third in each group). A small p-value shows a problem in the assignment, for example a group that lost customers.
- **Welch 95% CI.** Effect = mean of the email group − mean of the control group. The standard error is √(s₁²/n₁ + s₀²/n₀), and the CI is the effect ± t × standard error. The Welch test does not need equal variances in the two groups.
- **Power and MDE.** For n customers in each group and a standard deviation σ, MDE ≈ (z₀.₉₇₅ + z₀.₈₀) × σ × √(2/n) at 5% significance and 80% power. The code uses the exact t-test version (`power.t.test`). The inverse gives the customers needed for an effect: n ≈ 2 × σ² × (z₀.₉₇₅ + z₀.₈₀)² / effect².
- **Qini area.** Rank the customers by the predicted uplift. Take the top share g of the list. The Qini curve gives (mean spend of the email group − mean spend of the control group, in the top g) × g. A random order gives a straight line from 0 to the effect of "send to all". The Qini area is the mean distance between the curve and this line, at g = 5%, 10%, …, 100%. A higher area means a better order. An area of 0 or less means no better than a random order.
:::

## 3b. How we split the data

A model project splits the data into a training set and a test set. A randomized test needs a different split. The question here is not "Does a model predict well?". The question is "What does the email cause?". Thus the data has two uses, and each use needs its own split:

| Use | Question | Split | Who makes it |
|---|---|---|---|
| Effect (Steps 4a–4c) | What does the email cause, on average and in each segment? | Random assignment into three groups: no email, men's email, women's email | The data source, before the test |
| Uplift (Steps 4d and 5) | Which customers get the most from the email? | 5-fold cross-fit inside the men's email and the control group | This notebook |

**Random assignment.** The data source put each customer at random into one of the three groups. The control group then shows what the email groups do without an email. Thus a difference of means gives the causal effect, and no model must learn from the data. Branch 1 checks that the random assignment worked.

**Cross-fit for the uplift.** An uplift model learns from the same customers that it then puts in order. A model that scores the customers of its own training data finds noise and calls it uplift. Then the Qini curve looks good, but the order fails on new customers.

The fix is a cross-fit: cut the customers into five folds at random. For each fold, the model learns from the other four folds and gives an uplift to the customers of this fold. Thus each customer gets an uplift from a model that did not see that customer. We repeat this with 10 different random folds, because one cut of the folds can give a lucky result.

A single hold-out set (for example 70/30) is a simpler option. But less than 1% of the customers buy, so a test set of 30% has few buyers, and its Qini curve is noisy. With a cross-fit, each customer is in the test data one time. Rank by history needs no cross-fit, because it learns nothing from the test data.

Parameters: one third of the customers in each group (the planned split of the data source), 5 folds and 10 repeats for the uplift.

```{r}
#| label: design
#| code-summary: "Test design: group sizes, sample-ratio check, balance and the folds of the cross-fit"

# Purpose: Show the two splits of section 3b and the evidence of branch 1 (validity).
# Input:   `d` (with `arm`), `feat` (pre-test features, Step 2d), `SEED`, `RULES`.
# Output:  Table of the groups; N values of branch 1 (`d3_smd`, `d3_srm_p`, `d3_b1`) and of the folds.

# Random assignment: group sizes against the planned split of one third each.
grp <- table(d$arm)
smd_all <- sapply(c("mens", "womens"), function(a) sapply(feat, std_diff, arm = d$arm, a = a))
b1_smd <- max(abs(smd_all))
b1_srm <- srm_p(d$arm)
N$d3_smd <- formatC(b1_smd, format = "f", digits = 3)
N$d3_srm_p <- formatC(b1_srm, format = "f", digits = 2)
N$d3_b1 <- if (b1_smd < RULES$b1_smd && b1_srm > RULES$b1_srm_p) "passes" else "fails"

# Cross-fit: five folds of the men's email + control customers. Each fold is one fifth of them.
n_mc <- sum(d$arm != "womens")
N$d3_n_mc <- num(n_mc)
N$d3_n_fold <- num(n_mc / 5)
N$d3_buy_fold <- num(sum(d$conversion[d$arm != "womens"]) / 5)

kable(data.frame(
  Group = c("No email (control)", "Men's email", "Women's email"),
  Customers = num(as.vector(grp)),
  `Share of customers` = pct(as.vector(grp) / sum(grp), 2),
  `Planned share` = pct(rep(1 / 3, 3), 2),
  `Largest standardized difference against control` = c("", formatC(apply(abs(smd_all), 2, max), format = "f", digits = 3)),
  check.names = FALSE), row.names = FALSE, align = "lrrrr")
```

**How to read:** each row is one group. The last column gives the largest standardized difference of the pre-test features against the control group.

**So what:** the shares agree with the planned split (p-value `r N$d3_srm_p`), and the largest standardized difference is `r N$d3_smd`. Branch 1 `r N$d3_b1`, so a difference of means gives the effect of the email.

For the uplift, the men's email and the control group have `r N$d3_n_mc` customers. Each fold has about `r N$d3_n_fold` customers and about `r N$d3_buy_fold` buyers. This low number of buyers is the main limit of the uplift models in Step 4d.

## 3c. The primary metric and the power

::: {#dec-01 .decision}
### Which metric decides the test? {.unnumbered}

**Why this question matters.** The primary metric decides if the email "works". A metric that is easy to move but far from the money can approve an email that loses money. A metric that is close to the money but noisy can miss a profitable email. The test must also be large enough for the metric: if not, an effect of zero and a small effect look the same.

**Ways to do it.** The split axis is the place of the metric on the path from the email to the profit. The four places are a visit, a purchase, the dollars of the purchase, and the value after the test window. These four places cover all metrics of an email test, and each metric belongs to one of them.

| Place on the path | Metric | Advantage | Main risk | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Engagement | Email open or click; website visit | Many customers act, so the test has the most power. | An email can increase visits without more spend. The data has no opens or clicks. | Visit: possible. Test it. Opens and clicks: screened out (not in the data). |
| Purchase | Conversion (the customer buys) | Closer to the money than a visit. | Less than 1% of customers buy, so the test has less power. It ignores the size of each purchase. | Possible. Test it. |
| Dollars | Spend in the two weeks | Gives dollars. The profit is margin × spend − contact cost, so the profit needs spend. | Most customers spend $0 and a few spend a lot, so the noise is large. | Possible. Test it. |
| After the window | Spend over 12 months, or the customer lifetime value | Shows a long effect or fatigue. | The data stops after two weeks (as-03). | Screened out (not in the data) |

**Evidence.** For each metric, the code calculates the MDE of this test at 5% significance and 80% power. It compares the MDE with the observed effect of each email. It also gives the customers in each group that the test needs to find each observed effect (branch 2).

```{r}
#| label: dec-01-evidence
#| code-summary: "Evidence: MDE of each metric against the observed effect"

# Purpose: Compare the power of visit, conversion and spend for this test (dec-01, branch 2).
# Input:   `d`, `ALPHA`, `POWER`, mde_metric() (case03_helpers.R).
# Output:  `n_arm` (customers in the smallest group), `mde` (matrix: one column for each metric),
#          N values of the MDE and of the customers needed.

n_arm <- min(table(d$arm))
mde <- sapply(c(visit = "visit", conversion = "conversion", spend = "spend"),
              function(y) mde_metric(d[[y]], d$arm, n_arm))
mde <- rbind(mde, need = mde["need_w", ])  # Old row name: customers needed for the women's effect

N$mde_spend <- usd(mde["mde", "spend"])
N$eff_w_spend <- usd(mde["womens", "spend"])
N$eff_m_spend <- usd(mde["mens", "spend"])
N$need_w_spend <- num(mde["need_w", "spend"])
N$need_m_spend <- num(mde["need_m", "spend"])
N$need_ratio <- formatC(n_arm / mde["need_w", "spend"], format = "f", digits = 1)
N$need_ratio_m <- formatC(n_arm / mde["need_m", "spend"], format = "f", digits = 1)
N$d3_n_arm <- num(n_arm)
N$mde_conv <- pct(mde["mde", "conversion"], 2)
N$base_conv <- pct(mde["base", "conversion"], 2)
N$mde_conv_rel <- pct(mde["mde", "conversion"] / mde["base", "conversion"], 0)
N$mde_spend_rel <- pct(mde["mde", "spend"] / mde["base", "spend"], 0)
N$n_above_mde <- sum(mde[c("mens", "womens"), ] > rbind(mde["mde", ], mde["mde", ]))
N$d3_b2_power <- if (n_arm >= mde["need_m", "spend"]) "has" else "does not have"

f_metric <- function(x, y) if (y == "spend") usd(x, 3) else pct(x, 2)
kable(data.frame(
  Metric = c("Visit", "Conversion", "Spend"),
  `Control mean` = mapply(f_metric, mde["base", ], colnames(mde)),
  MDE = mapply(f_metric, mde["mde", ], colnames(mde)),
  `Effect, men's` = mapply(f_metric, mde["mens", ], colnames(mde)),
  `Effect, women's` = mapply(f_metric, mde["womens", ], colnames(mde)),
  `Customers needed, men's effect` = num(mde["need_m", ]),
  `Customers needed, women's effect` = num(mde["need_w", ]),
  check.names = FALSE), row.names = FALSE, align = "lrrrrrr")
```

**How to read:** the MDE is the smallest effect that this test finds in 80% of tests. An observed effect above the MDE is large enough for this test. The last two columns give the customers that each group needs to find the observed effect.

**So what:** of the 6 effects (2 emails × 3 metrics), `r N$n_above_mde` are larger than the MDE. For spend, the women's effect is only a little above the MDE.

::: {.choice}
**Decision.** Spend is the primary metric. Visit and conversion are secondary metrics: they help to explain the spend result.
:::

**Why.** Three reasons, from the most important:

1. **The decision is about profit, and profit needs dollars.** The profit of each email is margin × change in spend − contact cost. A visit or a conversion has no dollar value without a second assumption: the spend of each buyer.
2. **The test is large enough for spend.** The MDE of spend is `r N$mde_spend`. The men's email gives `r N$eff_m_spend`, and the women's email gives `r N$eff_w_spend`. To find the men's effect, the test needs `r N$need_m_spend` customers in each group. It has `r N$d3_n_arm`, or `r N$need_ratio_m` times this number. Thus the test `r N$d3_b2_power` the customers that branch 2 needs.
3. **The power is tight for the women's email.** To find the women's effect, the test needs `r N$need_w_spend` customers in each group, so it has only `r N$need_ratio` times this number. Thus a smaller effect than the women's effect is not clear in this test.

Spend has the least power of the three metrics. For spend, the MDE is `r N$mde_spend_rel` of the control mean. For conversion, it is `r N$mde_conv_rel` of the control mean (`r N$mde_conv` on a base of `r N$base_conv`). We accept the lower power, because only spend gives the dollars.

**What would change the decision.** If a test has fewer customers, for example a test in one segment, spend does not have sufficient power. Then use conversion as the primary metric, and calculate the dollars with the mean spend of a buyer.
:::

::: {.business-note}
**Business note.** The data source made a fair split: the three groups look the same before the test. The primary metric is spend, because the campaign decision needs dollars. The test can find an effect of `r N$mde_spend` for each customer, and the men's email gives `r N$eff_m_spend`. Step 4 measures the effect of each email and checks it with other methods.
:::

# Step 4. Build models {#step-4}

::: {.bridge}
Step 3 fixed the rules of the test and made spend the primary metric. The test can find an effect of `r N$mde_spend` for each customer, and the first look gives `r N$eff_m_spend` for the men's email. That first look is only a difference of two means.

This step answers four questions in order. How large is the effect of each email, with which method (4a)? Which version do we send (4b)? Does the effect change by segment (4c)? Which method puts the customers in order of uplift (4d)?
:::

::: {.purpose}
**Purpose.** This step measures the effect of each email and builds the tools that select the version and the customers. It supports this decision: send an email or not, which version, and to which customers.
:::

## 4a. Average effect

The average effect is the base of all later decisions. If the effect is not real, no version and no list of customers can make money. Two choices set the result: the method that compares the spend of two groups, and the use of the pre-test data.

::: {#dec-02 .decision}
### Which method measures the change in mean spend? {.unnumbered}

**Why this question matters.** The profit of the campaign is margin × change in mean spend × customers − contact cost. Thus the method must give the change in mean spend in dollars, with an interval that we can trust. Spend has a long right tail: `r N$spend_zero` of the customers spend $0, and a few spend up to `r N$spend_max`. A method that is wrong for this shape can give a false interval.

**Ways to do it.** The split axis is what the method compares between the two groups: the mean, the rank of each customer, or a model of the outcome. These three groups cover the usual methods, and each method belongs to one of them.

| What it compares | Method | Advantage | Main risk | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| The mean | Welch t-test | Simple. All reviewers know it. Gives the change in dollars. | With a long tail and a small sample, the interval can be wrong. | Possible. Test it. |
| The mean | Bootstrap of the difference of means | Gives the change in dollars. Needs no normal distribution. | More computation. It needs a seed to repeat the result. | Possible. Test it. |
| The rank | Mann-Whitney test | Not sensitive to large values. | It tests if one group usually spends more. It gives no change in dollars. | Possible. Test it as a check. |
| A model of the outcome | Two-part model (conversion × spend of a buyer), Tobit model, or a model of log(spend) | Shows where the effect comes from. | In a randomized test, the two-part model gives the same mean with more parts. Tobit needs a normal distribution. A log cannot use $0 and changes the question. | Screened out |

**Evidence.** The code calculates the three possible methods for the two emails. The bootstrap uses 2,000 samples with the seed of the setup chunk.

```{r}
#| label: dec-02-evidence
#| code-summary: "Evidence: three methods on the real spend"

# Purpose: Compare the Welch t-test, the Mann-Whitney test and the bootstrap on the spend (dec-02, branch 3).
# Input:   `d`, `SEED`, welch() and boot_diff() (case03_helpers.R).
# Output:  Table `dec02`, `boot_ci` (bootstrap 95% CI of each email, numbers), N values of the bootstrap.

B <- 2000
y0 <- d$spend[d$arm == "control"]
boot_ci <- matrix(NA_real_, 2, 2, dimnames = list(c("mens", "womens"), c("lo", "hi")))
dec02 <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("mens", "womens"), function(a) {
  y1 <- d$spend[d$arm == a]
  w <- welch(y1, y0)
  wt <- wilcox.test(y1, y0)
  bd <- boot_diff(y1, y0, B, SEED)
  boot_ci[a, ] <<- quantile(bd, c(0.025, 0.975))  # Keep the numbers for Step 6 (branch 3)
  data.frame(Email = rep(ifelse(a == "mens", "Men's", "Women's"), 3),
             Method = c("A. Welch t-test", "B. Mann-Whitney", "C. Bootstrap"),
             `Change in mean spend` = c(usd(w[["eff"]], 3), "not measured", usd(w[["eff"]], 3)),
             `95% CI` = c(ci_txt(w[["lo"]], w[["hi"]]), "not measured", ci_txt(boot_ci[a, 1], boot_ci[a, 2])),
             `p-value` = c(fmt_p(w[["p"]]), fmt_p(wt$p.value), fmt_p(2 * min(mean(bd <= 0), mean(bd >= 0)))),
             check.names = FALSE)
}))
N$boot_ci_m <- ci_txt(boot_ci["mens", 1], boot_ci["mens", 2])
N$boot_ci_w <- ci_txt(boot_ci["womens", 1], boot_ci["womens", 2])
N$n_arm_min <- num(min(table(d$arm)))
w_m <- welch(d$spend[d$arm == "mens"], y0)
N$welch_ci_m <- ci_txt(w_m[["lo"]], w_m[["hi"]])
kable(dec02, row.names = FALSE)
```

**How to read:** each email has three rows, one for each method. The Mann-Whitney test gives only a p-value.

**So what:** the Welch t-test and the bootstrap give almost the same interval for each email.

::: {.choice}
**Decision.** The Welch t-test. The bootstrap is a check (branch 3).
:::

**Why.** The business decision uses total dollars, so the method must measure the change in mean spend. For the men's email, the Welch interval is `r N$welch_ci_m`, and the bootstrap interval is `r N$boot_ci_m`. Each group has `r N$n_arm_min` or more customers, so the mean is close to a normal distribution, even with the long tail. The Welch t-test is simpler to explain and to repeat. The Mann-Whitney test gives no dollar value, so it cannot go into the profit calculation.

**What would change the decision.** If a group has fewer than about 5,000 customers, or the top 1% of customers give most of the spend, use the bootstrap.
:::

::: {#dec-03 .decision}
### Can the pre-test data make the interval smaller? {.unnumbered}

**Why this question matters.** A smaller interval gives a clearer decision with the same customers. In a later test, it can also give the same power with fewer customers, and thus a lower cost of the test. Each method that removes noise also adds a model that a reviewer must check.

**Ways to do it.** The split axis is how much pre-test data adjusts the outcome. The four groups are no data, one feature, all features in a linear model, and an ML prediction.

| Pre-test data | Method | Advantage | Main risk | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| None | Difference of means | Simple. No model. | The interval can be wider than necessary. | Possible. Test it. |
| One feature | CUPED with history | A standard method. It removes the part of the spend that history predicts. | It helps only if history predicts the spend in the test window. | Possible. Test it. |
| All features, linear | Regression adjustment (or post-stratification by segment, the same idea with cells) | Uses all the pre-test data. | More complex. A reviewer must check the model. | Possible. Test it. |
| All features, ML model | CUPAC: an ML prediction of the spend is the covariate | Can find curves and interactions. | A model to train and to approve. It helps only if the linear methods help. | Screened out if the linear methods give no gain |

**Evidence.** The code adjusts each metric of each email with the possible methods. The table gives the effect and the width of the 95% CI against no adjustment. A width of 100% means no gain. The effects also give branch 3: each adjusted effect must be within 10% of the unadjusted effect.

```{r}
#| label: dec-03-evidence
#| code-summary: "Evidence: CUPED and regression adjustment"

# Purpose: Compare no adjustment, CUPED and the regression adjustment for each metric (dec-03, branch 3).
# Input:   `d`, cuped() (case03_helpers.R), `RULES`.
# Output:  Table `dec03`, `adj_eff` (the spend effects of the three options, numbers), N values.

dec03 <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("visit", "conversion", "spend"), function(y) do.call(rbind, lapply(c("mens", "womens"), function(a) {
  s <- d[d$arm %in% c("control", a), ]
  s$t <- as.integer(s$arm == a)
  s$y_cuped <- cuped(s[[y]], s$history)
  fits <- list(A = lm(as.formula(paste(y, "~ t")), s),
               B = lm(y_cuped ~ t, s),
               C = lm(as.formula(paste(y, "~ t + lhist + recency + mens + womens + zip + newbie + channel")), s))
  se <- sapply(fits, function(f) summary(f)$coefficients["t", 2])
  data.frame(Metric = y, Email = ifelse(a == "mens", "Men's", "Women's"),
             `Effect, A` = coef(fits$A)["t"], `Effect, B` = coef(fits$B)["t"], `Effect, C` = coef(fits$C)["t"],
             `CI width B / A` = pct(se["B"] / se["A"]), `CI width C / A` = pct(se["C"] / se["A"]),
             r_hist = cor(s[[y]], s$history), gain = 1 - min(se) / se["A"], check.names = FALSE)
}))))
N$r_hist_spend <- formatC(max(dec03$r_hist[dec03$Metric == "spend"]), format = "f", digits = 3)
N$cuped_best <- pct(max(dec03$gain[dec03$Metric == "spend"]), 2)
N$cuped_visit <- pct(max(dec03$gain[dec03$Metric == "visit"]), 1)

# Branch 3: distance of each adjusted spend effect from the unadjusted effect.
adj_eff <- dec03[dec03$Metric == "spend", c("Email", "Effect, A", "Effect, B", "Effect, C")]
rownames(adj_eff) <- c("mens", "womens")
adj_dev <- abs(adj_eff[, c("Effect, B", "Effect, C")] / adj_eff[, "Effect, A"] - 1)
N$cuped_m <- usd(adj_eff["mens", "Effect, B"], 3)
N$reg_m <- usd(adj_eff["mens", "Effect, C"], 3)
N$ate_m_a <- usd(adj_eff["mens", "Effect, A"], 3)
N$adj_dev_m <- pct(max(adj_dev["mens", ]), 1)

dec03$r_hist <- NULL
dec03$gain <- NULL
kable(dec03, digits = 4, row.names = FALSE)
```

**How to read:** option A has no adjustment, option B uses CUPED with history, and option C uses the regression adjustment. The last two columns give the width of the interval of B and C against A.

**So what:** the adjustments do not change the effects, and they make the interval of spend almost no smaller.

::: {.choice}
**Decision.** No adjustment. CUPED and the regression adjustment stay as a check (branch 3).
:::

**Why.** The correlation of history with the spend in the test window is only `r N$r_hist_spend`. Thus CUPED and the regression make the interval of spend at most `r N$cuped_best` smaller. For visits, the gain is at most `r N$cuped_visit`. The effects stay the same: for the men's email, `r N$ate_m_a` with no adjustment, `r N$cuped_m` with CUPED and `r N$reg_m` with the regression. The largest distance is `r N$adj_dev_m`.

A simple method is better for the same result, and an ML adjustment cannot help when the linear methods find nothing.

**What would change the decision.** If the outcome repeats each month, CUPED can make the interval much smaller. For example, the monthly spend on a card is similar from one month to the next. In a card test, use CUPED with the spend of the three months before the test.
:::

### The effect of each email

The table gives the effect of each email on the three metrics, with the Welch t-test. The chart then compares the spend effect with the breakeven effect: contact cost / margin. If the effect is below the breakeven effect, the email loses money.

```{r}
#| label: ate
#| code-summary: "Effect of each email, with the Welch t-test"

# Purpose: The effect of each email on visit, conversion and spend (Welch t-test, dec-02).
# Input:   `d`, `MARGIN`, `COST`, welch() and breakeven() (case03_helpers.R).
# Output:  `ate` (all effects), `ATE`, `ATE_LO`, `ATE_HI` (spend effect of each email and its 95% CI), N values.

ate <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("visit", "conversion", "spend"), function(y) do.call(rbind, lapply(c("mens", "womens"), function(a) {
  y1 <- d[[y]][d$arm == a]; y0 <- d[[y]][d$arm == "control"]
  w <- welch(y1, y0)
  data.frame(metric = y, arm = a, eff = w[["eff"]], lo = w[["lo"]], hi = w[["hi"]],
             rel = w[["eff"]] / mean(y0), p = w[["p"]])
}))))
ATE <- setNames(ate$eff[ate$metric == "spend"], c("mens", "womens"))
ATE_LO <- setNames(ate$lo[ate$metric == "spend"], c("mens", "womens"))
ATE_HI <- setNames(ate$hi[ate$metric == "spend"], c("mens", "womens"))
N$ate_m <- usd(ATE["mens"]); N$ci_m <- ci_txt(ATE_LO["mens"], ATE_HI["mens"])
N$ate_w <- usd(ATE["womens"]); N$ci_w <- ci_txt(ATE_LO["womens"], ATE_HI["womens"])
N$rel_m <- pct(ate$rel[ate$metric == "spend" & ate$arm == "mens"], 0)
N$prof_m <- usd(MARGIN * ATE["mens"] - COST, 3)
N$prof_w <- usd(MARGIN * ATE["womens"] - COST, 3)
N$roi_m <- formatC(MARGIN * ATE["mens"] / COST, format = "f", digits = 1)
N$breakeven_eff <- usd(breakeven())
N$ate_lo_m <- usd(ATE_LO["mens"]); N$ate_lo_w <- usd(ATE_LO["womens"])
N$w_lo_vs_be <- if (ATE_LO["womens"] > breakeven()) "above" else "below"
N$m_lo_vs_be <- if (ATE_LO["mens"] > breakeven()) "above" else "below"
N$d4_b2_ci <- if (ATE_LO["mens"] > 0) "excludes" else "includes"

kable(data.frame(
  Metric = c("Visit", "Visit", "Conversion", "Conversion", "Spend", "Spend"),
  Email = rep(c("Men's", "Women's"), 3),
  Effect = ifelse(ate$metric == "spend", usd(ate$eff, 3), paste(formatC(100 * ate$eff, format = "f", digits = 2), "points")),
  `95% CI` = ifelse(ate$metric == "spend", ci_txt(ate$lo, ate$hi), paste0("[", formatC(100 * ate$lo, format = "f", digits = 2), ", ", formatC(100 * ate$hi, format = "f", digits = 2), "]")),
  `Change against control` = paste0("+", pct(ate$rel, 0)),
  `p-value` = fmt_p(ate$p), check.names = FALSE), row.names = FALSE, align = "llrrrr")
```

```{r}
#| label: ate-plot
#| code-summary: "Chart: spend effect of each email with the 95% CI and the breakeven effect"
#| fig-height: 3.2

# Purpose: Show the spend effect of each email against $0 and against the breakeven effect.
# Input:   `ATE`, `ATE_LO`, `ATE_HI`, breakeven(), `CS` and the chart functions (chart_style.R).
# Output:  Chart only.

yy <- c(mens = 2, womens = 1)
pcol <- c(mens = CS$blue, womens = CS$gray)
cs_setup(mar = c(3.6, 7.5, 0.6, 1.5))
plot(ATE, yy, xlim = c(0, max(ATE_HI) * 1.45), ylim = c(0.5, 2.6), pch = 19, cex = 1.4, col = pcol,
     yaxt = "n", xaxt = "n", xlab = "Change in mean spend for each customer, against no email", ylab = "")
segments(ATE_LO, yy, ATE_HI, yy, col = pcol, lwd = 3)
cs_dollar_axis(1)
axis(2, at = yy, labels = c("Men's email", "Women's email"), tick = FALSE, col.axis = CS$ink)
abline(v = breakeven(), lty = 2, col = CS$gray)
text(breakeven(), 2.55, paste0("Breakeven effect ", usd(breakeven())), pos = 4, cex = 0.75, col = CS$muted)
# Direct labels to the right of each interval: the effect and its 95% CI.
text(ATE_HI, yy, paste0(usd(ATE), "  ", ci_txt(ATE_LO, ATE_HI)), pos = 4, cex = 0.8, col = pcol, font = c(2, 1))
cs_title(paste0("The men's email adds ", N$ate_m, " of spend for each customer, ", N$roi_m, " times the breakeven"),
         "Change in mean spend in the two weeks after the email, with the Welch 95% CI")
```

**How to read:** each point is the change in mean spend of one email, against the control group. The line is the 95% CI. The dashed line is the breakeven effect at a 30% margin (as-01) and a $0.10 contact cost (as-02).

**So what:** the lower end of the men's interval is `r N$ate_lo_m`, `r N$m_lo_vs_be` the breakeven effect of `r N$breakeven_eff`. The lower end of the women's interval is `r N$ate_lo_w`, `r N$w_lo_vs_be` the breakeven effect.

Both emails increase visits, conversions and spend. The men's email increases the mean spend by `r N$ate_m` for each customer (95% CI `r N$ci_m`), or `r N$rel_m` more than the control group. The Welch CI `r N$d4_b2_ci` $0, as branch 2 asks. The women's email increases the mean spend by `r N$ate_w` (95% CI `r N$ci_w`).

At a 30% margin and a $0.10 contact cost, each men's email gives `r N$prof_m` of profit. Each women's email gives `r N$prof_w`. The ROI of the men's email is `r N$roi_m`. Thus both emails make money on average, and the men's email makes more. Section 4b examines if a mix of the two versions makes more than the men's email alone.

## 4b. Email version

Section 4a showed that both emails increase spend. The men's email adds `r N$ate_m` for each customer, and the women's email adds `r N$ate_w`. But the mean effect of a version mixes customers who buy men's products, women's products or both. The next question is: do we send one version to all customers, or the version that matches the products of each customer?

::: {#dec-04 .decision}
### Which email version do we send? {.unnumbered}

**Why this question matters.** The version sets the size of the effect for each customer, and thus the profit of the campaign. A second version doubles the creative work and makes the campaign harder to run. It earns its place only if it adds spend for some customers.

**Ways to do it.** The split axis is: does the version depend on the customer? If not, one version goes to all customers. If yes, a known feature or a model selects the version. A fifth way sends both versions to the same customer. Each way then goes through one filter: can this test measure its effect?

| Group | Option | Advantage | Main risk | Screen |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| One version for all | A. Men's email to all customers | One email. Simple to run. The largest mean effect. | Customers who buy only women's products can prefer the women's email. | Test |
| One version for all | B. Women's email to all customers | One email. | A smaller mean effect. | Test |
| Version by a known feature | C. Match the version to the product history | Each customer gets the products that they buy. | Two emails. It helps only if the women's email is better for some customers. | Test |
| Version by a model | D. A model predicts the effect of each version for each customer and selects the larger one | Uses all features. | The choice depends on the difference of two noisy uplift estimates. Less than 1% of customers convert. | Screened out: Section 4d tests uplift models for one email. A model for the difference of two emails has more noise. |
| Both versions | E. Send both emails to the same customer | No choice is necessary. | Two contact costs. Fatigue. | Screened out: the test has no group with both emails, so the data cannot measure the effect. |

**Evidence.** The table gives the spend effect of each version in each product history, with its Welch 95% CI. The last two columns compare the two versions directly. Then the code calculates the mean effect of option C. It adds the effect of the matched version in each product history, with the share of the customers as the weight.

```{r}
#| label: dec-04-evidence
#| code-summary: "Evidence: spend effect of each version by product history, and the mean effect of option C"

# Purpose: Compare the two versions in each product history, and option C against option A (dec-04).
# Input:   `d`, `ATE` (Section 4a).
# Output:  Table `dec04`. `eff_c` (mean effect of option C). N values for the text.

dec04 <- do.call(rbind, lapply(levels(d$buyer), function(b) {
  s <- d[d$buyer == b, ]
  # Welch t-test of each email against the control group in this product history.
  r <- sapply(c("mens", "womens"), function(a) {
    tt <- t.test(s$spend[s$arm == a], s$spend[s$arm == "control"])
    c(-diff(tt$estimate), tt$conf.int)
  })
  # Direct comparison of the two versions.
  dw <- t.test(s$spend[s$arm == "mens"], s$spend[s$arm == "womens"])
  data.frame(`Product history` = b, Customers = num(nrow(s)),
             `Effect, men's` = usd(r[1, "mens"]), `95% CI, men's` = ci_txt(r[2, "mens"], r[3, "mens"]),
             `Effect, women's` = usd(r[1, "womens"]), `95% CI, women's` = ci_txt(r[2, "womens"], r[3, "womens"]),
             `Men's minus women's` = usd(-diff(dw$estimate)), `p-value` = fmt_p(dw$p.value),
             check.names = FALSE)
}))
kable(dec04, row.names = FALSE, align = "lrrrrrrr")

# Option C: men's email to "mens only" and "both", women's email to "womens only".
eff_c <- sum(sapply(levels(d$buyer), function(b) {
  a <- if (b == "womens only") "womens" else "mens"
  mean(d$buyer == b) * (mean(d$spend[d$buyer == b & d$arm == a]) - mean(d$spend[d$buyer == b & d$arm == "control"]))
}))
N$eff_c <- usd(eff_c, 3)
N$ate_m3 <- usd(ATE["mens"], 3)
N$eff_c_gain <- unname(usd(eff_c - ATE["mens"], 3))
N$eff_c_gain_100k <- unname(usd(CAMPAIGN * MARGIN * (eff_c - ATE["mens"]), 0))
N$w_only_m <- dec04$`Effect, men's`[dec04$`Product history` == "womens only"]
N$w_only_w <- dec04$`Effect, women's`[dec04$`Product history` == "womens only"]
N$m_only_w <- dec04$`Effect, women's`[dec04$`Product history` == "mens only"]
N$m_only_w_ci <- dec04$`95% CI, women's`[dec04$`Product history` == "mens only"]
N$both_m <- dec04$`Effect, men's`[dec04$`Product history` == "both"]
N$both_w <- dec04$`Effect, women's`[dec04$`Product history` == "both"]
```

::: {.choice}
**Decision.** Option A: send the men's email to all customers.
:::

**Why.** The men's email increases spend in each product history. For the customers who buy only men's products, the women's email has no clear effect: `r N$m_only_w`, with a 95% CI of `r N$m_only_w_ci`. For the customers who buy both product types, the men's email gives `r N$both_m` and the women's email `r N$both_w`.

The women's email works as well as the men's email only for the customers who buy only women's products: `r N$w_only_w` against `r N$w_only_m`. Thus option C changes the version only where the two versions are equal. Option C gives a mean effect of `r N$eff_c`, and option A gives `r N$ate_m3`. The difference of `r N$eff_c_gain` adds only `r N$eff_c_gain_100k` of margin for 100,000 customers, but it needs a second email.

**What would change the decision.** If Marketing makes a new women's email with a larger effect for women's buyers, test option C again. The test then needs a group for each version in that product history.
:::

## 4c. Segment effects

Section 4b selected the men's email. From this section, the notebook uses only the men's email and the control group. The mean effect can hide a segment where the email loses money. The next question is: does the effect of the men's email change by segment, and how do we report it without false results?

::: {#dec-05 .decision}
### How do we report the effect in each segment? {.unnumbered}

**Why this question matters.** Marketing wants to know where the email pays for itself. Five features give many segments. If we test each segment at 5%, some segments show an effect by chance. A false segment effect can stop the email for customers where it makes money, or send it where it loses money.

**Ways to do it.** The split axis is: how does the report control the false results? It can use no control, correct each p-value, first test if the effect changes at all, or make the segment estimates smaller toward the mean. Each way then goes through one filter: can a reviewer check it without a new model?

| Group | Option | Advantage | Main risk | Screen |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| No control | A. Effect of each segment, p < 0.05 | Simple. | With many segments, some segments show an effect by chance. | Test |
| Correct each p-value | B. Effect of each segment, with the Holm correction | Controls the probability of one or more false results. | Less power for each segment. | Test |
| Test the change first | C. Interaction test for each feature. Then option B for the features with an interaction. | Examines only the features where the effect really changes. | Two steps. | Test |
| Estimates toward the mean | D. A hierarchical model that pulls each segment effect toward the mean effect | Uses all segments together. Fewer extreme results. | It needs a prior and a model review. The result depends on the prior. | Screened out: Section 4d tests a model that finds the customers with a large uplift. Each customer gets an uplift from a model that did not see that customer. |

**Evidence.** The first table gives the interaction test for each feature, with the Holm correction over the features. The last row tests a straight-line change of the effect with the history in dollars. The second table repeats options A and B on 50 placebo data sets. In each placebo data set, the code puts the treatment flag in a random order. Thus the true effect is zero in each segment, and each segment effect that a test finds is false.

::: {.tech-note}
**Technical note.** The interaction test for a feature *v* compares two linear models with an F-test: spend ~ *t* + *v* against spend ~ *t* × *v*. The second model gives one effect of the email for each level of *v*. A small p-value shows that the effect changes with *v*.

The Holm correction sorts the *k* p-values from small to large. It multiplies the *j*-th p-value by (*k* − *j* + 1) and keeps the order. It keeps the probability of one or more false results at 5% or less. The chart below uses a Bonferroni width for each interval: the Welch standard error times the normal quantile at 1 − 0.05 / (2*k*). This width is a safe bound for the Holm intervals.
:::

```{r}
#| label: dec-05-evidence
#| code-summary: "Evidence: interaction tests and a placebo test"

# Purpose: Test if the effect changes by segment, and measure the false results of options A and B (dec-05).
# Input:   `d`, `SEED`, `ALPHA`.
# Output:  `m` (men's email and control, with `t`), `seg_vars`, `inter` (interaction p-values),
#          `placebo`. N values for the text.

m <- d[d$arm != "womens", ]
m$t <- as.integer(m$arm == "mens")  # 1 = men's email, 0 = control
seg_vars <- c(`History bucket` = "hseg", `Product history` = "buyer", `New customer` = "newbie",
              Channel = "channel", `Area type` = "zip")
# F-test of the interaction for each feature.
inter <- sapply(seg_vars, function(v) {
  f0 <- lm(as.formula(paste("spend ~ t + factor(", v, ")")), m)
  f1 <- lm(as.formula(paste("spend ~ t * factor(", v, ")")), m)
  anova(f0, f1)[2, "Pr(>F)"]
})
lin <- summary(lm(spend ~ t * history, m))$coefficients
inter <- c(inter, `History (straight line)` = lin["t:history", 4])
kable(data.frame(Feature = names(inter), `Interaction p-value` = fmt_p(inter),
                 `Holm p-value` = fmt_p(p.adjust(inter, "holm")), check.names = FALSE), row.names = FALSE)

# Placebo: a random order of the treatment flag. Each segment effect that a test finds is false.
seg_tests <- function(dat) {
  unlist(lapply(seg_vars, function(v) sapply(split(dat, dat[[v]]), function(s) t.test(s$spend[s$t == 1], s$spend[s$t == 0])$p.value)))
}
n_seg <- length(seg_tests(m))
set.seed(SEED)
placebo <- replicate(50, {
  p <- m
  p$t <- sample(p$t)
  ps <- seg_tests(p)
  c(raw = sum(ps < ALPHA), holm = sum(p.adjust(ps, "holm") < ALPHA))
})
kable(data.frame(Option = c("A. p < 0.05", "B. Holm correction"),
                 `Mean number of false segment effects` = paste0(formatC(rowMeans(placebo), format = "f", digits = 2), " of ", n_seg),
                 `Placebo tests with one or more false results` = pct(rowMeans(placebo > 0), 0), check.names = FALSE), row.names = FALSE)
N$n_seg_tests <- n_seg
N$placebo_any <- pct(mean(placebo["raw", ] > 0), 0)
N$placebo_holm <- pct(mean(placebo["holm", ] > 0), 0)
N$n_inter <- sum(p.adjust(inter, "holm") < ALPHA)
N$min_raw <- names(inter)[which.min(inter)]
N$min_raw_p <- fmt_p(min(inter))
N$min_holm_p <- fmt_p(min(p.adjust(inter, "holm")))
N$lin_slope <- usd(100 * lin["t:history", 1])
```

::: {.choice}
**Decision.** Option C: the interaction test first, then the effect of each segment with the Holm correction. Report the segment effects as a description, not as a reason to target.
:::

**Why.** The five features give `r N$n_seg_tests` segments. The placebo data has no real effect, but option A finds one or more false segment effects in `r N$placebo_any` of the runs.

With the Holm correction, this share is `r N$placebo_holm`. In this test, `r N$n_inter` features have an interaction after the Holm correction. The smallest raw p-value is `r N$min_raw_p` (`r N$min_raw`), and its Holm p-value is `r N$min_holm_p`. Thus the data gives only weak evidence that the effect changes by segment.

The straight-line test points in one direction: each $100 of history adds about `r N$lin_slope` to the effect. Section 4d uses this signal: it puts the customers in order by history.

**What would change the decision.** If the business names one or two segments before the test, test only these segments. Then the correction is not necessary.
:::

The chart shows the effect of the men's email in each history bucket and each product history. Each interval has the Holm-adjusted width of the technical note above. Two reference lines help to read it. The first is the mean effect of Section 4a. The second is the breakeven effect: the contact cost divided by the margin (as-01, as-02). Above the breakeven effect, the email pays for itself.

```{r}
#| label: seg-plot
#| code-summary: "Chart: spend effect of the men's email by segment, with Holm-adjusted 95% intervals"
#| fig-height: 4.8

# Purpose: Show the segment effects of dec-05 against the mean effect and the breakeven effect.
# Input:   `m`, `ATE`, `ALPHA`, `COST` (as-02), `MARGIN` (as-01), `CS` and the functions of chart_style.R.
# Output:  `seg` (one row for each segment). Chart. N values for the text.

if (!exists("CS")) source("chart_style.R")  # The setup chunk sources it. This line keeps a part test alive.
seg <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("hseg", "buyer"), function(v) do.call(rbind, lapply(levels(m[[v]]), function(lv) {
  s <- m[m[[v]] == lv, ]
  tt <- t.test(s$spend[s$t == 1], s$spend[s$t == 0])
  data.frame(var = v, level = lv, n = nrow(s), eff = -diff(tt$estimate), se = tt$stderr, p = tt$p.value)
}))))
k <- nrow(seg)
z <- qnorm(1 - ALPHA / (2 * k))  # Bonferroni width. It is a safe bound for the Holm intervals.
seg$lo <- seg$eff - z * seg$se
seg$hi <- seg$eff + z * seg$se
seg$p_holm <- p.adjust(seg$p, "holm")
be_seg <- COST / MARGIN
N$breakeven_eff <- usd(be_seg)
N$n_seg_above <- sum(seg$eff > be_seg)
N$k_seg <- k
N$n_seg_holm <- sum(seg$p_holm < ALPHA & seg$eff > 0)
N$n_seg_lo_above <- sum(seg$lo > be_seg)
# History of $350 or more against less: the pattern that Section 4d uses.
hi_h <- m$history >= 350
N$eff_hist_hi <- usd(mean(m$spend[hi_h & m$t == 1]) - mean(m$spend[hi_h & m$t == 0]))
N$eff_hist_lo <- usd(mean(m$spend[!hi_h & m$t == 1]) - mean(m$spend[!hi_h & m$t == 0]))

# Labels: the segment and its number of customers.
buyer_lab <- c(`mens only` = "Men's products only", `womens only` = "Women's products only", both = "Both product types")
lab <- ifelse(seg$var == "hseg", paste("History", seg$level), buyer_lab[seg$level])
lab <- paste0(lab, "  (", num(seg$n), ")")
yy <- rev(seq_len(k))
pcol <- ifelse(seg$p_holm < ALPHA, CS$blue, CS$gray)

cs_setup(mar = c(3.6, 13, 1.6, 1.5))
plot(NA, xlim = range(c(seg$lo, seg$hi, 0)), ylim = c(0.5, k + 0.5), axes = FALSE,
     xlab = "Change in mean spend for each customer ($)", ylab = "")
axis(1, at = axTicks(1), labels = usd(axTicks(1), 0))  # usd() writes a plain minus sign
axis(2, at = yy, labels = lab, tick = FALSE, col.axis = CS$ink, cex.axis = 0.8)
abline(v = 0, col = CS$light_gray)
abline(h = sum(seg$var == "buyer") + 0.5, col = CS$light_gray, lty = 3)  # Line between the two features
# Reference lines with direct labels at the top: the mean effect and the breakeven effect.
abline(v = ATE["mens"], col = CS$navy, lty = 2, lwd = 1.2)
abline(v = be_seg, col = CS$muted, lty = 3, lwd = 1.2)
text(ATE["mens"], k + 0.9, paste0(" Mean effect ", N$ate_m), adj = c(0, 0.5), xpd = NA, col = CS$navy, cex = 0.75)
text(be_seg, k + 0.9, paste0("Breakeven ", N$breakeven_eff, " "), adj = c(1, 0.5), xpd = NA, col = CS$muted, cex = 0.75)
# Intervals and point effects. Blue: Holm p < 0.05. Gray: the others.
segments(seg$lo, yy, seg$hi, yy, col = pcol, lwd = 2.5)
points(seg$eff, yy, pch = 19, col = pcol, cex = 1.1)
cs_title(paste0("The effect beats the ", N$breakeven_eff, " breakeven in ", N$n_seg_above, " of ",
                N$k_seg, " segments, with wide intervals"),
         "Spend effect of the men's email, Holm-adjusted 95% intervals. Blue: Holm p < 0.05; gray: the others")
```

**How to read:** each row is one segment, with its number of customers in brackets. The dot is the spend effect of the men's email, and the line is its Holm-adjusted 95% interval. A blue line has a Holm p-value less than 0.05.

**So what:** the point effect is above the breakeven effect of `r N$breakeven_eff` in `r N$n_seg_above` of `r N$k_seg` segments. But only `r N$n_seg_holm` segments have a Holm p-value less than 0.05, and `r N$n_seg_lo_above` intervals are fully above the breakeven effect. Thus one feature at a time cannot show a segment where the email loses money. The effect is `r N$eff_hist_hi` for customers with $350 or more of history and `r N$eff_hist_lo` for the others. Section 4d tests if an order by history, or a model, finds the customers with the largest uplift.

## 4d. Uplift method

Section 4c found only weak evidence that the effect changes with one feature at a time. A combination of features can still find customers with a larger uplift. If the contact cost is high, the order of the customers by uplift decides who gets the email. Thus the last question of Step 4 is: which method puts the customers in this order?

::: {#dec-06 .decision}
### Which method puts the customers in order of uplift? {.unnumbered}

**Why this question matters.** A targeting rule sends the email to the top of a list. If the list has the wrong order, the rule removes customers who buy because of the email, and it keeps customers who do not. A complex model also needs a model review and a monthly check. Thus a model must give a clearly better order than a simple rule.

**Ways to do it.** The split axis is where the order comes from. It can come from one pre-test feature, a table of segments, a model of the outcome in each group, or a model of the uplift. These four groups cover the usual uplift methods, and each method belongs to one of them.

| Where the order comes from | Method | Advantage | Main risk | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| One pre-test feature | A. Rank by history (no model) | Simple. No model to approve. Customers who spent more in the past can buy more. | It ranks by the value of the customer, not directly by the uplift. | Possible. Test it as the baseline. |
| A table of segments | B. Segment table: history bucket × product history | Easy to read. | Each cell has few buyers, so each estimate is noisy. | Possible. Test it. |
| A model of the outcome in each group | C. T-learner: one logistic regression of the conversion in each group | Uses all features. A standard method. | The uplift is the difference of two noisy predictions. | Possible. Test it. |
| A model of the outcome in each group | S-learner or X-learner | The S-learner uses one model. The X-learner can help when the groups have different sizes. | Here the groups have the same size. A linear S-learner with no interaction gives the same uplift to all customers. | Screened out |
| A model of the uplift | D. Uplift tree on the transformed outcome | One model. The tree gives rules that a person can read. | The transformed outcome has a large variance for spend. | Possible. Test it. |
| A model of the uplift | Causal forest or uplift random forest | Strong on large data with many buyers. | Needs packages outside base R and rpart. With so few buyers, a forest of trees also fits noise. | Screened out |

**The rule before the evidence (branch 5).** We set the model rule in section 3a, before the rerun. An ML uplift model (C or D) replaces rank by history only if two conditions are true. Its mean Qini area is 20% or more higher than the area of rank by history. Its Qini area is more than 0 in at least 9 of 10 repeats. The segment table also uses estimates from the test data, so we apply the same bar to it.

::: {.tech-note}
**Technical note.** Settings of the methods. Each method uses only the men's email and the control group.

- **Cross-fit.** 5 folds, repeated 10 times with the seeds SEED + 1 to SEED + 10. Rank by history needs no folds, so its area is the same in each repeat.
- **B. Segment table.** For each cell of history bucket × product history in the training folds: mean spend of the email group − mean spend of the control group. A cell with no customers in the training folds gets an uplift of 0.
- **C. T-learner.** In each group, a logistic regression of the conversion on recency, log(history), product history, area type, new customer and channel. The uplift = (mean spend of a buyer × probability to buy) in the email group − the same in the control group.
- **D. Uplift tree.** The transformed outcome z = spend × (t − p) / (p × (1 − p)), with p the share of the email group. Its mean is the uplift. A regression tree on z (rpart) with at most 3 levels, at least 3,000 customers in each leaf and no cost-complexity limit (cp = 0).
- **Qini area.** At the top 5%, 10%, …, 100% of the list (section 3a). A tie in the score gets a random order.
:::

**Evidence.** For each repeat, the code gives each customer a cross-fitted uplift from each method. It then draws the Qini curve of each method and calculates its Qini area. The table gives the area over the 10 repeats and applies the model rule.

```{r}
#| label: dec-06-evidence
#| code-summary: "Evidence: four uplift methods with a 5-fold cross-fit, 10 repeats, and the model rule"

# Purpose: Compare four uplift methods by the Qini area and apply the model rule of branch 5 (dec-06).
# Input:   `m` (men's email + control, Step 4c), `SEED`, `RULES`, uplift_oof(), qini(), qini_area()
#          (case03_helpers.R).
# Output:  `p_t`, `GRID`, `preds`, `curves`, `area` (one row for each repeat), `OPT6`, table, N values.

p_t <- mean(m$t)            # Share of the email group
GRID <- seq(0.05, 1, 0.05)  # Top shares of the list for the Qini curve

REPS <- 10
preds <- lapply(seq_len(REPS), function(r) uplift_oof(SEED + r))
curves <- lapply(preds, function(p) { set.seed(SEED); sapply(colnames(p), function(cn) qini(p[, cn], m$spend, m$t)) })
area <- t(sapply(curves, qini_area))
OPT6 <- c(A = "A. Rank by history", B = "B. Segment table", C = "C. T-learner", D = "D. Uplift tree")

# The model rule of branch 5, set before the evidence.
gain6 <- colMeans(area) / mean(area[, "A"]) - 1     # Mean Qini area against rank by history (relative)
pos6 <- colSums(area > 0)                           # Repeats with a Qini area more than 0
pass6 <- gain6 >= RULES$b5_model_gain & pos6 >= RULES$b5_model_pos
pass6["A"] <- NA                                    # The baseline
cand <- names(which(pass6[c("B", "C", "D")]))
chosen6 <- if (length(cand)) cand[which.max(colMeans(area)[cand])] else "A"

kable(data.frame(Option = OPT6,
                 `Mean Qini area` = usd(colMeans(area), 3),
                 `Lowest of 10 repeats` = usd(apply(area, 2, min), 3),
                 `Highest of 10 repeats` = usd(apply(area, 2, max), 3),
                 `Repeats with area > 0` = paste(pos6, "of", REPS),
                 `Mean area against A` = c("baseline", paste0(ifelse(gain6[-1] > 0, "+", ""), pct(gain6[-1], 0))),
                 `Model rule` = c("baseline", ifelse(pass6[-1], "passes", "fails")),
                 check.names = FALSE), row.names = FALSE, align = "lrrrrrl")

best6 <- names(which.max(colMeans(area)))
N$best6 <- OPT6[best6]
N$chosen6 <- OPT6[chosen6]
N$b5_model <- if (chosen6 == "A") "keeps" else "replaces"
N$n_pass6 <- length(cand)
N$area_a <- usd(mean(area[, "A"]), 3)
N$area_b <- usd(mean(area[, "B"]), 3)
N$area_b_range <- ci_txt(min(area[, "B"]), max(area[, "B"]), function(x) usd(x, 3))
N$area_cd <- paste0(usd(mean(area[, "C"]), 3), " and ", usd(mean(area[, "D"]), 3))
N$gain_b <- pct(gain6[["B"]], 0); N$gain_c <- pct(gain6[["C"]], 0); N$gain_d <- pct(gain6[["D"]], 0)
N$pos_b <- pos6[["B"]]; N$pos_c <- pos6[["C"]]; N$pos_d <- pos6[["D"]]
```

```{r}
#| label: dec-06-plot
#| code-summary: "Chart: Qini curves of the four methods, first repeat"
#| fig-height: 4.6

# Purpose: Show the Qini curves of the first repeat against the line of a random order (dec-06).
# Input:   `curves`, `GRID`, `OPT6`, `CS` and the chart functions (chart_style.R).
# Output:  Chart only.

cv <- rbind(0, curves[[1]])
xs <- c(0, GRID) * 100
col6 <- c(A = CS$navy, B = CS$cyan, C = CS$gray, D = CS$gray)
lwd6 <- c(A = 2.8, B = 1.8, C = 1.5, D = 1.5)
cs_setup(mar = c(3.6, 5.4, 0.6, 1.5))
plot(xs, cv[, "A"], type = "n", ylim = range(0, cv), xlim = c(0, 100), xaxt = "n", yaxt = "n",
     xlab = "Share of customers that get the email, in the order of each method", ylab = "")
title(ylab = "Incremental spend for each customer", line = 3.6)  # More room for the dollar labels
axis(1, at = seq(0, 100, 20), labels = paste0(seq(0, 100, 20), "%"))
cs_dollar_axis(2)
lines(c(0, 100), c(0, cv[nrow(cv), "A"]), lty = 2, col = CS$light_gray, lwd = 1.5)
for (o in c("D", "C", "B", "A")) lines(xs, cv[, o], col = col6[o], lwd = lwd6[o])
# Direct labels in the empty space next to each curve: A and B above the curves, C and D below.
lab <- data.frame(o = c("A", "B", "C", "D"), x = c(25, 70, 65, 85),
                  ax = c(1.05, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5), ay = c(-0.6, -0.9, 1.8, 1.8))
for (j in seq_len(nrow(lab))) {
  o <- lab$o[j]; i <- which.min(abs(xs - lab$x[j]))
  text(xs[i], cv[i, o], OPT6[o], adj = c(lab$ax[j], lab$ay[j]), cex = 0.78,
       col = if (o == "A") CS$navy else if (o == "B") CS$cyan else CS$muted, font = if (o == "A") 2 else 1)
}
cs_title(paste0("Rank by history gives the largest Qini area: ", N$area_a, " for each customer"),
         "Qini curves of the first repeat of the 5-fold cross-fit; dashed line: random order")
```

**How to read:** each line starts at 0 and adds customers in the order of one method. The height is the incremental spend for each customer of the campaign. The dashed line is a random order. A curve above the dashed line puts the customers with a large uplift first.

**So what:** rank by history (navy) stays above the random order at each share. The T-learner and the uplift tree (gray) cross the random order, and their mean areas over 10 repeats are below 0.

::: {.choice}
**Decision.** Rank by history. The model rule `r N$b5_model` rank by history: `r N$n_pass6` of the three methods with estimates passes the rule.
:::

**Why.** Three reasons, from the most important:

1. **No model passes the rule.** The T-learner has a mean area `r N$gain_c` against rank by history, with an area more than 0 in `r N$pos_c` of 10 repeats. The uplift tree has `r N$gain_d`, with `r N$pos_d` of 10. The two models are not better than a random order (`r N$area_cd`). Less than 1% of the customers buy, so the models with more features fit noise.
2. **The segment table is not stable.** Its mean area is `r N$area_b` (`r N$gain_b` against rank by history), and it changes from repeat to repeat (`r N$area_b_range`). One cut of the folds can make it look better or worse than history.
3. **Rank by history is simple and stable.** It has the largest mean area, `r N$area_a`. It needs no model, so Marketing can use it without a model review.

**What would change the decision.** If a test has many more buyers, an ML model can find a pattern that history cannot show. Repeat this comparison with each new test and the same rule. Keep rank by history as the baseline.
:::

::: {.business-note}
**Business note.** The men's email increases the mean spend by `r N$ate_m` for each customer (95% CI `r N$ci_m`). This is `r N$roi_m` times the breakeven effect. The best order of the customers by uplift is the simplest one: rank by history. No ML model passes the rule of branch 5. Step 5 gives each customer an uplift from this order.
:::

# Step 5. Make predictions {#step-5}

::: {.bridge}
Step 4 selected the men's email and rank by history as the order of the customers. A targeting rule needs more than an order: it needs the uplift in dollars of each part of the list. Only then can we compare the uplift with the breakeven effect of `r N$breakeven_eff`. This step answers: what uplift does each customer get, and how sure are we?
:::

::: {.purpose}
**Purpose.** This step gives each customer an uplift on spend from the history quartile of the customer. It supports this decision: the list of customers for the email if the contact cost goes up (Step 7a).
:::

The prediction for a customer is the uplift of the history quartile of that customer. We use quartiles, because each quartile has about one quarter of the customers and enough buyers for an interval. Smaller groups give intervals that are too wide for a decision.

The code gives two estimates for each quartile:

- **The uplift of the quartile.** The mean spend of the email group − the mean spend of the control group, with the Welch 95% CI. All customers of the quartile give this estimate.
- **The cross-fitted uplift.** Each customer gets the uplift of the quartile from the other four folds (5-fold cross-fit). Thus the estimate of a customer never uses that customer. Step 7a uses this estimate in the breakeven rule. The range of the cross-fitted uplift over the five folds shows how much the data of one fold moves the estimate.

```{r}
#| label: uplift-quartile
#| code-summary: "Uplift on spend by history quartile, with the cross-fitted uplift"

# Purpose: The uplift on spend of each history quartile and the cross-fitted uplift of each customer (Step 5).
# Input:   `m`, `MARGIN`, `COST`, `SEED`, group_effect(), xfit_group() and breakeven() (case03_helpers.R).
# Output:  `qs` (quartile cuts), `m$hq` (history quartile), `uq` (uplift of each quartile with its 95% CI),
#          `uq_cf` (cross-fitted uplift of each customer), N values.

qs <- quantile(m$history, c(0.25, 0.50, 0.75))
m$hq <- cut(m$history, c(-Inf, qs, Inf), labels = c("Q1 (lowest)", "Q2", "Q3", "Q4 (highest)"))
uq <- group_effect(m, m$hq)
names(uq)[names(uq) == "level"] <- "q"
uq$lo_h <- as.vector(tapply(m$history, m$hq, min))
uq$hi_h <- as.vector(tapply(m$history, m$hq, max))
uq <- uq[, c("q", "n", "lo_h", "hi_h", "eff", "lo", "hi")]

# Cross-fitted uplift: the same folds as Step 7a (seed SEED + 1).
uq_cf <- xfit_group(m, m$hq, SEED + 1)
cf_mean <- tapply(uq_cf, m$hq, mean)
cf_fold <- tapply(seq_along(uq_cf), m$hq, function(i) range(uq_cf[i]))

kable(data.frame(`History quartile` = uq$q, `History range` = paste(usd(uq$lo_h, 0), "to", usd(uq$hi_h, 0)),
                 Customers = num(uq$n), `Uplift on spend` = usd(uq$eff), `95% CI` = ci_txt(uq$lo, uq$hi),
                 `Cross-fitted uplift, mean` = usd(cf_mean),
                 `Cross-fitted uplift, range of 5 folds` = sapply(cf_fold, function(r) ci_txt(r[1], r[2])),
                 `Profit for each email at $0.10` = usd(MARGIN * uq$eff - COST), check.names = FALSE),
      row.names = FALSE, align = "llrrrrrr")

N$q4_eff <- usd(uq$eff[4]); N$q4_cut <- usd(qs[3], 0)
N$q4_ci <- ci_txt(uq$lo[4], uq$hi[4])
N$q13 <- paste(usd(min(uq$eff[1:3])), "to", usd(max(uq$eff[1:3])))
N$q_min_profit <- usd(min(MARGIN * uq$eff - COST), 3)
N$q_n <- num(min(uq$n))
N$n_q_above <- sum(uq$eff > breakeven())
N$n_q_lo_above <- sum(uq$lo > breakeven())
N$q_lo_min <- usd(min(uq$lo))
N$cf_range <- paste(usd(min(sapply(cf_fold, min))), "to", usd(max(sapply(cf_fold, max))))
N$q4_cf_range <- ci_txt(cf_fold[[4]][1], cf_fold[[4]][2])
N$q4_ratio <- formatC(uq$eff[4] / mean(uq$eff[1:3]), format = "f", digits = 1)
# Does the top quartile stay above the other quartiles in each fold?
q4_top <- cf_fold[[4]][1] > max(sapply(cf_fold[1:3], max))
N$q4_order <- if (q4_top) "stays on top in each fold" else "does not stay on top in each fold"
```

```{r}
#| label: uplift-quartile-plot
#| code-summary: "Chart: uplift on spend by history quartile, with the 95% CI and the breakeven effect"
#| fig-height: 4

# Purpose: Show the uplift of each history quartile against the breakeven effect (Step 5).
# Input:   `uq`, breakeven(), `CS` and the chart functions (chart_style.R).
# Output:  Chart only.

xq <- seq_len(nrow(uq))
qcol <- ifelse(xq == 4, CS$blue, CS$navy)
cs_setup(mar = c(3.6, 5.4, 0.6, 7))
plot(xq, uq$eff, ylim = range(0, uq$lo, uq$hi), xlim = c(0.6, 4.4), pch = 19, cex = 1.3, col = qcol,
     xaxt = "n", yaxt = "n", xlab = "History quartile (spend in the 12 months before the test)", ylab = "")
title(ylab = "Uplift on spend for each customer", line = 3.6)  # More room for the dollar labels
segments(xq, uq$lo, xq, uq$hi, col = qcol, lwd = 3)
axis(1, at = xq, labels = paste0(uq$q, "\n", usd(uq$lo_h, 0), " to ", usd(uq$hi_h, 0)), padj = 0.5, cex.axis = 0.75)
cs_dollar_axis(2)
abline(h = 0, col = CS$light_gray)
abline(h = breakeven(), lty = 2, col = CS$gray)
cs_label_end(4.4, breakeven(), paste0("Breakeven ", usd(breakeven())), col = CS$muted)
text(xq, uq$eff, usd(uq$eff), pos = 4, offset = 0.7, cex = 0.8, col = qcol, font = ifelse(xq == 4, 2, 1))
cs_title(paste0("The top history quartile adds ", N$q4_eff, " of spend; the other quartiles ", N$q13),
         "Uplift of the men's email on spend for each customer, with the Welch 95% CI")
```

**How to read:** each point is the uplift of one history quartile, with its 95% CI. The dashed line is the breakeven effect at a $0.10 contact cost. A quartile above the line makes money with each email.

**So what:** the point estimate is above the breakeven effect in `r N$n_q_above` of 4 quartiles. The interval is fully above it in only `r N$n_q_lo_above` of 4 quartiles, so the uplift of a quartile is not certain.

The uplift is `r N$q13` in the three lower quartiles. In the top quartile (history more than `r N$q4_cut`), it is `r N$q4_eff` (95% CI `r N$q4_ci`). At a contact cost of $0.10, each quartile is profitable, but the lowest profit is only `r N$q_min_profit` for each email.

The cross-fitted uplift of a customer goes from `r N$cf_range`. In the top quartile, the range is `r N$q4_cf_range`. Thus the estimate of a quartile moves with the fold, and the top quartile `r N$q4_order`.

::: {.business-note}
**Business note.** Each customer now has an uplift from the history quartile. The top quartile gives `r N$q4_eff` for each customer, `r N$q4_ratio` times the mean of the other quartiles. Thus the top quartile is the first group to keep if the contact cost goes up. Step 6 checks the recommended policy against the five branches of section 3a. Step 7a then compares "send to all" with the rules that use this uplift.
:::

# Step 6. Evaluate {#step-6}

::: {.bridge}
Steps 4 and 5 gave the evidence one piece at a time. The men's email increases spend, it is the better version, and each history quartile is profitable at the base contact cost. Now we must judge the recommended policy as a whole: send the men's email to all customers. This step uses the five branches of the evaluation framework of Step 3a, one at a time.
:::

::: {.purpose}
**Purpose.** This step answers: *is the policy "men's email to all customers" valid, large enough, robust, profitable and better than a targeting rule?* It supports this decision: approve the policy for the launch with a holdout.
:::

The table repeats the five rules of Step 3a. We set these rules before the rerun of this version, and we do not change them after a result. If a result fails a rule, this step reports the failure and what it means.

| Branch | Question | Rule |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Validity | Do the groups differ only by the email? | The largest absolute standardized difference is less than 0.05. The p-value of the sample-ratio check is more than 0.01. |
| 2. Effect | Does the men's email change spend, and is the test large enough? | The Welch 95% CI excludes 0. Each group has at least the customers for 80% power at the observed effect. |
| 3. Robustness | Does the effect hold with other methods? | The bootstrap 95% CI excludes 0. The CUPED effect and the regression effect are each within 10% of the unadjusted effect. |
| 4. Business value | Does the recommended policy make money? | The profit for 100,000 customers is more than 0, and the lower end of its 95% CI is more than 0. |
| 5. Targeting | Does a targeting rule or an uplift model beat "send to all"? | The policy follows the model rule and the policy rule of Step 3a. |

## 6a. Branch 1: validity

The question: do the three groups differ only by the email? The data source put each customer into a group at random. A random split gives groups that are equal on average, but a fault in the split can make them different. If the groups differ before the email, the difference of the means is not the effect of the email.

Two checks answer the question, because they find different faults:

- **Standardized difference.** It compares the mean of each pre-test feature in each email group with the control group. It finds a group with different customers.
- **Sample-ratio check.** It compares the number of customers in each group with an equal split. It finds a group that lost or gained customers.

[Step 2d](#randomization) gives the full table of the standardized differences. This section applies the rule of Step 3a to it.

```{r}
#| label: eval-validity
#| code-summary: "Branch 1: largest standardized difference and the sample-ratio check"

# Purpose: Measure branch 1 (validity) of the evaluation framework of Step 3a.
# Input:   `feat`, `d` (contract C2), `RULES` (Step 3a).
# Output:  `RULES` (if Step 3a did not make it), `e1_smd`, `e1_srm`, `b1_pass`, N$e1_*.

# The chart style of the notebook. The setup chunk loads it. This guard keeps the part usable alone.
if (!exists("CS")) source("chart_style.R")

# The rules of the evaluation framework: `RULES` of Step 3a. The fallback has the same values (the brief of
# round 2), for a run without the chunk of Step 3a. We set the rules before the rerun.
if (!exists("RULES")) {
  RULES <- list(
    b1_smd = 0.05,          # Branch 1: largest absolute standardized difference less than 0.05
    b1_srm_p = 0.01,        # Branch 1: p-value of the sample-ratio check more than 0.01
    b3_adj_dev = 0.10,      # Branch 3: each adjusted effect within 10% of the unadjusted effect
    b5_model_gain = 0.20,   # Branch 5: an ML uplift model needs a 20% higher mean Qini area ...
    b5_model_pos = 9,       # ... and a Qini area more than 0 in 9 or more of the repeats
    b5_policy_level = 0.90  # Branch 5: the 90% interval of the gain of a targeting rule must be above 0
  )
}

# Standardized difference of each pre-test feature: (mean of the email group - mean of control) / sd.
smd_arm <- function(a) sapply(feat, function(x) (mean(x[d$arm == a]) - mean(x[d$arm == "control"])) / sd(x))
smd_all <- cbind(mens = smd_arm("mens"), womens = smd_arm("womens"))
e1_smd <- max(abs(smd_all))
e1_smd_feat <- rownames(smd_all)[which.max(apply(abs(smd_all), 1, max))]
# Sample-ratio check: chi-square test of the group sizes against an equal split.
e1_srm <- chisq.test(table(d$arm))$p.value

b1_pass <- e1_smd < RULES$b1_smd && e1_srm > RULES$b1_srm_p
N$e1_smd <- formatC(e1_smd, format = "f", digits = 3)
N$e1_smd_feat <- e1_smd_feat
N$e1_srm <- formatC(e1_srm, format = "f", digits = 2)
N$e1_n_feat <- ncol(feat)
N$b1_verdict <- if (b1_pass) "The policy passes branch 1." else "The policy fails branch 1."

kable(data.frame(
  Check = c("Largest absolute standardized difference (both emails against control)", "Sample-ratio check: chi-square p-value"),
  Result = c(N$e1_smd, N$e1_srm),
  Rule = c("Less than 0.05", "More than 0.01"), check.names = FALSE), row.names = FALSE, align = "lrl")
```

The largest standardized difference of the `r N$e1_n_feat` pre-test features is `r N$e1_smd` (`r N$e1_smd_feat`), against the limit of 0.05. The p-value of the sample-ratio check is `r N$e1_srm`, against the limit of 0.01. `r N$b1_verdict` Thus a difference of the means gives the causal effect of the email.

## 6b. Branch 2: effect

The question: does the men's email change spend, and is the test large enough to trust the answer? A test with too few customers can find an effect by chance, and its estimate is often too large. Thus the rule has two parts:

- The Welch 95% CI of the spend effect excludes 0.
- Each group has at least the customers that a test needs for 80% power at the observed effect, at 5% significance.

```{r}
#| label: eval-effect
#| code-summary: "Branch 2: Welch CI of the spend effect and the customers for 80% power"

# Purpose: Measure branch 2 (effect): the Welch CI and the size of the test at the observed effect.
# Input:   `d`, `ATE`, `ATE_LO`, `ATE_HI` (contract C3), `ALPHA`, `POWER`.
# Output:  `e2_need`, `e2_have`, `e2_power`, `b2_pass`, N$e2_*.

# Pooled standard deviation of spend in the three groups (the same as the power of Step 3c).
s_pool <- sqrt(mean(tapply(d$spend, d$arm, var)))
e2_have <- min(table(d$arm))
e2_need <- power.t.test(delta = ATE[["mens"]], sd = s_pool, sig.level = ALPHA, power = POWER)$n
# Power of this test at the observed effect.
e2_power <- power.t.test(n = e2_have, delta = ATE[["mens"]], sd = s_pool, sig.level = ALPHA)$power

b2_pass <- ATE_LO[["mens"]] > 0 && e2_have >= e2_need
N$e2_ci <- ci_txt(ATE_LO[["mens"]], ATE_HI[["mens"]])
N$e2_ate <- usd(ATE[["mens"]])
N$e2_need <- num(ceiling(e2_need))
N$e2_have <- num(e2_have)
N$e2_ratio <- formatC(e2_have / e2_need, format = "f", digits = 1)
N$e2_power <- pct(e2_power, 0)
N$b2_verdict <- if (b2_pass) "The policy passes branch 2." else "The policy fails branch 2."

kable(data.frame(
```
