```{r}
  Check = c("Spend effect of the men's email, Welch 95% CI", "Customers in the smallest group",
            "Customers for 80% power at the observed effect", "Power of this test at the observed effect"),
  Result = c(paste(N$e2_ate, N$e2_ci), N$e2_have, N$e2_need, N$e2_power),
  Rule = c("The CI excludes 0", "At least the customers for 80% power", "", ""), check.names = FALSE),
  row.names = FALSE, align = "lrl")
```

The men's email increases the mean spend by `r N$e2_ate` for each customer (95% CI `r N$e2_ci`). The CI excludes 0. At this effect, a test needs `r N$e2_need` customers in each group for 80% power. The smallest group has `r N$e2_have`, or `r N$e2_ratio` times this number, and the power is `r N$e2_power`. `r N$b2_verdict`

## 6c. Branch 3: robustness

The question: does the effect hold if we use other methods? The Welch CI assumes that the mean of the spend has a normal distribution. Spend has a long right tail, so a reviewer can doubt this. The pre-test data can also change the estimate. Thus the rule uses three other methods:

- **Bootstrap.** It needs no normal distribution. The code repeats the bootstrap of Step 4a with the same seed and 2,000 samples, so the CI is the same.
- **CUPED with history.** It removes the part of the spend that history predicts.
- **Regression adjustment.** It adds all pre-test features to a linear regression.

The two adjusted effects come from the evidence of the variance-reduction decision in Step 4a.

```{r}
#| label: eval-robust
#| code-summary: "Branch 3: bootstrap CI and the adjusted effects against the unadjusted effect"

# Purpose: Measure branch 3 (robustness): bootstrap CI, CUPED effect and regression effect of the men's email.
# Input:   `d`, `dec03` (contract C3), `SEED`, `ATE`.
# Output:  `e3_boot`, `e3_adj` (effects A, B and C), `b3_pass`, N$e3_*.

# Bootstrap: the same code and seed as dec-02, so the interval is the interval of Step 4a.
y1 <- d$spend[d$arm == "mens"]
y0 <- d$spend[d$arm == "control"]
set.seed(SEED)
bd <- replicate(2000, mean(y1[sample.int(length(y1), replace = TRUE)]) - mean(y0[sample.int(length(y0), replace = TRUE)]))
e3_boot <- quantile(bd, c(0.025, 0.975))

# Effects A (no adjustment), B (CUPED) and C (regression) for spend, men's email, from dec03.
# If dec03 has other column names, fit the three models again with the method of dec-03.
cols3 <- c("Metric", "Email", "Effect, A", "Effect, B", "Effect, C")
if (all(cols3 %in% names(dec03))) {
  r3 <- dec03[dec03$Metric == "spend" & dec03$Email == "Men's", ]
  e3_adj <- c(A = r3[["Effect, A"]], B = r3[["Effect, B"]], C = r3[["Effect, C"]])
} else {
  s3 <- d[d$arm %in% c("control", "mens"), ]
  s3$t <- as.integer(s3$arm == "mens")
  theta <- cov(s3$spend, s3$history) / var(s3$history)
  s3$y_cuped <- s3$spend - theta * (s3$history - mean(s3$history))
  e3_adj <- c(A = coef(lm(spend ~ t, s3))[["t"]], B = coef(lm(y_cuped ~ t, s3))[["t"]],
              C = coef(lm(spend ~ t + lhist + recency + mens + womens + zip + newbie + channel, s3))[["t"]])
}
e3_dev <- abs(e3_adj[c("B", "C")] / e3_adj[["A"]] - 1)  # Relative change against the unadjusted effect

b3_pass <- e3_boot[[1]] > 0 && all(e3_dev <= RULES$b3_adj_dev)
N$e3_boot <- ci_txt(e3_boot[[1]], e3_boot[[2]])
N$e3_cuped <- usd(e3_adj[["B"]], 3)
N$e3_reg <- usd(e3_adj[["C"]], 3)
N$e3_unadj <- usd(e3_adj[["A"]], 3)
N$e3_dev_max <- pct(max(e3_dev), 1)
N$b3_verdict <- if (b3_pass) "The policy passes branch 3." else "The policy fails branch 3."

kable(data.frame(
  Method = c("Welch t-test (no adjustment)", "Bootstrap, 2,000 samples", "CUPED with history", "Regression adjustment, all features"),
  `Effect on spend` = c(N$e3_unadj, N$e3_unadj, N$e3_cuped, N$e3_reg),
  `95% CI` = c(N$e2_ci, N$e3_boot, "", ""),
  `Change against no adjustment` = c("", "", pct(e3_dev[["B"]], 1), pct(e3_dev[["C"]], 1)),
  Rule = c("", "The CI excludes 0", "Within 10%", "Within 10%"), check.names = FALSE),
  row.names = FALSE, align = "lrrrl")
```

The bootstrap 95% CI is `r N$e3_boot`, almost the same as the Welch CI, and it excludes 0. The CUPED effect is `r N$e3_cuped`, and the regression effect is `r N$e3_reg`. The unadjusted effect is `r N$e3_unadj`. The largest change is `r N$e3_dev_max`, against the limit of 10%. `r N$b3_verdict`

## 6d. Branch 4: business value

The question: does the recommended policy make money, also at the low end of the effect? A positive effect is not sufficient. Each email has a contact cost, so the effect must be more than the breakeven effect. The rule uses the base margin of 30% (as-01) and the base contact cost of $0.10 (as-02), for one campaign of 100,000 customers (as-04).

::: {.tech-note}
**Technical note.** For a campaign of n customers, with margin m, contact cost c and spend effect u, the incremental profit is n × (m × u − c). The profit is a straight line in u. Thus the 95% CI of the profit comes directly from the Welch 95% CI of u. The breakeven effect is c / m.
:::

```{r}
#| label: eval-value
#| code-summary: "Branch 4: incremental profit of the men's email to all, with its 95% CI"

# Purpose: Measure branch 4 (business value) at the base margin and contact cost (as-01, as-02, as-04).
# Input:   `ATE`, `ATE_LO`, `ATE_HI`, `MARGIN`, `COST`, `CAMPAIGN`.
# Output:  `e4_prof` (profit, lower end, upper end), `b4_pass`, N$e4_*.

# Profit = customers x (margin x effect - contact cost). The CI of the effect gives the CI of the profit.
e4_prof <- CAMPAIGN * (MARGIN * c(est = ATE[["mens"]], lo = ATE_LO[["mens"]], hi = ATE_HI[["mens"]]) - COST)
b4_pass <- e4_prof[["est"]] > 0 && e4_prof[["lo"]] > 0
N$e4_prof <- usd(e4_prof[["est"]], 0)
N$e4_ci <- ci_txt(e4_prof[["lo"]], e4_prof[["hi"]], function(x) usd(x, 0))
N$e4_be <- usd(COST / MARGIN)
N$e4_lo_eff <- usd(ATE_LO[["mens"]])
N$e4_cost <- usd(COST)
N$e4_margin <- pct(MARGIN, 0)
N$e4_campaign <- num(CAMPAIGN)
N$b4_verdict <- if (b4_pass) "The policy passes branch 4." else "The policy fails branch 4."

kable(data.frame(
  Check = c("Incremental profit for 100,000 customers", "95% CI of the profit", "Breakeven effect (contact cost / margin)",
            "Lower end of the 95% CI of the effect"),
  Result = c(N$e4_prof, N$e4_ci, N$e4_be, N$e4_lo_eff),
  Rule = c("More than 0", "Lower end more than 0", "", "More than the breakeven effect"), check.names = FALSE),
  row.names = FALSE, align = "lrl")
```

At a margin of `r N$e4_margin` and a contact cost of `r N$e4_cost`, the men's email to all gives `r N$e4_prof` for `r N$e4_campaign` customers. The 95% CI of the profit is `r N$e4_ci`. The lower end of the effect, `r N$e4_lo_eff`, is above the breakeven effect of `r N$e4_be`. `r N$b4_verdict` The margin and the contact cost are assumptions, so Step 7c changes them.

## 6e. Branch 5: targeting

The question: can a smaller list of customers make more money than "send to all"? Step 5 showed that the top history quartile has the largest uplift. If the contact cost is high, an email to the low quartiles can lose money. The rule of Step 3a has two parts:

- **Model rule.** An ML uplift model replaces "rank by history" only if two conditions are true. Its mean Qini area is 20% or more higher, and its area is more than 0 in at least 9 of 10 repeats. The evidence comes from Step 4d.
- **Policy rule.** A targeting rule replaces "send to all" only if the 90% interval of its gain is above 0 at the base contact cost.

The recommended policy passes if it follows both rules. The policy rule compares two targeting rules with "send to all":

- **Top 25% by history.** The email goes only to the top history quartile.
- **Breakeven rule by history quartile.** The email goes to a quartile only if the margin on its cross-fitted uplift is more than the contact cost.

The code calculates the profit of each rule for six contact costs, from $0.05 to $0.30. Branch 5 uses only the base cost. Step 7a uses the full table to select the targeting rule for other costs. Thus this table is also the evidence for that decision.

::: {.tech-note}
**Technical note.** The profit of a rule for each customer in the campaign is s × (m × û − c). Here s is the share of customers that the rule selects. The value û is the mean spend of the treated customers minus the mean spend of the control customers in that selection.

The breakeven rule uses the cross-fitted uplift of each history quartile, with 5 folds. Thus each customer gets an uplift from folds that do not contain that customer. The 90% interval of the gain comes from 500 bootstrap samples of the customers. Each rule and each cost use the same samples, so the code compares the rules on the same data.
:::

```{r}
#| label: dec-07-evidence
#| code-summary: "Branch 5 and the evidence for the targeting rule: profit of each rule at six contact costs"

# Purpose: Measure branch 5 (targeting): the model rule (Qini area, dec-06) and the policy rule (gain against
#          "send to all", 90% bootstrap interval). The table is also the evidence for dec-07 (Step 7a).
# Input:   `m` with `t`, `spend`, `hq` (contracts C4, C5), `area`, `MARGIN`, `COST`, `CAMPAIGN`, `SEED`.
# Output:  Contract C6: `policy_profit`, `u_q`, `all_sel`, `top_q`, `dec07`, `k100`. Also `boot_idx`,
#          `b5_model`, `b5_policy`, `b5_pass`, N$b5_*. Existing N names of dec-07 (a_base, cost_sig and others).

# Helper of case03_helpers.R. The definition below is the same, for a run without that file.
if (!exists("policy_profit")) {
  policy_profit <- function(sel, y, t, cost, margin = MARGIN) {
    # Profit for each customer in the campaign. Customers outside the selection get no email.
    share <- mean(sel)
    if (share == 0) return(0)
    eff <- mean(y[sel & t == 1]) - mean(y[sel & t == 0])
    share * (margin * eff - cost)
  }
}

# --- Model rule (dec-06 evidence): ML models against rank by history ---
# Columns of `area`: A rank by history, B segment table, C T-learner, D uplift tree (Step 4d).
area_mean <- colMeans(area)
b5_model <- data.frame(
  model = c("B", "C", "D"),
  gain = area_mean[c("B", "C", "D")] / area_mean[["A"]] - 1,
  pos = colSums(area[, c("B", "C", "D")] > 0))
b5_model$replaces <- b5_model$gain >= RULES$b5_model_gain & b5_model$pos >= RULES$b5_model_pos
ml_models <- c("C", "D")  # The T-learner and the uplift tree are the ML models. B is a table of means.
model_ok <- !any(b5_model$replaces[b5_model$model %in% ml_models])

# --- Policy rule: targeting rules against "send to all" ---
# Cross-fitted uplift of each history quartile (5 folds)
set.seed(SEED + 1)
fold <- sample(rep(1:5, length.out = nrow(m)))
u_q <- numeric(nrow(m))
for (k in 1:5) {
  tr <- m[fold != k, ]; te <- fold == k
  uu <- tapply(tr$spend[tr$t == 1], tr$hq[tr$t == 1], mean) - tapply(tr$spend[tr$t == 0], tr$hq[tr$t == 0], mean)
  u_q[te] <- uu[as.character(m$hq[te])]
}

COSTS <- c(0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.20, 0.25, 0.30)
all_sel <- rep(TRUE, nrow(m))
top_q <- m$hq == "Q4 (highest)"
# The same 500 bootstrap samples for each rule and each cost: the gains are paired.
set.seed(SEED)
boot_idx <- replicate(500, sample.int(nrow(m), replace = TRUE), simplify = FALSE)
boot_gain <- function(sel, cst) {
  # 90% bootstrap interval of the gain of a rule against "send to all", for each customer.
  g <- sapply(boot_idx, function(i) policy_profit(sel[i], m$spend[i], m$t[i], cst) - policy_profit(all_sel[i], m$spend[i], m$t[i], cst))
  quantile(g, c((1 - RULES$b5_policy_level) / 2, (1 + RULES$b5_policy_level) / 2))
}

dec07 <- do.call(rbind, lapply(COSTS, function(cst) {
  sel_c <- MARGIN * u_q > cst
  ib <- boot_gain(top_q, cst); ic <- boot_gain(sel_c, cst)
  data.frame(cost = cst, a = policy_profit(all_sel, m$spend, m$t, cst), b = policy_profit(top_q, m$spend, m$t, cst),
             c = policy_profit(sel_c, m$spend, m$t, cst), share_c = mean(sel_c),
             b_lo = ib[[1]], b_hi = ib[[2]], c_lo = ic[[1]], c_hi = ic[[2]])
}))
k100 <- function(x) usd(CAMPAIGN * x, 0)  # Profit for each customer -> profit for one campaign
iv <- function(lo, hi) ci_txt(CAMPAIGN * lo, CAMPAIGN * hi, function(x) usd(x, 0))

# Branch 5 at the base contact cost (as-02)
base <- dec07[dec07$cost == COST, ]
b5_policy <- c(top = base$b_lo > 0, rule = base$c_lo > 0)  # TRUE: the rule replaces "send to all"
b5_pass <- model_ok && !any(b5_policy)

# Existing N names of the dec-07 evidence (the decision text of Step 7a and the summary use them)
N$a_base <- k100(base$a)
N$b_base <- k100(base$b)
N$c_share_base <- pct(base$share_c, 0)
N$c_base_gain <- k100(base$c - base$a)
sig_b <- dec07$cost[dec07$b_lo > 0]
N$has_sig <- length(sig_b) > 0
N$cost_sig <- if (N$has_sig) usd(min(sig_b)) else "more than $0.30"
N$b_gain_030 <- k100(dec07$b[dec07$cost == 0.30] - dec07$a[dec07$cost == 0.30])
N$c_vs_b_030 <- if (dec07$c[dec07$cost == 0.30] < dec07$b[dec07$cost == 0.30]) "less" else "more"
N$cost_zero_all <- usd(MARGIN * ATE[["mens"]])

# New N names of branch 5
fmt_gain <- function(g) paste0(ifelse(g >= 0, "+", ""), pct(g, 0))
N$b5_area_a <- usd(area_mean[["A"]], 3)
best_ml <- ml_models[which.max(area_mean[ml_models])]  # The ML model with the largest mean Qini area
N$b5_best_ml <- c(C = "the T-learner", D = "the uplift tree")[[best_ml]]
N$b5_best_ml_gain <- fmt_gain(b5_model$gain[b5_model$model == best_ml])
N$b5_best_ml_pos <- b5_model$pos[b5_model$model == best_ml]
N$b5_seg_gain <- fmt_gain(b5_model$gain[b5_model$model == "B"])
N$b5_seg_pos <- b5_model$pos[b5_model$model == "B"]
N$b5_top_iv <- iv(base$b_lo, base$b_hi)
N$b5_rule_iv <- iv(base$c_lo, base$c_hi)
N$b5_model_txt <- if (model_ok) "No ML model passes the model rule, so rank by history stays." else
  "An ML model passes the model rule, so it must replace rank by history."
N$b5_policy_txt <- if (!any(b5_policy)) "No targeting rule passes the policy rule at the base cost, so \"send to all\" stays." else
  "A targeting rule passes the policy rule at the base cost, so it must replace \"send to all\"."
N$b5_verdict <- if (b5_pass) "The policy passes branch 5." else "The policy fails branch 5."

# Table 1: the model rule
kable(data.frame(
  Option = c("B. Segment table", "C. T-learner", "D. Uplift tree"),
  `ML model` = c("No", "Yes", "Yes"),
  `Mean Qini area` = usd(area_mean[c("B", "C", "D")], 3),
  `Change against rank by history` = fmt_gain(b5_model$gain),
  `Repeats with area > 0` = paste(b5_model$pos, "of", nrow(area)),
  `Replaces rank by history` = ifelse(b5_model$replaces, "Yes", "No"), check.names = FALSE),
  row.names = FALSE, align = "llrrrl",
  caption = paste0("Model rule. Rank by history has a mean Qini area of ", N$b5_area_a, "."))

# Table 2: the policy rule, for each contact cost (Step 7a uses the full table)
kable(data.frame(`Contact cost` = usd(dec07$cost),
                 `A. Send to all` = k100(dec07$a),
                 `B. Top 25%` = k100(dec07$b),
                 `B minus A, 90% interval` = iv(dec07$b_lo, dec07$b_hi),
                 `C. Breakeven rule` = k100(dec07$c),
                 `C sends to` = pct(dec07$share_c, 0),
                 `C minus A, 90% interval` = iv(dec07$c_lo, dec07$c_hi), check.names = FALSE),
      row.names = FALSE, align = "rrrrrrr",
      caption = "Policy rule. Profit for 100,000 customers. Branch 5 uses the row of the base contact cost ($0.10).")
```

**Model rule.** Rank by history has a mean Qini area of `r N$b5_area_a`. The best ML model is `r N$b5_best_ml`, with a change of `r N$b5_best_ml_gain` against the limit of +20%. Its area is more than 0 in `r N$b5_best_ml_pos` of 10 repeats. `r N$b5_model_txt` The segment table is not an ML model. For information, its change is `r N$b5_seg_gain`, with an area more than 0 in `r N$b5_seg_pos` of 10 repeats.

**Policy rule.** At the base contact cost, "send to all" gives `r N$a_base` for 100,000 customers. The top 25% gives `r N$b_base`, and the 90% interval of its gain is `r N$b5_top_iv`. The breakeven rule sends to `r N$c_share_base` of the customers, and the interval of its gain is `r N$b5_rule_iv`. `r N$b5_policy_txt`

`r N$b5_verdict` The result depends on the contact cost. The gain of the top 25% is above 0 with 90% confidence from a contact cost of `r N$cost_sig`. Step 7a uses this result for the targeting rule.

## 6f. Summary of the evaluation

The table collects one result for each branch, with the rule of Step 3a.

```{r}
#| label: evaluate
#| code-summary: "Summary: the recommended policy against the rule of each branch"

# Purpose: Collect the result of the recommended policy (men's email to all) for each branch (6a–6e).
# Input:   Results of sections 6a–6e.
# Output:  Table `evaluation`, N$n_pass, N$fail_list.

evaluation <- data.frame(
  Branch = c("1. Validity", "2. Effect", "3. Robustness", "4. Business value", "5. Targeting"),
  Metric = c("Largest absolute standardized difference; sample-ratio p-value",
             "Welch 95% CI of the spend effect; customers in each group / customers for 80% power",
             "Bootstrap 95% CI; largest change of the CUPED and the regression effect",
             "Profit for 100,000 customers, with its 95% CI",
             "Best ML model against rank by history (Qini area); 90% interval of the gain of the top 25% at $0.10"),
  Result = c(paste0(N$e1_smd, "; ", N$e1_srm),
             paste0(N$e2_ci, "; ", N$e2_have, " / ", N$e2_need),
             paste0(N$e3_boot, "; ", N$e3_dev_max),
             paste0(N$e4_prof, " ", N$e4_ci),
             paste0(N$b5_best_ml_gain, ", ", N$b5_best_ml_pos, " of 10; ", N$b5_top_iv)),
  Rule = c("Less than 0.05; more than 0.01",
           "Excludes 0; at least the customers for 80% power",
           "Excludes 0; within 10%",
           "More than 0; lower end more than 0",
           "+20% or more and 9 of 10; interval above 0 (then targeting replaces send to all)"),
  Pass = ifelse(c(b1_pass, b2_pass, b3_pass, b4_pass, b5_pass), "Yes", "No"))
failed <- tolower(sub("^\\d\\. ", "", evaluation$Branch[evaluation$Pass == "No"]))
N$n_pass <- sum(evaluation$Pass == "Yes")
N$fail_list <- if (length(failed)) paste(failed, collapse = ", ") else "none"
kable(evaluation, row.names = FALSE, align = "lllll")
```

The recommended policy passes `r N$n_pass` of the 5 branches. The branches that fail are: `r N$fail_list`.

Two results need attention, also when a branch passes:

- **Power (branch 2).** The test has `r N$e2_ratio` times the customers for 80% power at the effect of the men's email. A test of one segment has fewer customers, so it cannot find an effect of this size.
- **Contact cost (branches 4 and 5).** Both results use the base contact cost of `r N$e4_cost` (as-02). The data does not give this cost. At `r N$cost_sig` or more, the top 25% by history beats "send to all".

::: {.business-note}
**Business note.** The men's email to all customers passes `r N$n_pass` of the 5 branches of the evaluation framework. It gives `r N$e4_prof` for each campaign of 100,000 customers (95% CI `r N$e4_ci`). At the base contact cost, no targeting rule and no ML model beats "send to all". The full contact cost decides the targeting rule, and the data does not give it. Step 7 changes this result into a policy for each contact cost, a dollar value and a rollout plan.
:::

# Step 7. Implementation {#step-7}

::: {.bridge}
Step 6 showed that the men's email to all customers passes `r N$n_pass` of the 5 branches of the evaluation framework. At the base contact cost, no targeting rule beats "send to all". But the contact cost is an assumption (as-02), and the data does not give it. A result on test data is not yet a policy.

This step answers four questions. Which rule selects the customers at each contact cost? How much money does the policy make? Does the choice hold for other margins and costs? How do we confirm the result after the launch?
:::

::: {.purpose}
**Purpose.** This step changes the evaluation into a targeting rule, a dollar value and a rollout plan. It supports this decision: launch the men's email to all customers with a holdout, and the contact cost at which the list becomes shorter.
:::

## 7a. From result to policy

A test gives the effect of the email. A policy says which customers get the email. The breakeven rule links the two. It sends the email to a customer only if the incremental margin is more than the contact cost. At a margin of `r N$e4_margin` and a contact cost of `r N$e4_cost`, the breakeven effect is `r N$e4_be` of spend for each customer.

::: {.tech-note}
**Technical note.** The breakeven rule sends the email to a customer if m × û(q) > c. Here m is the margin (as-01) and c is the contact cost (as-02). The value û(q) is the cross-fitted uplift of the history quartile q of the customer (Step 5). A rule with a fixed list, for example the top 25% by history, does not use c. Its profit falls more slowly with c, because it sends fewer emails.
:::

::: {#dec-07 .decision}
### Which rule selects the customers for the email? {.unnumbered}

**Why this question matters.** The contact cost decides if an email to a customer with a small uplift pays for itself. If the list is too long, the emails to customers with a small uplift lose money. If the list is too short, the policy loses the profit of customers who buy because of the email.

**Ways to do it.** A rule can select the customers with four kinds of information. Each kind adds information to the kind before it:

| Information that the rule uses | Rule | Advantage | Main risk |
|---|---|---|---|
| None | A. Send to all customers. (No email to any customer is the other rule with no information.) | Simple. No estimate to trust. It gets all of the positive mean effect. | It sends to customers where the email can lose money. "No email" loses the profit of branch 4, so we screen it out. |
| A fixed share by history | B. Top 25% by history | Simple. A quarter of the contact cost. It keeps the quartile with the largest uplift. | The list does not change with the contact cost. |
| The uplift of each quartile and the contact cost | C. Breakeven rule by history quartile | It sends only where the margin is more than the cost. The list changes with the cost. | It depends on four noisy estimates and on the contact cost. |
| The uplift of each customer from an ML model | T-learner or uplift tree | It can find customers that history does not show. | No ML model beats rank by history (branch 5, Step 4d). We screen it out. |

**Evidence.** The policy-rule table of [Step 6e](#step-6) gives the profit of rules A, B and C for 100,000 customers at six contact costs. It also gives the 90% interval of the gain of B and C against A. The chart below shows the profit of each rule for each contact cost from $0 to $0.35. It also gives the contact cost at which rule B starts to give more than rule A.

```{r}
#| label: dec-07-plot
#| code-summary: "Chart: profit for 100,000 customers against the contact cost, for the three rules"
#| fig-height: 4.6

# Purpose: Show the profit of each targeting rule against the contact cost (dec-07, as-02).
# Input:   `policy_profit`, `all_sel`, `top_q`, `u_q`, `m`, `MARGIN`, `COST`, `CAMPAIGN`, `N`, `CS`.
# Output:  Line chart, N$cost_cross (contact cost where the top 25% starts to beat "send to all").

cost_grid <- seq(0, 0.35, 0.01)
prof <- sapply(cost_grid, function(cst) c(all = policy_profit(all_sel, m$spend, m$t, cst),
                                          top = policy_profit(top_q, m$spend, m$t, cst),
                                          rule = policy_profit(MARGIN * u_q > cst, m$spend, m$t, cst)))
prof_k <- CAMPAIGN * prof / 1000  # $ thousand for one campaign

# Profit of a fixed list is a straight line in the cost: p(c) = p(0) - share x c. Thus the two lines cross at
# c = (p_all(0) - p_top(0)) / (1 - share of the top 25%).
cost_cross <- (policy_profit(all_sel, m$spend, m$t, 0) - policy_profit(top_q, m$spend, m$t, 0)) / (1 - mean(top_q))
N$cost_cross <- usd(cost_cross)

cs_setup(mar = c(3.6, 4.6, 0.6, 9.5))
plot(cost_grid, prof_k["all", ], type = "n", ylim = range(0, prof_k), xlim = c(0, 0.35),
     xlab = "Full contact cost of one email ($)", ylab = "Profit for 100,000 customers ($ thousand)")
abline(h = 0, col = CS$light_gray)
# The base contact cost (as-02) as a reference line
abline(v = COST, col = CS$gray, lty = 2)
text(COST, par("usr")[4], paste0(" Base cost ", usd(COST), " (as-02)"), adj = c(0, 1), cex = 0.75, col = CS$muted)
lines(cost_grid, prof_k["rule", ], col = CS$gray, lwd = 1.8)
lines(cost_grid, prof_k["top", ], col = CS$cyan, lwd = 2.2)
lines(cost_grid, prof_k["all", ], col = CS$navy, lwd = 2.5)
# The one point: the cost where the top 25% starts to give more than "send to all"
y_cross <- CAMPAIGN * policy_profit(top_q, m$spend, m$t, cost_cross) / 1000
points(cost_cross, y_cross, pch = 19, col = CS$blue, cex = 1.3)
text(cost_cross, y_cross, paste0("  Lines cross at ", N$cost_cross), adj = c(0, -0.8), cex = 0.8, col = CS$blue, font = 2)
# Direct labels at the line ends. Move labels apart if the ends are near each other.
n_end <- length(cost_grid)
ends <- prof_k[, n_end]
dy <- c(all = 0, top = 0, rule = 0)
if (abs(ends["top"] - ends["rule"]) < 0.06 * diff(range(prof_k))) dy[c("top", "rule")] <- if (ends["top"] >= ends["rule"]) c(0.7, -0.7) else c(-0.7, 0.7)
cs_label_end(0.35, ends["all"], "A. Send to all", col = CS$navy, bold = TRUE, dy = dy["all"])
cs_label_end(0.35, ends["top"], "B. Top 25% by history", col = CS$cyan, dy = dy["top"])
cs_label_end(0.35, ends["rule"], "C. Breakeven rule", col = CS$gray, dy = dy["rule"])
cs_title(paste0("Send to all earns the most until the contact cost passes ", N$cost_cross),
         "Profit for one campaign of 100,000 customers, men's email, margin 30% (as-01)")
```

**How to read:** each line is one rule. The x-axis is the full cost of one email, and the dashed line marks the base cost of `r N$e4_cost`. The blue point is the cost where the top 25% starts to give more than "send to all".

**So what:** at the base cost, "send to all" gives the most profit, `r N$a_base` for 100,000 customers. Above `r N$cost_cross`, the top 25% by history gives more, but the gain is reliable only from `r N$cost_sig`.

::: {.choice}
**Decision.** At the base contact cost of `r N$e4_cost`, rule A: send the men's email to all customers. If the full contact cost is `r N$cost_sig` or more, use rule B: send only to the top 25% by history.
:::

**Why.** At `r N$e4_cost`, rule A gives `r N$a_base` for 100,000 customers, and rule B gives `r N$b_base`. Each quartile is still profitable at this cost, so a shorter list loses money. Rule C gives `r N$c_base_gain` against rule A, because the noise of the quartile estimates excludes some profitable customers.

Between `r N$cost_cross` and `r N$cost_sig`, rule B gives more on the point estimate, but the 90% interval of its gain contains 0. From `r N$cost_sig`, the interval is above 0, so the policy rule of branch 5 lets rule B replace rule A. At $0.30, rule B gives `r N$b_gain_030` more than rule A, and rule C gives `r N$c_vs_b_030` than rule B.

**What would change the decision.** The contact cost decides the choice. If Marketing confirms a full cost of `r N$cost_sig` or more, use rule B. A cost of this size is possible if the unsubscribe rate is high, or if the offer has a discount. If the contact cost is more than `r N$cost_zero_all`, "send to all" loses money. If a new test has many more buyers, compare the ML models again (Step 4d).
:::

## 7b. Dollar impact

The dollar impact uses the decision of 7a at the base cost: the men's email to all customers. The formula is: incremental profit = 100,000 × (0.30 × change in mean spend − $0.10). The table compares this policy with the women's email to all and with no email.

```{r}
#| label: dollar
#| code-summary: "Dollar impact for one campaign of 100,000 customers"

# Purpose: Give the dollar impact of each version for one campaign (as-01, as-02, as-04).
# Input:   `ATE`, `ATE_LO`, `ATE_HI`, `MARGIN`, `COST`, `CAMPAIGN`.
# Output:  Contract C6: `d_m`, `d_w` (profit for each customer). Table `imp`, N$imp_*.

d_w <- MARGIN * ATE[["womens"]] - COST
d_m <- MARGIN * ATE[["mens"]] - COST
ci_prof <- function(a) ci_txt(CAMPAIGN * (MARGIN * ATE_LO[[a]] - COST), CAMPAIGN * (MARGIN * ATE_HI[[a]] - COST), function(x) usd(x, 0))
imp <- data.frame(
  Policy = c("No email", "Women's email to all", "Men's email to all (recommended)"),
  `Emails sent` = num(CAMPAIGN * c(0, 1, 1)),
  `Incremental spend` = usd(CAMPAIGN * c(0, ATE[["womens"]], ATE[["mens"]]), 0),
  `Incremental margin` = usd(CAMPAIGN * MARGIN * c(0, ATE[["womens"]], ATE[["mens"]]), 0),
  `Contact cost` = usd(CAMPAIGN * COST * c(0, 1, 1), 0),
  `Incremental profit` = usd(CAMPAIGN * c(0, d_w, d_m), 0),
  `95% CI of the profit` = c("", ci_prof("womens"), ci_prof("mens")),
  check.names = FALSE)
kable(imp, row.names = FALSE, align = "lrrrrrr")
N$imp_m <- usd(CAMPAIGN * d_m, 0)
N$imp_diff <- usd(CAMPAIGN * (d_m - d_w), 0)
N$imp_m_lo <- usd(CAMPAIGN * (MARGIN * ATE_LO[["mens"]] - COST), 0)
N$imp_m_hi <- usd(CAMPAIGN * (MARGIN * ATE_HI[["mens"]] - COST), 0)
N$imp_roi <- formatC(MARGIN * ATE[["mens"]] / COST, format = "f", digits = 1)
```

The men's email to all gives `r N$imp_m` for each campaign of 100,000 customers. The 95% CI of the effect gives a range of `r N$imp_m_lo` to `r N$imp_m_hi`. Each $1 of contact cost gives `r N$imp_roi` dollars of incremental margin. The men's email gives `r N$imp_diff` more than the women's email. At the base cost, the version is the lever. The targeting rule adds money only at a high contact cost.

## 7c. Sensitivity check

The margin (as-01) and the contact cost (as-02) are assumptions. The check changes both and gives the profit of the two simple rules. The "Indicated choice" column uses a simple rule: the top 25% must give 25% more profit than "send to all". This margin protects the choice against the noise of the estimate.

```{r}
#| label: sensitivity
#| code-summary: "Sensitivity: profit of each rule by margin and contact cost"

# Purpose: Show how the margin (as-01) and the contact cost (as-02) change the choice of dec-07.
# Input:   `policy_profit`, `all_sel`, `top_q`, `m`, `k100`.
# Output:  Contract C6: `grid` (profit and indicated choice for each combination). N$n_all, N$n_grid, N$n_top.

grid <- expand.grid(cost = c(0.05, 0.10, 0.20, 0.30), margin = c(0.20, 0.30, 0.40))
grid$all <- mapply(function(mg, cst) policy_profit(all_sel, m$spend, m$t, cst, mg), grid$margin, grid$cost)
grid$top <- mapply(function(mg, cst) policy_profit(top_q, m$spend, m$t, cst, mg), grid$margin, grid$cost)
# The top 25% must give 25% more than "send to all", as a protection against noise.
grid$choice <- ifelse(pmax(grid$all, grid$top) <= 0, "No email",
                      ifelse(grid$top - grid$all > 0.25 * abs(grid$all), "Top 25% by history", "Send to all"))
kable(data.frame(Margin = pct(grid$margin, 0), `Contact cost` = usd(grid$cost),
                 `Profit, send to all` = k100(grid$all), `Profit, top 25%` = k100(grid$top),
                 `Indicated choice` = grid$choice, check.names = FALSE),
      row.names = FALSE, align = "rrrrl")
N$n_all <- sum(grid$choice == "Send to all"); N$n_grid <- nrow(grid)
N$all_low_cost <- all(grid$choice[grid$cost <= COST] == "Send to all")
N$n_top <- sum(grid$choice == "Top 25% by history")
N$n_none <- sum(grid$choice == "No email")
N$low_cost_txt <- if (N$all_low_cost) "It is the choice in each combination with a contact cost of $0.10 or less." else
  "It is not the choice in each combination with a contact cost of $0.10 or less."
```

::: {.assumption}
**Assumption check.** The contact cost (as-02) has the largest effect on the choice. "Send to all" is the choice in `r N$n_all` of `r N$n_grid` combinations. `r N$low_cost_txt` The top 25% is the choice in `r N$n_top` combinations, all with a high cost or a low margin. "No email" is the choice in `r N$n_none` combinations. Confirm the full contact cost with Marketing before the launch.
:::

## 7d. Rollout

The test result covers two weeks (as-03). After the launch, the effect can become smaller, and customers can unsubscribe. A holdout is a random group of customers that gets no email after the launch. It shows the effect of the email over time, with the same causal logic as the test.

::: {#dec-08 .decision}
### Which share of customers do we keep as a holdout after the launch? {.unnumbered}

**Why this question matters.** Each customer in the holdout gets no email, so the holdout costs profit. A holdout that is too small cannot show if the email still pays for itself. Then a fall of the effect stays hidden, and the campaign can lose money for months.

**Ways to do it.** The size of the holdout is one number. Thus the options are points on one scale: none, small, medium and large.

| Option | Advantage | Disadvantage |
|---|---|---|
| A. No holdout | No lost profit. | We cannot see if the effect becomes smaller or if customers unsubscribe. We screen it out. |
| B. 5% holdout | Small lost profit. | Less power. |
| C. 10% holdout | Good power to show that the email still pays for itself. | More lost profit. |
| D. 20% holdout | Most power. | Twice the lost profit of option C. |

**Evidence.** The holdout must show that the email still pays for itself. Thus the test asks: is the effect more than the breakeven effect of `r N$e4_be`? The table gives the power of this test for one campaign of 100,000 customers, with a one-sided test at 5%. The lost profit is the profit that the holdout customers do not give.

::: {.tech-note}
**Technical note.** Let s be the standard deviation of spend in the test, n the customers of the campaign and h the share of the holdout. The standard error of the effect is se = s × √(1 / (n(1 − h)) + 1 / (nh)). The power to show an effect above the breakeven effect b, if the true effect is u, is Φ((u − b) / se − z₀.₉₅).
:::

```{r}
#| label: dec-08-evidence
#| code-summary: "Evidence: power and lost profit of each holdout size"

# Purpose: Compare the power and the lost profit of each holdout size (dec-08).
# Input:   `m`, `COST`, `MARGIN`, `CAMPAIGN`, `ALPHA`, `ATE`, `d_m`.
# Output:  Contract C6: `sd_spend`. N$pow_*, N$lost_*, N$hw_10, N$hold_pct.

sd_spend <- sqrt(mean(tapply(m$spend, m$t, var)))
be <- COST / MARGIN
hold <- c(0.05, 0.10, 0.20)
se_h <- sapply(hold, function(h) sd_spend * sqrt(1 / (CAMPAIGN * (1 - h)) + 1 / (CAMPAIGN * h)))
# One-sided test: is the effect more than the breakeven effect?
pow <- function(true_eff) pnorm((true_eff - be) / se_h - qnorm(1 - ALPHA))
kable(data.frame(Option = c("B. 5%", "C. 10%", "D. 20%"),
                 `Holdout customers` = num(CAMPAIGN * hold),
                 `Half-width of the 95% CI` = usd(qnorm(1 - ALPHA / 2) * se_h),
                 `Power if the effect stays at the test result` = pct(pow(ATE[["mens"]]), 0),
                 `Power if the effect falls by 20%` = pct(pow(0.8 * ATE[["mens"]]), 0),
                 `Lost profit for each campaign` = usd(CAMPAIGN * hold * d_m, 0), check.names = FALSE),
      row.names = FALSE, align = "lrrrrr")
N$pow_10 <- pct(pow(ATE[["mens"]])[2], 0); N$pow_5 <- pct(pow(ATE[["mens"]])[1], 0); N$pow_20 <- pct(pow(ATE[["mens"]])[3], 0)
N$pow_10_fall <- pct(pow(0.8 * ATE[["mens"]])[2], 0)
N$lost_10 <- usd(CAMPAIGN * 0.10 * d_m, 0); N$lost_20 <- usd(CAMPAIGN * 0.20 * d_m, 0)
N$hw_10 <- usd(qnorm(1 - ALPHA / 2) * se_h[2])
N$hold_pct <- pct(hold[2], 0)  # The choice of dec-08 (option C)
```

::: {.choice}
**Decision.** Option C, a `r N$hold_pct` holdout.
:::

**Why.** If the effect stays at the test result, a 10% holdout shows that the email pays for itself with `r N$pow_10` power. A 5% holdout gives only `r N$pow_5`. A 20% holdout gives `r N$pow_20`, but it doubles the lost profit to `r N$lost_20`. The lost profit of option C is `r N$lost_10` for each campaign. This is a small price to know if the email still makes money.

If the effect falls by 20%, the power of a 10% holdout is only `r N$pow_10_fall` in one campaign. Thus the kill criteria below use two campaigns, not one.

**What would change the decision.** If a campaign has more than 200,000 customers, use 5%, because the holdout keeps the same number of customers. If the campaigns repeat each month, combine the holdouts of two or three campaigns.
:::

### Metrics and kill criteria {.unnumbered}

The holdout gives the primary metric for each campaign. The table gives the metrics, the limits and the action for each limit.

| Metric | Type | Target or limit | Action |
|---|---|---|---|
| Incremental spend for each customer (email group minus holdout) | Primary | More than `r N$e4_be` (the breakeven effect at `r N$e4_cost`) | If it is less for two campaigns, stop "send to all". Send only to the top 25% by history. |
| Conversion rate | Secondary | More than the holdout | If the spend effect falls but conversion stays, examine the order size. |
| Unsubscribe rate | Guardrail | Less than 0.5 points more than the holdout. [Confirm with Marketing.]{.placeholder} | If it is more, update the contact cost (as-02). Then use the targeting rule of 7a again. |
| Complaints | Guardrail | No increase | Stop the campaign. |

::: {.business-note}
**Business note.** At the base contact cost, send the men's email to all customers. It gives `r N$imp_m` for each campaign of 100,000 customers (range `r N$imp_m_lo` to `r N$imp_m_hi`). If the full contact cost is `r N$cost_sig` or more, send only to the top 25% by history. Keep a 10% holdout. It costs `r N$lost_10` for each campaign.

If the effect stays below `r N$e4_be` for two campaigns, stop "send to all". Part 2 shows how other teams can use the same method.
:::

# Part 2: Use in other teams {#part-2}

::: {.bridge}
Steps 0 to 7 used one randomized test to answer one marketing question. The method has four parts: a random split, a primary metric with sufficient power, the effect in dollars, and a holdout after the launch. Case 01 left two questions that historical data cannot answer, because each loan got only one price and one collection treatment. Part 2 shows how the same method answers them.
:::

::: {.purpose}
**Purpose.** This part shows how the method of this notebook applies to two open questions of case 01. It supports these decisions: the design of a pricing test, and the design of a collections test.
:::

The two questions come from the revised case 01. The next chunk records its facts, so that the text and the power calculation use the same values.

```{r}
#| label: case01-facts
#| code-summary: "Facts from the revised case 01: rate increase for zero NPV, default rates, volumes, recoveries"

# Purpose: Record the facts of the revised case 01 that Part 2 uses (Part 2: Pricing, Part 2: Recoveries).
# Input:   None. The values come from case 01 (2015 loans of Lending Club, prices of 2015).
# Output:  `rate_up` (points of interest rate for zero NPV, by grade), `pricing` (grades A–C), `rec01`, N$p2_*.

# Increase of the interest rate (points) that makes the NPV of the 2015 loans equal to zero, by grade
rate_up <- c(A = 0.3, B = 0.1, C = 1.0, D = 2.7, E = 6.0, F = 12.9, G = 19.7)
# Grades A–C: the pricing test of case 01 (an increase of 1 point or less)
pricing <- data.frame(grade = c("A", "B", "C"), bad = c(0.054, 0.119, 0.195), loans_2015 = c(70107, 91672, 77363))
pricing$rate_up <- rate_up[pricing$grade]
# Recoveries (Part 2: Recoveries of case 01)
rec01 <- list(rate = 0.110, top20_balance = 0.455, top20_gbm = 0.462)

N$p2_up_ac <- paste(paste0(names(rate_up)[1:3], " +", formatC(rate_up[1:3], format = "f", digits = 1)), collapse = ", ")
N$p2_up_max_ac <- formatC(max(rate_up[1:3]), format = "f", digits = 1)
N$p2_up_dg <- paste0(formatC(min(rate_up[4:7]), format = "f", digits = 1), " to ", formatC(max(rate_up[4:7]), format = "f", digits = 1))
N$p2_rec <- pct(rec01$rate)
N$p2_top_bal <- pct(rec01$top20_balance)
N$p2_top_gbm <- pct(rec01$top20_gbm)
N$p2_two_pts_a <- pct(0.02 / pricing$bad[1], 0)
```

## Pricing test for grades A to C (case 01, Part 2: Pricing)

**The question.** Case 01 shows that the 2015 loans lost money in every grade at 2015 prices. The increase of the interest rate for an NPV of zero is small in grades A to C: `r N$p2_up_ac` points. In grades D to G, it is `r N$p2_up_dg` points. The market may not accept such an increase, so a cutoff is the better tool for D to G. Thus case 01 recommends a pricing test for grades A to C only.

**Why a test.** A price increase can change two things that the NPV calculation keeps fixed: the default rate and the volume. The historical data cannot measure this effect, because the price depends on the risk. A borrower with a higher price is also a riskier borrower. A random test gives each applicant the old price or the new price by chance, so the difference comes from the price.

**The primary metric.** The default rate decides if the higher price pays for itself, so it is the primary metric. The take-up rate of the offer is the second metric, because a higher price can reduce the volume.

**The detectable change.** The test must find a change of the default rate that matters for the NPV. The price changes by `r N$p2_up_max_ac` points or less, so the change of the default rate is probably small. A fixed change of 2 points is `r N$p2_two_pts_a` of the grade A rate. A test for 2 points can miss a real effect in grade A. Thus we use a relative change: 10% of the 2015 default rate of each grade. [Confirm the detectable change with Risk.]{.placeholder}

::: {.tech-note}
**Technical note.** The code uses `power.prop.test` with the default rate of the grade as p₁ and 1.1 × p₁ as p₂, at 5% significance (two-sided) and 80% power. The test has two groups of equal size: the old price and the new price. The months of volume are 2 × (loans in each group) / (loans in 2015 / 12). This value assumes that all new loans of the grade go into the test.
:::

```{r}
#| label: pricing-power
#| code-summary: "Power for a pricing test of grades A–C: loans in each group to find a 10% change of the default rate"

# Purpose: Size the pricing test of case 01 for grades A–C (method of Step 3c).
# Input:   `pricing`, `ALPHA`, `POWER`.
# Output:  Table `pricing` with the loans in each group and the months of volume, N$p2_*.

REL_CHANGE <- 0.10  # Detectable change: 10% of the default rate of the grade (relative)
loans_needed <- function(p, rel) ceiling(power.prop.test(p1 = p, p2 = p * (1 + rel), sig.level = ALPHA, power = POWER)$n)
pricing$delta <- pricing$bad * REL_CHANGE
pricing$n <- sapply(pricing$bad, loans_needed, rel = REL_CHANGE)
pricing$months <- 2 * pricing$n / (pricing$loans_2015 / 12)
# For comparison: a larger change of 20% needs about a quarter of the loans.
pricing$n20 <- sapply(pricing$bad, loans_needed, rel = 0.20)
pricing$months20 <- 2 * pricing$n20 / (pricing$loans_2015 / 12)

kable(data.frame(Grade = pricing$grade,
                 `Rate increase for zero NPV (points)` = formatC(pricing$rate_up, format = "f", digits = 1),
                 `Default rate 2015` = pct(pricing$bad),
                 `Detectable change (points)` = formatC(100 * pricing$delta, format = "f", digits = 2),
                 `Loans in each group` = num(pricing$n),
                 `Loans in 2015` = num(pricing$loans_2015),
                 `Months of volume for two groups` = formatC(pricing$months, format = "f", digits = 1),
                 `Months for a 20% change` = formatC(pricing$months20, format = "f", digits = 1), check.names = FALSE),
      row.names = FALSE, align = "lrrrrrrr")

mo <- setNames(pricing$months, pricing$grade)
N$p2_months_a <- formatC(mo[["A"]], format = "f", digits = 1)
N$p2_months_b <- formatC(mo[["B"]], format = "f", digits = 1)
N$p2_months_c <- formatC(mo[["C"]], format = "f", digits = 1)
N$p2_months_a20 <- formatC(pricing$months20[pricing$grade == "A"], format = "f", digits = 1)
N$p2_n_a <- num(pricing$n[pricing$grade == "A"])
N$p2_delta_a <- formatC(100 * pricing$delta[pricing$grade == "A"], format = "f", digits = 2)
```

Grades B and C have sufficient volume for a test in `r N$p2_months_b` and `r N$p2_months_c` months. Grade A has the lowest default rate, so a 10% change is only `r N$p2_delta_a` points. The test needs `r N$p2_n_a` loans in each group, or `r N$p2_months_a` months of volume. If Risk accepts a change of 20% for grade A, the test needs `r N$p2_months_a20` months.

Two limits apply to the design:

- **The lifetime default rate comes late.** We know it only after 36 months. Thus the test must use an early metric, for example the default rate at 12 months on book. This rate is lower than the lifetime rate, so the test needs more loans than the table shows.
- **One price change for each grade.** A test of one increase in each grade gives one point on the price curve. To find the best price, a later test can use two or three increases.

## Collections test (case 01, Part 2: Recoveries)

**The question.** Case 01 shows that the net recovery is about `r N$p2_rec` of the principal in each segment. The top 20% of charged-off loans by balance holds `r N$p2_top_bal` of the net recovery dollars, and a GBM holds `r N$p2_top_gbm`. Thus a model does not find better accounts than a rank by balance. The real lever is the choice between a sale of the debt and in-house collection. The data cannot measure this choice, because each loan got only one treatment.

**The test design.** The same method as this notebook applies. Each step of this notebook has a match in the collections test:

1. **Random split.** Put the charged-off loans at random into two groups: sale of the debt, and in-house collection. Use a sample-ratio check and the standardized differences of Step 6a.
2. **Primary metric.** The net dollars for each $1 of principal at the charge-off, after 12 months. For a sale, it is the sale price. For in-house collection, it is the net recovery minus the cost of the collection.
3. **Effect and power.** Use the Welch CI of Step 6b. The net recovery has a long right tail, like spend, so check the result with the bootstrap of Step 6c.
4. **Targeting.** Rank by balance is the baseline, as rank by history is the baseline in this notebook. If a model beats this baseline with the model rule of Step 6e, use the uplift method of Step 4d.
5. **Holdout.** After the decision, keep a random share of the loans with the other treatment, as in Step 7d.

Case 02 uses the same champion/challenger logic for the fraud policy: a random 10% of the transactions goes to the new policy.

::: {.business-note}
**Business note.** The method of this notebook answers the two open questions of case 01. A pricing test for grades A to C needs about `r N$p2_months_c` months of grade C volume and `r N$p2_months_a` months of grade A volume. A collections test compares a sale of the debt with in-house collection, on loans with a random treatment. The conclusion collects the results of all steps.
:::

# Conclusion {#conclusion}

::: {.bridge}
The notebook started with two questions from leadership: do we send the email to all customers, and which version do we send? Steps 0 to 7 answered them with one randomized test. Part 2 then showed how other teams can use the same method.
:::

## The answer

Send the men's email to all customers. It increases the mean spend by `r N$e2_ate` for each customer (95% CI `r N$e2_ci`). For each campaign of 100,000 customers, it gives `r N$imp_m` of incremental profit, with a range of `r N$imp_m_lo` to `r N$imp_m_hi`. It gives `r N$imp_diff` more than the women's email.

The policy passes `r N$n_pass` of the 5 branches of the evaluation framework. The branches that fail are: `r N$fail_list`. At the base contact cost of `r N$e4_cost`, no targeting rule and no ML uplift model beats "send to all". A shorter list pays only if the full contact cost is `r N$cost_sig` or more.

## Recommendation

1. **Send the men's email to all customers.** At the base contact cost, it gives the most profit of all rules ([Step 7a](#dec-07)).
2. **Confirm the full contact cost before the launch.** If Marketing confirms a cost of `r N$cost_sig` or more, send only to the top 25% by history ([Step 7a](#dec-07)). If the cost is more than `r N$cost_zero_all`, "send to all" loses money.
3. **Keep a 10% holdout.** It shows with `r N$pow_10` power that the email still pays for itself, and it costs `r N$lost_10` for each campaign ([Step 7d](#dec-08)).
4. **Stop "send to all" if the effect falls.** If the incremental spend stays below `r N$e4_be` for two campaigns, send only to the top 25% by history ([Step 7d](#step-7)).
5. **Use the same method for the open questions of case 01.** A pricing test for grades A to C, and a test of a debt sale against in-house collection ([Part 2](#part-2)).

## What a reviewer should challenge

These limits can change the result most. Each one has a control.

| Limitation | Effect on the result | Control, or what to do next |
|---|---|---|
| The contact cost of `r N$e4_cost` is an assumption (as-02). The data does not give unsubscribes. | The contact cost decides if a targeting rule beats "send to all". | The profit chart of Step 7a and the sensitivity check of Step 7c. Measure the unsubscribe rate as a guardrail and update the cost. |
| The margin of `r N$e4_margin` is an assumption (as-01). | The profit changes with the margin. At a low margin and a high cost, the top 25% is the better rule. | The sensitivity check of Step 7c uses 20% and 40%. Finance confirms the margin. |
| The effect window is two weeks (as-03). | The long-term effect is not known. It can be larger or smaller. | Keep the 10% holdout for three months (Step 7d). |
| Less than 1% of customers convert. | Each segment effect has a wide interval. The ML uplift models fit noise. | Rank by history. Repeat the comparison with each new test, with the model rule of Step 3a. |
| The gain of the top 25% at the base cost is near the limit of the policy rule. | A small change of the data or of the cost can change the targeting rule. | The decision uses the 90% interval, not the point estimate. Confirm the cost before a high-cost campaign. |
| I examined the segment effects before I selected the uplift method, on the same data. | The gain of a targeting rule can be too high. | The cross-fitted uplift reduces this risk. A new test confirms the rule before a high-cost campaign. |
| The data is from one retailer in 2008 (as-05). | The size of each effect is different for a card offer. | The method stays the same. Repeat the analysis on the bank data. |

Other limits have a small effect. The data source cut the spend at its largest value, so a few large orders can be larger in reality. The test has only one email version for each group, so it cannot show the best combination of versions.

## Next steps

1. Business case deck (6–8 slides): the men's email to all customers, the breakeven contact cost and the 10% holdout.
2. Confirm the contact cost (as-02) and the margin (as-01) with Marketing and Finance.
3. Design the pricing test for grades A to C with case 01 (Part 2: Pricing). Add it to the pricing one-pager.
4. Design the collections test (debt sale or in-house collection) with case 01 (Part 2: Recoveries). Add it to the collections one-pager.

# Appendix A: data dictionary {#data-dictionary .unnumbered}

The table gives each column of the Hillstrom file, then each feature that this notebook codes from them. The meaning of a raw column comes from the description of the MineThatData challenge (Hillstrom, 2008). The other parts of the table come from this notebook:

- **Role.** The time of the value against the email (Step 2b): a pre-test feature, the test group or an outcome. A coded feature has the role of its source.
- **Type.** The type of the value in R: a flag (0 or 1), a whole number, a number, a text or a category.
- **Values.** The code calculates this column from the data. A flag gives the share of 1. A number gives the range and the mean. A category gives each level with its number of customers.
- **Use.** The steps of this notebook that use the column.

The coded features `t` and `hq` exist only in the analysis set `m` (men's email and control group, Section 4c). Their values come from `m`.

::: {.data-dictionary-table}

```{r}
#| label: data-dictionary
#| code-summary: "Data dictionary: meaning, role, type, values and use of each column"

# Purpose: Build Appendix A: one row for each raw column and each coded feature, with values from the data.
# Input:   `d`, `m` (with `t` and `hq`), `COL_ROLE` (Step 2b).
# Output:  Table `dictionary`. N$n_dict_rows.

# Meaning of each column. Raw columns: the challenge description. Coded columns: the rule of the code.
MEANING <- c(
  recency = "Months since the last purchase of the customer, before the test.",
  history_segment = "History bucket: the dollars of the last 12 months in seven groups, with a number prefix.",
  history = "History: the dollars that the customer spent in the 12 months before the test.",
  mens = "1 if the customer bought men's products in the last 12 months.",
  womens = "1 if the customer bought women's products in the last 12 months.",
  zip_code = "Area type of the customer address. The data source writes \"Surburban\" for suburban.",
  newbie = "1 if the customer is a new customer in the last 12 months.",
  channel = "Channel of the purchases in the last 12 months. The load chunk changes the text into a factor.",
  segment = "Test group of the data source: no email, men's email or women's email.",
  visit = "1 if the customer visited the website in the two weeks after the email.",
  conversion = "1 if the customer bought something in the two weeks after the email.",
  spend = "Dollars that the customer spent in the two weeks after the email. The data source caps the value (Step 2c).",
  arm = "Test group as a factor, from segment: control, mens, womens.",
  buyer = "Product history, from mens and womens: men's only, women's only, or both.",
  hseg = "History bucket without the number prefix, from history_segment, in the order of the dollars.",
  zip = "Area type as a factor, from zip_code.",
  lhist = "Natural log of the history, from history.",
  t = "Treatment flag in m: 1 = men's email, 0 = control group.",
  hq = "History quartile in m: four groups with the same number of customers, from history."
)
USE <- c(
  recency = "Balance check (2d), regression adjustment (4a), uplift models (4d)",
  history_segment = "Source of hseg",
  history = "Balance check (2d), CUPED (4a), segment test (4c), order by history (4d, Step 5, Step 7)",
  mens = "Source of buyer. Balance check (2d), uplift models (4d)",
  womens = "Source of buyer. Balance check (2d), uplift models (4d)",
  zip_code = "Source of zip",
  newbie = "Balance check (2d), segment effects (4c), uplift models (4d)",
  channel = "Balance check (2d), segment effects (4c), uplift models (4d)",
  segment = "Source of arm",
  visit = "Secondary metric (3c), baseline (2e)",
  conversion = "Secondary metric (3c), baseline (2e), T-learner (4d)",
  spend = "Primary metric (3c). All effects and the profit (Steps 4-7)",
  arm = "The groups of each comparison",
  buyer = "Email version (4b), segment effects (4c), segment table (4d)",
  hseg = "Segment effects (4c), segment table (4d)",
  zip = "Balance check (2d), segment effects (4c), uplift models (4d)",
  lhist = "Regression adjustment (4a), T-learner (4d)",
  t = "Uplift models (4d), predictions (Step 5), policy profit (Step 7)",
  hq = "Uplift by history quartile (Step 5), targeting rule (Step 7)"
)
RAW <- names(COL_ROLE)
CODED <- c(arm = "segment", buyer = "mens, womens", hseg = "history_segment", zip = "zip_code",
           lhist = "history", t = "segment", hq = "history")

col_type <- function(x) {
  # Returns the type of a column in plain words.
  if (is.factor(x)) "Category"
  else if (is.character(x)) "Text"
  else if (all(x %in% c(0, 1))) "Flag (0 or 1)"
  else if (is.integer(x) || all(x == round(x))) "Whole number"
  else "Number"
}
col_values <- function(x) {
  # Returns the values of a column, calculated from the data.
  if (is.factor(x) || is.character(x)) {
    tb <- table(x)
    paste0(names(tb), ": ", num(as.vector(tb)), collapse = "; ")
  } else if (all(x %in% c(0, 1))) {
    paste0("Share of 1: ", pct(mean(x)))
  } else {
    dg <- if (all(x == round(x))) 0 else 2  # No decimals for whole numbers
    paste0("From ", num(min(x), dg), " to ", num(max(x), dg), "; mean ", num(mean(x), 2))
  }
}

rows <- c(RAW, names(CODED))
dictionary <- data.frame(
  Column = ifelse(rows %in% RAW, rows, paste0(rows, " (coded from ", CODED[rows], ")")),
  Meaning = MEANING[rows],
  Role = ifelse(rows %in% RAW, COL_ROLE[rows],
                ifelse(rows %in% c("arm", "t"), "Test group", "Pre-test feature")),
  Type = sapply(rows, function(r) col_type(if (r %in% c("t", "hq")) m[[r]] else d[[r]])),
  Values = sapply(rows, function(r) col_values(if (r %in% c("t", "hq")) m[[r]] else d[[r]])),
  Use = USE[rows], check.names = FALSE)
# Check: each row has a meaning and a use.
stopifnot(!anyNA(dictionary$Meaning), !anyNA(dictionary$Use))
N$n_dict_rows <- nrow(dictionary)
kable(dictionary, row.names = FALSE)
```

:::

# Reader guides: decisions, assumptions and glossary {#reader-guides .unnumbered}

This appendix holds the reference material of the notebook. Click a title to open it.

[]{#how-to-read-notebook}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## How to read this notebook

- Read the text to follow the logic. Click **Show code** to see the code for a step.
- The notebook follows the steps of a model project, from Step 0 to Step 7. Part 2 applies the same method to two questions of case 01.
- Each step starts with a gray block. This block says what the step before showed, and the question of this step.
- A blue block records a decision. It starts with a question. Then it gives the possible methods, the evidence, the decision and the reason.
- A gray-blue block (**Technical note**) gives the method in detail for a data scientist. A business reader can skip it.
- A green block is a business note. It gives the result of a step for a manager.
- [Appendix A](#data-dictionary) gives the meaning of each column in the data.
- The business case deck gives the recommendation for leadership: [decks/03-test-and-learn.pdf]{.placeholder}.

Each team can read only the part that it needs.

| Part | Question | Team |
|---|---|---|
| [Step 0](#step-0) | What is the business problem? | All |
| [Steps 1–3](#step-1) | Did the randomization work? Is the test large enough to find the effect that matters? | Marketing, all test owners |
| [Step 4](#step-4) | Does the email increase spend? Which version do we send? Does the effect change by segment? | Marketing |
| [Steps 5–6](#step-5) | Which customers have the largest uplift? Is the policy good enough for the launch? | Marketing, model risk |
| [Step 7](#step-7) | Which customers get the email? What is the dollar value? How do we confirm the result after the launch? | Marketing, Finance, CX and operations |
| [Part 2](#part-2) | How does the method apply to a pricing test and a collections test? | Product and pricing, collections |
:::

[]{#decision-log}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Decision log

The decision blocks in the text show only the question. This log gives each decision an ID for a model risk review. Click the question to go to the decision.

| ID | Question | Decision | Step |
|---|---|---|---|
| dec-01 | [Which metric decides the test?](#dec-01) | Spend. Visit and conversion are secondary metrics. | 3c |
| dec-02 | [Which method measures the change in mean spend?](#dec-02) | Welch t-test. The bootstrap is a check. | 4a |
| dec-03 | [Can the pre-test data make the interval smaller?](#dec-03) | No adjustment. History does not predict the spend in the test window. | 4a |
| dec-04 | [Which email version do we send?](#dec-04) | The men's email to all customers. | 4b |
| dec-05 | [How do we report the effect in each segment?](#dec-05) | Interaction test first. Then the effect of each segment with the Holm correction. The evidence for different effects is weak. | 4c |
| dec-06 | [Which method puts the customers in order of uplift?](#dec-06) | Rank by history. The rule before the evidence: an ML model replaces it only if its Qini area is 20% or more higher. | 4d |
| dec-07 | [Which rule selects the customers for the email?](#dec-07) | Send to all at the base contact cost. Send only to the top 25% by history if the contact cost is high. | 7a |
| dec-08 | [Which share of customers do we keep as a holdout after the launch?](#dec-08) | 10% | 7d |
:::

[]{#assumption-register}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Assumption register

| ID | Assumption | Value | Source | Effect if the value is wrong |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| as-01 | Contribution margin on incremental spend | 30% | Assumption: gross margin of an apparel retailer, minus the cost of delivery and returns. [Confirm with Finance.]{.placeholder} | Large. The profit of each email goes up or down with the margin. The sensitivity check of Step 7c uses 20% and 40%. |
| as-02 | Full cost of one email | $0.10 | Assumption: the cost to send, plus the cost of creative work, plus the future value that we lose when a customer unsubscribes. The data does not give unsubscribes. [Confirm with Marketing.]{.placeholder} | Large. This value decides if targeting is better than "send to all". Step 7a gives the contact cost at which the targeting rule changes. |
| as-03 | Effect window | Two weeks after the email | The test design of the dataset | The long-term effect is not known. It can be larger (more future purchases) or smaller (fatigue). |
| as-04 | Size of one campaign | 100,000 customers | Assumption, for the dollar values | No effect on the decision. The dollar values scale with the number of customers. |
| as-05 | Proxy | An email from a retailer to its customers is a proxy for a card offer to card customers | The public data has no bank test | The size of each effect is different for a bank. The method stays the same. |
:::

[]{#glossary}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Glossary

The words in this table are technical names. The notebook uses each name only with the meaning below.

| Technical name | Meaning in this notebook |
|---|---|
| A/B test | A test that puts customers into groups at random. Each group gets a different treatment. |
| Randomized test | A test where the data source, not the customer, selects the group of each customer at random. Thus a difference of means gives the causal effect. Same meaning as "A/B test". |
| Treatment | The action that the test examines. In this case, the men's email or the women's email. |
| Control group | The customers that get no email. |
| Holdout | The customers that get no email after the launch. They show the effect of the email over time. |
| Proxy | Data from a similar decision that takes the place of the real data. Here, the email of a retailer takes the place of a card offer (as-05). |
| Visit | The customer visited the website in the two weeks after the email. |
| Conversion | The customer bought something in the two weeks after the email. |
| Spend | The dollars that the customer spent in the two weeks after the email. |
| Spend cap | The largest spend value in the data. The data source cut the larger values to this value. |
| History | The dollars that the customer spent in the 12 months before the test. |
| Standardized difference | The difference of the means of a pre-test feature in two groups, divided by the standard deviation of the feature. It shows if the groups are the same before the test. |
| Sample-ratio check | A chi-square test of the group sizes against the planned split. A small p-value shows a problem in the assignment. |
| Average treatment effect (ATE) | The mean outcome of a treatment group minus the mean outcome of the control group. |
| Significance level | The probability of a false result "effect found" when the effect is zero. This notebook uses 5%. |
| Power | The probability that the test finds an effect of a given size. This notebook uses 80%. |
| MDE | Minimum detectable effect. The smallest effect that the test can find with the selected power and significance level. |
| Confidence interval (CI) | A range that contains the true effect in 95% of tests. |
| Welch t-test | A t-test that does not need equal variances in the two groups. |
| Bootstrap | A method that samples the data again many times, with replacement, to estimate the uncertainty of a result. |
| CUPED | Controlled experiment with pre-experiment data. A method that removes the part of the outcome that the pre-test data predicts. |
| Regression adjustment | A linear regression of the outcome on the treatment and the customer features. |
| Uplift | The change of an outcome that a treatment causes for a customer. |
| Segment effect | The ATE in one group of customers, for example the customers with more than $500 of history. |
| Interaction test | An F-test that compares a model with one effect for all customers against a model with one effect for each segment. |
| Holm correction | A correction of the p-values when we test many segments. It keeps the probability of one or more false results at 5%. |
| Cross-fit | A method that estimates the uplift of each customer with a model that did not see that customer. "Cross-fitted" has the same meaning. |
| Two-part model | A model of spend in two parts: the probability of a purchase, and the spend of a buyer. |
| Tobit model | A regression model for an outcome with many values at zero. |
| CUPAC | A version of CUPED that uses the prediction of an ML model as the pre-test covariate. |
| S-learner | An uplift model with one model for all customers. The treatment is one of its features. |
| X-learner | An uplift model in two stages. It uses the T-learner and then corrects the uplift in each group. |
| Causal forest | A random forest that estimates the uplift of each customer directly. |
| T-learner | An uplift model with two models: one for the treatment group and one for the control group. The uplift is the difference of the two predictions. |
| Transformed outcome | An outcome that has the same mean as the uplift. A normal regression model on it gives an uplift model. |
| ML uplift model | An uplift model that learns from many features: here the T-learner and the uplift tree. |
| Qini curve | The incremental spend from the top x% of customers, in the order of the predicted uplift. |
| Qini area | The mean distance between the Qini curve of a model and the line of a random order. Higher is better. |
| Rank by history | A targeting rule with no model: it sends the email first to the customers with the largest history. |
| Send to all | The policy that sends the email to each customer in the campaign. |
| Targeting rule | A rule that sends the email only to some customers, for example the top 25% by history. |
| Incremental margin | The contribution margin multiplied by the incremental spend. |
| Contact cost | The full cost of one email. See as-02. |
| Breakeven effect | The uplift on spend at which the incremental margin equals the contact cost: contact cost / margin. |
| Breakeven rule | A rule that sends the email to a customer if the incremental margin is more than the contact cost. |
| Decision layer | The step that changes the effect into a policy and a dollar value, with the margin and the contact cost. |
| ROI | Incremental margin divided by the total contact cost. |
| Evaluation framework | The five branches (validity, effect, robustness, business value, targeting) with the rules that the result must pass (Step 3a). |
| Model rule | The rule of branch 5 for the uplift method. An ML uplift model replaces rank by history only if its Qini area is 20% or more higher. |
| Policy rule | The rule of branch 5 for the list of customers. A targeting rule replaces "send to all" only if the 90% interval of its gain is above 0. |
| Guardrail metric | A metric that must not become worse, for example the unsubscribe rate. |
| Kill criteria | The results that stop a rollout. |
| Champion/challenger test | A test that sends a random share of the cases to a new policy and the rest to the current policy. |
| Business note | A short result of a step for a manager. |
| Technical note | Detail of a method for a data scientist. A business reader can skip it. |
:::

# Appendix B: reproducibility {.unnumbered}

The notebook uses only base R, `knitr` and `rpart`. `rpart` comes with each R installation. The setup chunk sets the seed, so each run gives the same bootstrap samples and the same folds.

```{r}
#| label: session-info
#| code-summary: "Package versions and the seed"

# Purpose: Print the versions of R and of the packages, and the seed, for reproducibility.
# Input:   `SEED` (setup chunk).
# Output:  Text.

cat("Seed:", SEED, "\n\n")
sessionInfo()
```

# Appendix C: functions used in the analysis {#functions .unnumbered}

Steps 3 to 7 use the functions in the file `case03_helpers.R`. They give the checks of the test design, the effect with its CI, the power and the bootstrap. They also give CUPED, the profit of a policy, the uplift models and the Qini curve. The charts use the functions in `chart_style.R`. A reviewer can read the full source of both files below, without a separate file.

```{r}
#| label: helpers-source
#| output: asis
#| code-summary: "Show the source of case03_helpers.R and chart_style.R"

# Purpose: Show the source of the two helper files in the notebook (Appendix C).
# Input:   Files case03_helpers.R and chart_style.R (next to this notebook).
# Output:  The source of each file as an R code block, or a note if the file does not exist.

fence <- strrep("`", 3)  # A literal fence here would end the chunk in the .qmd file
for (f in c("case03_helpers.R", "chart_style.R")) {
  cat("\n**File `", f, "`**\n\n", sep = "")
  if (file.exists(f)) {
    cat(fence, "r\n", paste(readLines(f, warn = FALSE), collapse = "\n"), "\n", fence, "\n", sep = "")
  } else {
    cat("*The file `", f, "` does not exist. The functions are in the chunks of the steps.*\n", sep = "")
  }
}
```
